explanations.c: A false transmitter is a substance like octopamine that is stored and released like a neurotransmitter but fails to produce the normal physiological response.
explanations.d: A postganglionic neuron blocker is a drug class that stops transmission, not the imposter substance itself.
explanations.e: A sympathomimetic mimics the effects of the sympathetic nervous system; octopamine as a false transmitter does the opposite (it reduces sympathetic effectiveness).

ankiCards: A substance stored in vesicles and released but lacking true transmitter effectiveness is a {{c1::false transmitter}}.
An example of a false transmitter mentioned in high-yield terms is {{c1::octopamine}}.
False transmitters replace {{c1::norepinephrine}} in the synaptic vesicles.
When a false transmitter is released, the physiological response is {{c1::decreased/lacking}}.
Octopamine is to norepinephrine as a {{c1::false}} transmitter is to a true transmitter.
keyPoints: False transmitters (e.g., octopamine) 'cheat' the vesicle storage system.
They are released during nerve stimulation.
They have very low activity at adrenergic receptors.
This leads to a reduction in sympathetic nervous system effectiveness.
This mechanism is relevant for some antihypertensive drugs (e.g., methyldopa).
microReview: False Transmitter: Stored? Yes. Released? Yes. Effective? No. Result: Reduced sympathetic tone.
examinerTraps: The examiner might use 'antagonist' as a distractor, but an antagonist binds a receptor. A false transmitter acts by replacing the ligand in the storage/release phase.
sourceQuote: False transmitter: Substance, for example, octopamine, stored in vesicles and released into synaptic cleft but lacking the effectiveness of the true transmitter, norepinephrine

stem: Which of the following drug classes acts primarily by blocking the transmission of signals at the level of the nicotinic receptors in the autonomic ganglia?

explanations.a: ACE inhibitors act by preventing the conversion of Angiotensin I to Angiotensin II, primarily in the lungs/vasculature.
explanations.b: Calcium channel blockers act on L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle and the heart.
explanations.c: Ganglion blockers (e.g., hexamethonium) block the nicotinic receptors at the synapse between pre- and post-ganglionic neurons in both the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems.
explanations.d: Beta-blockers act on adrenergic receptors on the heart and kidney.
explanations.e: Alpha-blockers act on adrenergic receptors on vascular smooth muscle.

ankiCards: Hexamethonium is an example of a {{c1::ganglion blocker}}.
Ganglion blockers work by inhibiting {{c1::nicotinic}} receptors in the autonomic ganglia.
The drug class acting on the 'Ganglia' according to the classification chart is {{c1::ganglion blockers}}.
Sympathoplegics can be divided into CNS, {{c1::ganglia}}, nerve terminal, and receptor blockers.
Ganglionic blockade affects both the {{c1::sympathetic}} and {{c1::parasympathetic}} systems.
keyPoints: Sympathoplegic drugs reduce sympathetic influence on the CV system.
They act at four sites: CNS, Ganglia, Terminals, or Receptors.
Ganglion blockers are rarely used now due to broad side effects.
They interfere with the nicotinic acetylcholine transmission in ganglia.
Hexamethonium is the classic prototype mentioned in text.
microReview: CNS (Clonidine) -> Ganglia (Hexamethonium) -> Nerve Terminal (Guanethidine/Reserpine) -> Receptor (Prazosin/Propranolol).
examinerTraps: The examiner may use 'prazosin' or 'propranolol' as distractors; remember these are receptor blockers (post-ganglionic), not ganglion blockers (at the level of the ganglia).
sourceQuote: Sympathoplegics—blockers of... Ganglia (hexamethonium)

stem: A 70-year-old man with a history of hypertension is started on an alpha-receptor antagonist. He is advised to be careful when getting out of bed in the morning to avoid fainting. What is the pharmacological term for the condition the physician is trying to prevent?

explanations.a: Reflex tachycardia is an increase in heart rate, which might occur, but 'fainting when getting out of bed' is specifically caused by the blood pressure drop.
explanations.b: Orthostatic hypotension (or postural hypotension) is a drop in blood pressure when assuming an upright posture, often exacerbated by drugs that interfere with the baroreceptor reflex or sympathetic tone.
explanations.c: Rebound hypertension occurs upon drug withdrawal, not as a side effect of taking the drug.
explanations.d: Malignant hypertension is an extreme emergency elevation in BP, the opposite of what is happening when the patient stands up.
explanations.e: Essential hypertension is the baseline disease, not the side effect.

ankiCards: Hypotension on assuming an upright posture is known as {{c1::orthostatic}} hypotension.
Another name for orthostatic hypotension is {{c1::postural}} hypotension.
Alpha-blockers are a common cause of {{c1::orthostatic}} hypotension.
Orthostatic hypotension results from a failure of the {{c1::baroreceptor}} reflex to compensate for gravity.
Dizziness upon standing is a classic symptom of {{c1::orthostatic hypotension}}.
keyPoints: Orthostatic hypotension is a common side effect of antihypertensives.
It is defined as a significant drop in BP upon standing.
Sympathoplegics and vasodilators are common culprits.
It reflects an impairment of the normal baroreceptor-mediated vasoconstriction.
Patients should be warned about 'first-dose' phenomena with certain alpha-blockers.
microReview: Stand up -> Gravity pulls blood down -> Normal: Baroreceptors fire, vessels constrict -> Drug-induced: Vessels don't constrict -> BP drops -> Orthostatic Hypotension.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'orthostatic hypotension' with 'reflex tachycardia'. Tachycardia is the *compensation* for the drop; the hypotension is the *problem* causing the syncope.
sourceQuote: Orthostatic hypotension: Hypotension on assuming upright posture; postural hypotension

stem: Which molecular component is responsible for the recycling of norepinephrine from the synaptic cleft back into the nerve terminal?

explanations.a: VMAT (Catecholamine vesicle pump) transports NE from the cytoplasm into the vesicle, not from the synapse to the terminal.
explanations.b: ACE converts Angiotensin I to II.
explanations.c: NET (Norepinephrine Transporter), also called the catecholamine reuptake pump, is responsible for the reuptake of NE from the synapse back into the terminal.
explanations.d: MAO is an enzyme that degrades catecholamines in the cytoplasm; it is not a transporter.
explanations.e: Nicotinic receptors are for acetylcholine in the ganglia, not for norepinephrine reuptake.

ankiCards: The catecholamine reuptake pump is also known as {{c1::NET}}.
NET stands for {{c1::norepinephrine transporter}}.
The function of NET is {{c1::recycling}} norepinephrine after release into the synapse.
Inhibition of NET would lead to {{c1::increased}} levels of norepinephrine in the synapse.
NET is located on the {{c1::nerve terminal}} membrane.
keyPoints: Termination of NE action is primarily via reuptake (NET).
NET is a high-affinity transporter.
Recycled NE can be repackaged into vesicles via VMAT.
NET is a target for several drugs (though the text focuses on reuptake as a term).
Differentiating NET (terminal) from VMAT (vesicle) is crucial.
microReview: Reuptake = NET (Recycling). Storage = VMAT (Vesicles).
examinerTraps: Watch for 'catecholamine vesicle pump' vs 'catecholamine reuptake pump'. They sound similar but are diametrically different in location (vesicle vs terminal membrane).
sourceQuote: Catecholamine reuptake pump: Nerve terminal transporter responsible for recycling norepinephrine after release into the synapse; also called norepinephrine transporter (NET)

stem: A patient with hypertension is treated with a centrally acting sympathoplegic. If the medication is stopped abruptly, the patient may experience a sudden rise in blood pressure, potentially exceeding baseline levels. What is the correct term for this phenomenon?

explanations.a: Postural hypotension is a drop in BP upon standing, not a rise after stopping a drug.
explanations.b: Reflex tachycardia is a change in heart rate, usually following a drop in BP.
explanations.c: Rebound hypertension is an elevated blood pressure (usually above pretreatment levels) resulting from the loss of an antihypertensive drug's effect, common with drugs like clonidine.
explanations.d: False transmission refers to the use of imposter neurotransmitters like octopamine.
explanations.e: Baroreceptor resetting is a physiological adaptation to chronic high BP, not a term for the acute withdrawal effect.

ankiCards: Elevated BP (above pretreatment) after stopping a drug is called {{c1::rebound}} hypertension.
Rebound hypertension often results from the loss of an {{c1::antihypertensive}} drug effect.
{{c1::Centrally}} acting sympathoplegics like clonidine are notorious for rebound effects.
Rebound hypertension is a risk when a patient is {{c1::non-compliant}} or stops medication suddenly.
To avoid rebound hypertension, drugs should be {{c1::tapered}} slowly.
keyPoints: Rebound hypertension is a 'withdrawal' phenomenon.
BP can spike dangerously high, leading to hypertensive emergency.
Most associated with CNS sympathoplegics (e.g., clonidine).
Reflects a sudden surge in sympathetic activity.
Prevention involves gradual tapering of the dose.
microReview: Stop drug -> Sympathetic surge -> BP higher than before treatment -> Rebound Hypertension.
examinerTraps: The examiner may call it 'hypertensive emergency' (which it might become), but the question asks for the *term for the phenomenon* related to drug withdrawal, which is 'rebound hypertension'.
sourceQuote: Rebound hypertension: Elevated blood pressure (usually above pretreatment levels) resulting from loss of antihypertensive drug effect

stem: Under the 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines, a patient presents with an average blood pressure reading of 135/84 mm Hg. Which of the following best describes this patient's hypertensive status?

explanations.a: Elevated blood pressure is defined as 120-129 systolic and less than 80 diastolic.
explanations.b: Stage 1 hypertension is defined as 130-139 systolic or 80-89 diastolic. 135/84 falls exactly in this range.
explanations.c: Stage 2 hypertension is defined as 140/90 mm Hg or higher.
explanations.d: Hypertensive emergency involves significantly higher pressures (usually >180/120) with acute end-organ damage.
explanations.e: Secondary hypertension refers to an underlying cause (e.g., renal artery stenosis), not a specific pressure range.

ankiCards: AHA/ACC 2017 guidelines define Stage 1 hypertension as systolic {{c1::130-139}} or diastolic {{c1::80-89}} mm Hg.
AHA/ACC 2017 guidelines define Stage 2 hypertension as systolic {{c1::≥140}} or diastolic {{c1::≥90}} mm Hg.
Elevated blood pressure is defined as systolic {{c1::120-129}} and diastolic {{c1::<80}} mm Hg.
The primary risk factors associated with hypertension include myocardial infarction, {{c1::heart failure}}, and {{c1::stroke}}.
In modern hypertension management, {{c1::systolic}} pressure is considered at least as important as diastolic pressure.
keyPoints: Hypertension is a major risk factor for MI, stroke, and heart failure.
2017 AHA/ACC guidelines lowered the threshold for diagnosis.
Stage 2: ≥140/90 mm Hg.
Elevated BP: 120-129 / <80 mm Hg.
microReview: Hypertension classification is now more aggressive. Patients above 130/80 are considered hypertensive (Stage 1), necessitating lifestyle changes and potentially pharmacological intervention depending on cardiovascular risk.
examinerTraps: Confusing the old JNC 7 guidelines (140/90 for Stage 1) with the current 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines (130/80 for Stage 1).
sourceQuote: According to the 2017 guidelines, average systolic pressure greater than 120 but less than 130 mm Hg is considered elevated, pressure equal to or greater than 130/80 mm Hg but less than 140/89 is considered stage 1 hypertension.

stem: A 55-year-old male is prescribed a drug that acts at the postganglionic nerve terminal to reduce the amount of norepinephrine stored in synaptic vesicles. Which protein is the most likely target of this medication?

explanations.a: NET (the catecholamine reuptake pump) is responsible for recycling norepinephrine from the synapse back into the cytoplasm.
explanations.b: VMAT (the catecholamine vesicle pump) transports norepinephrine from the cytoplasm into storage vesicles. Drugs like reserpine block this, leading to neurotransmitter depletion.
explanations.c: ACE converts Angiotensin I to Angiotensin II; it does not affect vesicular storage in nerve terminals.
explanations.d: Alpha-1 receptors are postsynaptic targets, not terminal storage transporters.
explanations.e: Calcium channels trigger release but do not govern the storage of catecholamines into vesicles.

ankiCards: The protein responsible for pumping catecholamines from neural cytoplasm into storage vesicles is {{c1::VMAT (Vesicle Monoamine Transporter)}}.
The {{c1::NET (Norepinephrine Transporter)}} is the catecholamine reuptake pump responsible for recycling norepinephrine after release.
Blocking {{c1::VMAT}} leads to a depletion of norepinephrine in the nerve terminals.
Drugs acting on {{c1::nerve terminals}} (e.g., reserpine) are classified as sympathoplegics.
{{c1::VMAT}} is also known as the catecholamine vesicle pump.
keyPoints: VMAT transports catecholamines into vesicles.
NET recycles catecholamines from the synapse.
Inhibition of VMAT depletes neurotransmitter stores.
This mechanism targets the sympathetic nerve terminal.
It is one level of sympathoplegic action.
microReview: Pharmacological control of blood pressure often targets the sympathetic nervous system at various levels: CNS outflow, ganglia, nerve terminals (VMAT/NET), or receptors (Alpha/Beta).
examinerTraps: Mixing up VMAT (vesicle storage) with NET (reuptake from synapse). Both involve catecholamine transport but in different locations.
sourceQuote: Catecholamine vesicle pump: Storage vesicle transporter that pumps catecholamine from neural cytoplasm into the storage vesicle; also called vesicle monoamine transporter (VMAT)

stem: A 62-year-old female with a long history of untreated hypertension presents to the emergency department with severe headache and confusion. Her blood pressure is 210/130 mm Hg. Physical examination reveals retinal hemorrhages. Which of the following terms best describes her clinical presentation?

explanations.a: Essential hypertension is hypertension of unknown etiology, not a description of an acute crisis.
explanations.b: Reflex tachycardia is a compensatory increase in heart rate due to a drop in BP, often caused by vasodilators.
explanations.c: Hypertensive emergency is severe hypertension with evidence of acute end-organ damage (e.g., encephalopathy, retinal hemorrhages).
explanations.d: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in BP upon standing.
explanations.e: Secondary hypertension refers to hypertension with a specific identifiable cause (e.g., renal artery stenosis).

ankiCards: A hypertensive emergency is severe hypertension associated with {{c1::acute end-organ damage}}.
Common signs of end-organ damage in hypertensive crises include {{c1::retinal hemorrhages}}, {{c1::encephalopathy}}, and {{c1::renal damage}}.
Hypertensive emergency is sometimes referred to historically as {{c1::malignant hypertension}}.
Clinical signs like angina or stroke in the setting of severe hypertension indicate a {{c1::hypertensive emergency}}.
Essential hypertension is also known as {{c1::primary}} hypertension.
keyPoints: Hypertensive emergency requires acute BP reduction.
Must have end-organ damage (brain, heart, kidney, eyes).
High BP alone (without damage) is often called hypertensive urgency.
Retinal hemorrhages are a hallmark sign of ocular end-organ damage.
Prompt treatment is necessary to prevent permanent injury.
microReview: Distinguishing emergency from urgency depends on the presence of acute damage (retinal bleed, stroke, heart failure, renal failure) rather than just the absolute BP value.
examinerTraps: Using 'Hypertensive Urgency' interchangeably with 'Emergency'. Urgency has high BP but NO acute end-organ damage.
sourceQuote: Hypertensive emergency: An accelerated form of severe hypertension associated with rising blood pressure and rapidly progressing damage to vessels and end organs.

stem: Which of the following physiologic mechanisms serves as the primary autonomic homeostatic control for maintaining blood pressure and is often the target of compensatory changes when antihypertensive drugs are administered?

explanations.a: RAAS is a hormonal system, not the primary rapid autonomic reflex.
explanations.b: The baroreceptor reflex involves sensory input from the carotid sinus and aorta to the vasomotor center to rapidly adjust BP.
explanations.c: Tubuloglomerular feedback is a renal local mechanism for GFR regulation.
explanations.d: ANP is a hormonal response to atrial stretch.
explanations.e: Chemoreceptors respond primarily to blood gases and pH, not primarily to BP homeostasis.

ankiCards: The primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis is the {{c1::baroreceptor reflex}}.
Sensory input for the baroreceptor reflex originates in the {{c1::carotid sinus}} and {{c1::aorta}}.
The baroreceptor reflex outputs signals via the {{c1::parasympathetic}} and {{c1::sympathetic}} motor nerves.
Lowering blood pressure often triggers a {{c1::reflex tachycardia}} via the baroreceptor reflex.
The central processing center for the baroreceptor reflex is the {{c1::vasomotor center}}.
keyPoints: Baroreceptor reflex is rapid-acting.
Sensors are in the carotid sinus and aortic arch.
Integrates in the medulla (vasomotor center).
Explains reflex tachycardia when vasodilators are used.
It is the reason for initial resistance to some mono-therapies.
microReview: The baroreceptor reflex is the body's 'thermostat' for BP. When a drug lowers BP, the reflex tries to pull it back up by increasing sympathetic tone (increasing heart rate and peripheral resistance).
examinerTraps: Assuming the baroreceptor reflex only handles high blood pressure. It handles both high and low BP fluctuations.
sourceQuote: Baroreceptor reflex: Primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis; involves sensory input from carotid sinus and aorta to the vasomotor center.

stem: A patient is treated with a drug that acts as a 'false transmitter.' This substance is stored in vesicles and released but is less effective than the endogenous neurotransmitter. Which of the following endogenous molecules does this 'false transmitter' primarily replace?

explanations.a: Acetylcholine is the transmitter for the parasympathetic system; false transmitters in HTN therapy usually target the sympathetic system.
explanations.b: Dopamine is a precursor but not the primary transmitter replaced by molecules like octopamine in peripheral nerves.
explanations.c: False transmitters like octopamine are stored and released in place of norepinephrine, leading to reduced sympathetic effect.
explanations.d: Serotonin is not the target of antihypertensive false transmitters.
explanations.e: Epinephrine is primarily a hormone from the adrenal medulla; norepinephrine is the neurotransmitter of the postganglionic sympathetic terminal.

ankiCards: A {{c1::false transmitter}} is a substance stored in vesicles and released into the synaptic cleft but lacking effectiveness.
An example of a false transmitter is {{c1::octopamine}}.
False transmitters replace {{c1::norepinephrine}} in the synaptic vesicles.
The use of false transmitters results in {{c1::decreased}} sympathetic stimulation of receptors.
False transmitters are associated with drugs that act on {{c1::nerve terminals}}.
keyPoints: False transmitters mimic the structure of NE.
They are packaged into vesicles by VMAT.
When the nerve fires, the 'weak' transmitter is released.
This results in less activation of alpha and beta receptors.
Octopamine is the classic biochemical example.
microReview: Sympathoplegics can act at four levels. The nerve terminal level involves depletion of NE (reserpine) or replacement of NE with a less potent molecule (false transmitters).
examinerTraps: Thinking a false transmitter blocks the receptor. It actually works 'upstream' by being released instead of the normal neurotransmitter.
sourceQuote: False transmitter: Substance, for example, octopamine, stored in vesicles and released into synaptic cleft but lacking the effectiveness of the true transmitter, norepinephrine.

stem: A 48-year-old male is started on a potent vasodilator for blood pressure control. One week later, he complains that his heart feels like it is 'racing.' Which of the following drug classes could be added to mitigate this specific compensatory effect?

explanations.a: Alpha-blockers can actually cause further reflex tachycardia by lowering BP without suppressing the heart.
explanations.b: Reflex tachycardia is mediated by sympathetic output to the heart; Beta-blockers (like propranolol) directly inhibit this cardiac response.
explanations.c: ACE inhibitors affect RAAS; they do not directly block the sympathetic tachycardia reflex.
explanations.d: Diuretics reduce volume but do not prevent the baroreceptor-mediated increase in heart rate.
explanations.e: While some CCBs (verapamil/diltiazem) slow the heart, beta-blockers are the classic choice to pair with vasodilators to block reflex tachycardia.

ankiCards: {{c1::Reflex tachycardia}} results from the lowering of blood pressure via the baroreceptor reflex.
Direct vasodilators frequently cause {{c1::reflex tachycardia}} as a compensatory mechanism.
{{c1::Beta-blockers}} are commonly used to prevent tachycardia associated with vasodilator therapy.
Tachycardia occurs because the vasomotor center increases {{c1::sympathetic}} output when BP drops.
The baroreceptor reflex involves sensory input from the {{c1::aorta}} and {{c1::carotid sinus}}.
keyPoints: Vasodilators trigger the baroreceptor reflex.
Reduced BP -> Reduced baroreceptor firing -> Increased sympathetic outflow.
Increased sympathetic outflow -> increased heart rate (tachycardia).
Beta-blockers antagonize this sympathetic effect on the heart.
This is a common example of multi-drug rationale in HTN.
microReview: When you bypass the brain's control of BP using a peripheral vasodilator, the brain 'fights back' using the sympathetic nervous system to increase heart rate. Beta-blockers 'mute' this fight-back response.
examinerTraps: Choosing an ACE inhibitor to stop tachycardia. RAAS handles volume and long-term resistance, while the Baroreceptor reflex handles the heart rate (tachycardia).
sourceQuote: Reflex tachycardia: Tachycardia resulting from lowering of blood pressure; mediated by the baroreceptor reflex.

stem: A patient with hypertension is found to have coarctation of the aorta. This specific case of hypertension would be classified as which of the following?

explanations.a: Essential hypertension (primary) is hypertension of unknown etiology.
explanations.b: Primary hypertension is another name for essential hypertension (no known cause).
explanations.c: Secondary hypertension is caused by a diagnosable abnormality, such as aortic coarctation or renal artery stenosis.
explanations.d: Malignant hypertension is an old term for hypertensive emergency/severe rapid damage.
explanations.e: Elevated blood pressure is a specific range (120-129 systolic), not a classification of etiology.

ankiCards: Hypertension of unknown etiology is called {{c1::essential}} or {{c1::primary}} hypertension.
Hypertension caused by a diagnosable abnormality like renal artery stenosis is called {{c1::secondary}} hypertension.
An example of an abnormality causing secondary hypertension is {{c1::aortic coarctation}}.
Most patients with hypertension have {{c1::essential (primary)}} hypertension.
{{c1::Essential}} hypertension is the term for hypertension with no identifiable cause.
keyPoints: Most HTN is 'Essential' (90-95% of cases).
Secondary HTN suggests a fixable underlying problem.
Common causes of secondary HTN: Renal disease, endocrine tumors, coarctation.
Identification is crucial as it might be curable.
Essential and Primary are synonyms.
microReview: In boards, if they give you a specific disease (like Conn syndrome or renal stenosis) causing the high BP, the answer is Secondary HTN. If they don't give a cause, it's Essential HTN.
examinerTraps: Confusing 'Essential' with 'Secondary'. Essential means the cause is *not* known (essential to the person), not that the drug is essential.
sourceQuote: Secondary hypertension: Hypertension caused by a diagnosable abnormality, eg, aortic coarctation, renal artery stenosis.

stem: Which of the following drug-mechanism pairs correctly identifies a medication acting on the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)?

explanations.a: Aliskiren is a direct renin inhibitor, not an ACE inhibitor.
explanations.b: Captopril is an ACE inhibitor, not an ARB.
explanations.c: Losartan is an Angiotensin Receptor Blocker (ARB), not a renin inhibitor.
explanations.d: Aliskiren is the primary clinical example of a direct renin inhibitor.
explanations.e: Captopril acts via the RAAS; it is not classified as a direct vasodilator (like hydralazine).

ankiCards: The drug {{c1::Aliskiren}} acts as a direct renin inhibitor.
{{c1::Captopril}} is an example of an Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor.
{{c1::Losartan}} is an example of an Angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB).
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and renin inhibitors all target the {{c1::RAAS}} system.
Drugs in the RAAS antagonist class are used to prevent cardiovascular conditions like {{c1::heart failure}}.
keyPoints: RAAS has three main pharmacological targets.
Renin (Aliskiren).
ACE (Captopril, etc.).
Angiotensin II Receptors (Losartan, etc.).
All three ultimately reduce Angiotensin II effect or production.
microReview: The RAAS pathway: Renin (inhibited by Aliskiren) converts Angiotensinogen to Angiotensin I. ACE (inhibited by Captopril) converts Angiotensin I to Angiotensin II. Angiotensin II acts on Receptors (blocked by Losartan).
examinerTraps: Swapping the names of ARBs and ACE inhibitors. ACE inhibitors usually end in '-pril', and ARBs usually end in '-sartan'.
sourceQuote: Angiotensin antagonists: Renin inhibitor (aliskiren), ACE inhibitors (captopril), Receptor blockers (losartan).

stem: A 70-year-old patient with hypertension is treated with a ganglion-blocking drug. He reports feeling very dizzy whenever he stands up from a seated position. Which term best describes this adverse effect?

explanations.a: Rebound hypertension is high BP following the sudden withdrawal of a drug.
explanations.b: Orthostatic (postural) hypotension is a significant drop in BP when assuming an upright posture, common with drugs that interfere with autonomic reflexes.
explanations.c: Hypertensive emergency is acute high BP with organ damage.
explanations.d: Essential hypertension is a diagnosis of etiology.
explanations.e: Reflex tachycardia is an increase in heart rate, which might accompany hypotension, but the dizziness itself is due to the BP drop.

ankiCards: {{c1::Orthostatic hypotension}} is defined as hypotension upon assuming an upright posture.
Orthostatic hypotension is also known as {{c1::postural}} hypotension.
Drugs that block {{c1::autonomic (ganglia/sympathetic)}} reflexes often cause orthostatic hypotension.
The dizziness a patient feels upon standing is typically due to {{c1::orthostatic hypotension}}.
Ganglion-blocking drugs like {{c1::hexamethonium}} are associated with severe orthostatic effects.
keyPoints: Orthostatic hypotension occurs with posture changes.
It results from failure of the baroreceptor reflex to compensate for gravity.
Sympathoplegics are the primary culprits.
Common in elderly patients or those on multiple agents.
Also known as postural hypotension.
microReview: Normally, standing up causes blood to pool in the legs. The baroreceptor reflex detects the drop in BP and immediately constricts vessels and increases HR. If drugs block this reflex (sympathoplegics), the BP stays low and the patient feels dizzy.
examinerTraps: Using 'Reflex tachycardia' as a description for 'dizziness'. Dizziness is the symptom of the hypotension; tachycardia is a response to it.
sourceQuote: Orthostatic hypotension: Hypotension on assuming upright posture; postural hypotension.

stem: Which of the following drug classes acts by interfering with sympathetic outflow from the central nervous system (CNS)?

explanations.a: ACE inhibitors work on the RAAS, primarily in the lungs/vasculature.
explanations.b: CCBs work directly on vascular smooth muscle and the heart.
explanations.c: Clonidine is a classic example of a drug that reduces sympathetic outflow from the CNS vasomotor center.
explanations.d: Postganglionic neuron blockers (like reserpine) work at the nerve terminal, not the CNS.
explanations.e: Ganglion blockers work at the nicotinic receptors in the autonomic ganglia, outside the CNS.

ankiCards: {{c1::Clonidine}} is an example of a drug that acts on CNS sympathetic outflow.
Drugs that act on the central nervous system to treat hypertension are called {{c1::centrally acting sympathoplegics}}.
Sympathoplegics can be divided into CNS-acting, {{c1::ganglion}}-blocking, and {{c1::nerve terminal}}-blocking drugs.
The site of action for clonidine is the {{c1::CNS}}.
{{c1::Sympathoplegics}} reduce blood pressure by reducing the effects or release of norepinephrine.
keyPoints: Sympathoplegics work at four different anatomical sites.
CNS: reduces 'brain drive' to the heart/vessels (e.g., Clonidine).
Ganglia: blocks nicotinic transmission (e.g., Hexamethonium).
Terminals: depletes NE or prevents release (e.g., Reserpine).
Receptors: Alpha or Beta blockade (e.g., Prazosin/Propranolol).
microReview: If the drug works in the 'brain' to lower BP, it's a centrally acting sympathoplegic. If it works on the 'wires', it's a ganglion or terminal blocker. If it works on the 'end-organs', it's a receptor blocker.
examinerTraps: Confusing 'postganglionic' (nerve terminal) with 'central' (brain). Clonidine is central; Reserpine is terminal.
sourceQuote: Sympathoplegics—blockers of: CNS sympathetic outflow (clonidine), Nerve terminals (guanethidine, reserpine), Ganglia (hexamethonium), Alpha or beta receptors (prazosin, propranolol).

stem: A 58-year-old male presents for a routine check-up. His blood pressure readings today average 148/94 mm Hg. He has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. Physical examination and basic metabolic panel are unremarkable. According to the current 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines, which of the following classifications best describes his cardiovascular status?

explanations.a: Elevated blood pressure is defined as a systolic pressure between 120-129 mm Hg with a diastolic less than 80 mm Hg.
explanations.b: Stage 1 hypertension is defined as a systolic pressure of 130-139 mm Hg or a diastolic of 80-89 mm Hg.
explanations.c: Stage 2 hypertension is defined as a systolic pressure equal to or greater than 140 mm Hg or a diastolic equal to or greater than 90 mm Hg. This patient's 148/94 mm Hg fits this category.
explanations.d: Hypertensive emergency involves severe hypertension (usually >180/120) with evidence of acute end-organ damage (e.g., encephalopathy, MI), which this patient does not have.
explanations.e: Secondary hypertension refers to hypertension with a specific diagnosable cause (e.g., renal artery stenosis), but the classification of the pressure level itself remains Stage 2.

ankiCards: According to 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines, Stage 2 hypertension is defined as BP ≥{{c1::140/90}} mm Hg.
Elevated blood pressure is defined as systolic {{c1::120-129}} mm Hg and diastolic <80 mm Hg.
Stage 1 hypertension is defined as systolic {{c1::130-139}} or diastolic {{c1::80-89}} mm Hg.
The 2017 guidelines state that {{c1::systolic}} pressure is now considered at least as important as diastolic pressure.
Most patients with Stage 1 or Stage 2 hypertension are {{c1::deserving of treatment}}.
keyPoints: Stage 2 hypertension starts at 140/90 mm Hg.
Stage 1 hypertension is 130-139/80-89 mm Hg.
Elevated BP is 120-129/<80 mm Hg.
Systolic pressure is a critical risk factor alongside diastolic.
Early prevention and treatment are urged by 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines.
microReview: Blood pressure categories: Normal (<120/80), Elevated (120-129/<80), Stage 1 (130-139 or 80-89), Stage 2 (≥140 or ≥90).
examinerTraps: Students often confuse the old JNC 7 limits (140/90 for Stage 1) with the 2017 AHA/ACC limits (140/90 for Stage 2).
sourceQuote: pressure equal to or greater than 130/80 mm Hg but less than 140/89 is con - sidered stage 1 hypertension , while pressures equal to or greater than 140/90 are considered stage 2 hypertension .

stem: A novel pharmacological agent is developed that selectively inhibits the primary autonomic mechanism responsible for blood pressure homeostasis. This mechanism involves sensory input from the carotid sinus and aorta communicating with the vasomotor center. Which of the following describes the most likely physiological consequence of inhibiting this mechanism during a sudden drop in blood pressure?

options.a: Increased parasympathetic output to the SA node
options.c: Activation of the catecholamine vesicle pump

explanations.a: Inhibition of the baroreceptor reflex would prevent the normal compensatory decrease in parasympathetic tone that occurs when BP drops.
explanations.b: The baroreceptor reflex is the primary mechanism for BP homeostasis. If inhibited, the heart cannot increase rate via sympathetic activation (reflex tachycardia) in response to falling BP.
explanations.c: The catecholamine vesicle pump (VMAT) is a cellular transporter, not the primary systemic reflex mechanism.
explanations.d: Enhanced reuptake (NET) would decrease synaptic norepinephrine, which is unrelated to the inhibition of the sensory-motor reflex arc itself.
explanations.e: While renal perfusion may drop, the specific question asks for the consequence of inhibiting the homeostatic reflex (baroreceptor reflex).

ankiCards: The {{c1::baroreceptor reflex}} is the primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis.
Sensory input for the baroreceptor reflex comes from the {{c1::carotid sinus}} and {{c1::aorta}}.
The vasomotor center output for BP control is via {{c1::parasympathetic}} and {{c1::sympathetic}} motor nerves.
{{c1::Reflex tachycardia}} results from the lowering of blood pressure mediated by the baroreceptor reflex.
Inhibition of the baroreceptor reflex prevents compensatory changes in {{c1::heart rate}} during BP fluctuations.
keyPoints: Baroreceptor reflex involves carotid/aortic sensors.
Output is both sympathetic and parasympathetic.
Reflex tachycardia is a compensatory response to hypotension.
This reflex is essential for homeostasis.
Vasomotor center processes the sensory input.
microReview: Baroreceptor Reflex: ↓BP → ↓Stretch → ↓Firing to Medulla → ↑Sympathetic/↓Parasympathetic → ↑HR/↑SVR.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the reflex itself with the cellular transporters (NET/VMAT). The reflex is the 'system' level response.
sourceQuote: Baroreceptor reflex Primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis; involves sensory input from carotid sinus and aorta to the vasomotor center

stem: A 45-year-old woman is prescribed a direct-acting vasodilator for severe hypertension. Shortly after taking the first dose, she experiences a rapid heart rate and palpitations. This reaction is a known physiological response to the abrupt lowering of blood pressure. Which of the following best names this specific phenomenon?

explanations.a: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in BP upon standing, not the heart rate increase following BP reduction.
explanations.b: Reflex tachycardia is specifically defined as tachycardia resulting from the lowering of blood pressure, mediated by the baroreceptor reflex.
explanations.c: Rebound hypertension occurs when a drug effect wears off or is stopped abruptly, causing BP to spike above pretreatment levels.
explanations.d: False neurotransmission involves substances like octopamine and does not primarily describe the heart rate response to vasodilators.
explanations.e: End-organ damage refers to vascular damage in the heart, kidney, or brain, not a physiological reflex.

ankiCards: {{c1::Reflex tachycardia}} is the term for increased heart rate in response to decreased blood pressure.
Reflex tachycardia is mediated by the {{c1::baroreceptor reflex}}.
Direct-acting vasodilators often cause {{c1::reflex tachycardia}} as a side effect.
{{c1::Orthostatic hypotension}} is hypotension that occurs when assuming an upright posture.
{{c1::Rebound hypertension}} is elevated BP resulting from the loss of an antihypertensive drug effect.
keyPoints: Vasodilators trigger reflex tachycardia.
The baroreceptor reflex detects the drop in BP.
Reflex tachycardia involves increased sympathetic discharge to the SA node.
Orthostatic hypotension relates to posture.
Rebound hypertension is a withdrawal-like phenomenon.
microReview: Reflex Tachycardia: Common with Hydralazine, Nitrates, and Nifedipine (DHP-CCBs) due to rapid BP drop triggering the baroreceptors.
examinerTraps: Wait for the patient to 'stand up' to choose orthostatic hypotension; if the question focuses on the 'rapid heart rate' following a 'BP drop', it's reflex tachycardia.
sourceQuote: Reflex tachycardia Tachycardia resulting from lowering of blood pressure; mediated by the baroreceptor reflex

stem: A research study investigates a drug that inhibits the storage of norepinephrine in neural vesicles by blocking the transporter responsible for moving catecholamines from the neural cytoplasm into the storage vesicle. Which of the following is the correct name for this transporter?

explanations.a: NET is the reuptake pump on the plasma membrane, not the vesicle membrane.
explanations.b: VMAT (Catecholamine vesicle pump) is responsible for transporting catecholamines from the cytoplasm into storage vesicles.
explanations.c: The reuptake pump is synonymous with NET, which functions at the synapse/plasma membrane.
explanations.d: Ganglionic receptors are involved in signal transmission between pre- and post-ganglionic neurons, not vesicle storage.
explanations.e: ACE is an enzyme in the RAAS pathway that converts Angiotensin I to II.

ankiCards: The {{c1::vesicle monoamine transporter (VMAT)}} pumps catecholamines into storage vesicles.
Another name for the catecholamine vesicle pump is {{c1::VMAT}}.
VMAT moves catecholamines from the {{c1::neural cytoplasm}} into the {{c1::storage vesicle}}.
The {{c1::norepinephrine transporter (NET)}} is responsible for recycling NE from the synapse.
The {{c1::catecholamine reuptake pump}} is also called the norepinephrine transporter (NET).
keyPoints: VMAT = Vesicle Monoamine Transporter.
NET = Norepinephrine Transporter.
VMAT is the target of drugs like Reserpine.
VMAT is located on the vesicle membrane.
NET is located on the presynaptic plasma membrane.
microReview: Nerve terminal transport: VMAT (Cytoplasm → Vesicle); NET (Synapse → Cytoplasm).
examinerTraps: Students often swap NET and VMAT. Remember: V is for Vesicle (VMAT), N is for Norepinephrine/Net uptake (NET).
sourceQuote: Catecholamine vesicle pump Storage vesicle transporter that pumps catecholamine from neural cytoplasm into the storage vesicle; also called vesicle monoamine transporter (VMAT)

stem: Which of the following describes a substance that is stored in synaptic vesicles and released into the synaptic cleft, but lacks the effectiveness of the true neurotransmitter norepinephrine?

explanations.a: End-organ mediators are usually the active substances (like NE or ACh) or local factors.
explanations.b: Secondary messengers (e.g., cAMP) act inside the cell after a receptor is activated.
explanations.c: A false transmitter (e.g., octopamine) is stored and released like a transmitter but has little or no effect on the postsynaptic receptors.
explanations.d: Postganglionic blockers are drugs that stop transmission, not the substances released themselves.
explanations.e: Baroreceptor agonists are not a standard pharmacological class described in this context; baroreceptors are sensory structures.

ankiCards: A {{c1::false transmitter}} is a substance stored in vesicles that lacks the effectiveness of norepinephrine.
An example of a false transmitter is {{c1::octopamine}}.
False transmitters are released into the {{c1::synaptic cleft}} during nerve stimulation.
False transmitters compete with {{c1::norepinephrine}} for storage in vesicles.
Substitution of NE with a false transmitter {{c1::decreases}} sympathetic effectiveness.
keyPoints: False transmitters displace NE.
Octopamine is the classic example.
They are stored in vesicles and released by exocytosis.
They lead to reduced sympathetic tone.
Their presence results in 'ineffective' transmission.
microReview: False Transmitter (e.g., Octopamine): Stored/Released like NE, but fails to activate receptors properly → Functional Sympatholysis.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'false transmitter' with 'reuptake inhibitor'. One replaces the signal; the other increases the duration of the signal.
sourceQuote: False transmitter Substance, for example, octopamine, stored in vesicles and released into synaptic cleft but lacking the effectiveness of the true transmitter, norepinephrine

stem: A 62-year-old patient with a history of poorly controlled hypertension presents to the emergency department with a blood pressure of 210/130 mm Hg. The patient is confused, and funduscopic examination reveals retinal hemorrhages. Which of the following terms best describes this clinical presentation?

explanations.a: Essential hypertension is simply hypertension of unknown etiology; it does not describe the acuity or severity of this presentation.
explanations.b: While the BP meets Stage 2 criteria, the presence of acute end-organ damage (confusion, retinal hemorrhages) makes 'Hypertensive emergency' the more specific and clinically relevant term.
explanations.c: Hypertensive emergency (or 'malignant hypertension') is severe hypertension associated with rapidly progressing damage to end organs (e.g., encephalopathy, retinal hemorrhages).
explanations.d: Secondary hypertension refers to an underlying cause (like renal artery stenosis), which is not specified here.
explanations.e: Rebound hypertension follows the withdrawal of certain drugs and may not necessarily present with end-organ damage.

ankiCards: A {{c1::hypertensive emergency}} is severe hypertension with rapidly progressing end-organ damage.
Signs of hypertensive emergency include {{c1::encephalopathy}}, {{c1::retinal hemorrhages}}, or {{c1::angina}}.
Hypertensive emergency is also known as {{c1::malignant}} hypertension.
End-organ damage in the {{c1::kidney}}, {{c1::retina}}, or {{c1::brain}} signals a hypertensive emergency.
Rising blood pressure with signs of a {{c1::stroke}} or {{c1::myocardial infarction}} indicates an emergency.
keyPoints: Hypertensive Emergency = High BP + End-organ damage.
End-organs include heart, brain, kidney, and eyes.
Malignant hypertension is an older term for this state.
Retinal hemorrhages are a classic sign.
Requires immediate parenteral treatment.
microReview: Hypertensive Urgency: BP >180/120 without end-organ damage. Hypertensive Emergency: BP >180/120 WITH end-organ damage (stroke, MI, renal failure, etc.).
examinerTraps: The examiner may give a very high BP without symptoms. If no end-organ damage is mentioned, it is an urgency, not an emergency.
sourceQuote: Hypertensive emergency (“malignant hypertension”) An accelerated form of severe hypertension associated with rising blood pressure and rapidly progressing damage to vessels and end organs.

stem: A patient is evaluated for hypertension that is found to be caused by a specific, diagnosable abnormality: aortic coarctation. Which of the following is the correct classification for this type of hypertension?

explanations.a: Primary hypertension is hypertension of unknown etiology.
explanations.b: Essential hypertension is another name for primary hypertension (unknown etiology).
explanations.c: Secondary hypertension is hypertension caused by a diagnosable abnormality, such as aortic coarctation or renal artery stenosis.
explanations.d: Malignant hypertension refers to the severity and presence of end-organ damage, not the etiology.
explanations.e: Elevated blood pressure is a category for BP 120-129/<80 mm Hg.

ankiCards: {{c1::Secondary}} hypertension is caused by a diagnosable abnormality.
Examples of secondary hypertension include {{c1::aortic coarctation}} and {{c1::renal artery stenosis}}.
{{c1::Essential}} hypertension is also called primary hypertension.
Primary hypertension has an {{c1::unknown}} etiology.
{{c1::Secondary}} hypertension accounts for a small percentage of hypertensive patients compared to primary.
keyPoints: Essential = Primary = Unknown cause.
Secondary = Identifiable cause.
Common causes of secondary HTN: Renal disease, Coarctation, Endocrine disorders.
Treatment of the cause often cures secondary HTN.
Secondary HTN should be suspected in very young or very old patients with new onset HTN.
microReview: HTN Etiology: 90-95% is Essential (Primary). 5-10% is Secondary.
examinerTraps: Essential and Primary are synonyms. If both are options, they are likely distractors for Secondary.
sourceQuote: Secondary hypertension Hypertension caused by a diagnosable abnormality, eg, aortic coarctation, renal artery stenosis

stem: Which of the following pharmacologic mechanisms is primarily responsible for the recycling of norepinephrine back into the nerve terminal after its release into the synaptic cleft?

explanations.a: VMAT pumps catecholamines into vesicles from the cytoplasm, not from the synapse.
explanations.b: The catecholamine vesicle pump is synonymous with VMAT.
explanations.c: The norepinephrine transporter (NET), also called the catecholamine reuptake pump, is responsible for recycling NE from the synapse back into the terminal.
explanations.d: ARBs block receptors, they do not participate in neurotransmitter recycling.
explanations.e: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are diuretics acting in the proximal tubule.

ankiCards: The {{c1::norepinephrine transporter (NET)}} is responsible for recycling NE after its release into the synapse.
Another name for NET is the {{c1::catecholamine reuptake pump}}.
NET is located on the {{c1::nerve terminal}} membrane.
Inhibition of NET leads to {{c1::increased}} concentrations of NE in the synapse.
The {{c1::catecholamine vesicle pump}} (VMAT) is different from the reuptake pump (NET).
keyPoints: NET = Reuptake from synapse.
VMAT = Uptake into vesicles.
NET is the main way the sympathetic signal is terminated.
NET is also known as Uptake 1.
Cocaine and TCAs inhibit NET.
microReview: Synaptic NE termination: 1. Reuptake (NET - most important), 2. Diffusion, 3. Enzymatic degradation (COMT/MAO).
examinerTraps: The prompt asks for 'recycling... back into the terminal'. This is NET. If it asks for 'storage into vesicles', it is VMAT.
sourceQuote: Catecholamine reuptake pump Nerve terminal transporter responsible for recycling norepinephrine after release into the synapse; also called norepinephrine transporter (NET)

stem: A patient is taking a sympathoplegic drug that specifically blocks transmission by an action in the terminals of the postganglionic nerves. Which of the following drugs represents this specific class of antihypertensives?

explanations.a: Hexamethonium is a ganglion blocker, not a postganglionic nerve terminal blocker.
explanations.b: Clonidine is a centrally acting alpha-2 agonist that reduces sympathetic outflow from the CNS.
explanations.c: Guanethidine (and reserpine) are nerve terminal blockers that act in the postganglionic neuron terminals.
explanations.d: Prazosin is an alpha-1 receptor blocker that acts on the effector organ, not the nerve terminal.
explanations.e: Captopril is an ACE inhibitor, affecting the RAAS system.

ankiCards: {{c1::Postganglionic neuron blockers}} act in the terminals of the postganglionic nerves.
Examples of postganglionic nerve terminal blockers include {{c1::guanethidine}} and reserpine.
{{c1::Hexamethonium}} is a drug that blocks autonomic ganglia.
{{c1::Clonidine}} is a sympathoplegic that acts on CNS sympathetic outflow.
{{c1::Prazosin}} is a sympathoplegic that blocks alpha receptors.
keyPoints: Sympathoplegics are categorized by site of action.
Nerve terminal blockers: Guanethidine, Reserpine.
CNS-active: Clonidine, Methyldopa.
Ganglion blockers: Hexamethonium (rarely used).
Receptor blockers: Prazosin, Propranolol.
microReview: Sympathoplegic sites: 1. CNS (Clonidine), 2. Ganglia (Hexamethonium), 3. Terminals (Guanethidine), 4. Receptors (Alpha/Beta blockers).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'Nerve terminal blockers' (Guanethidine) with 'Ganglion blockers' (Hexamethonium). Both reduce NE release but at different locations in the circuit.
sourceQuote: Postganglionic neuron blocker Drug that blocks transmission by an action in the terminals of the postganglionic nerves

stem: A 50-year-old male with long-standing hypertension has been taking a medication that he suddenly stops because he ran out of refills. Within 24 hours, he experiences a headache, sweating, and his blood pressure is measured at 170/110 mm Hg, which is significantly higher than his original untreated baseline of 150/95 mm Hg. Which of the following terms describes this event?

explanations.a: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in BP with posture changes.
explanations.b: Secondary hypertension is HTN due to a specific underlying disease, not drug withdrawal.
explanations.c: Rebound hypertension is elevated BP (usually above pretreatment levels) resulting from the loss of an antihypertensive drug effect, often seen with clonidine.
explanations.d: Reflex tachycardia is an increase in heart rate following a drop in BP, not a rise in BP.
explanations.e: Essential hypertension is the term for primary hypertension and doesn't describe this acute withdrawal phenomenon.

ankiCards: {{c1::Rebound hypertension}} is elevated BP resulting from the loss of an antihypertensive drug effect.
Rebound hypertension often results in pressures {{c1::above}} pretreatment levels.
Sudden withdrawal of {{c1::clonidine}} is a classic cause of rebound hypertension.
Symptoms of rebound hypertension can include {{c1::headache}} and sweating.
{{c1::Postural}} hypotension is another name for orthostatic hypotension.
keyPoints: Rebound HTN = Sudden spike after stopping meds.
Often exceeds the original baseline BP.
Common with centrally acting alpha-2 agonists.
Can be life-threatening.
Requires gradual tapering of medications.
microReview: Withdrawal syndromes: Clonidine → Rebound HTN (massive sympathetic surge); Beta-blockers → Tachycardia/Ischemia.
examinerTraps: If the BP just goes back to the old baseline, it's just 'loss of effect'. If it goes *higher* than the old baseline, it's 'rebound'.
sourceQuote: Rebound hypertension Elevated blood pressure (usually above pretreatment levels) resulting from loss of antihyperten - sive drug effect

stem: A 52-year-old male presents for a routine check-up. He has no significant medical history and currently takes no medications. Physical examination reveals a blood pressure of 136/84 mm Hg. This reading is confirmed by an average of three separate measurements over the course of two weeks. Which of the following classifications best describes this patient's current cardiovascular status?

explanations.a: Elevated blood pressure is defined as a systolic pressure between 120-129 mm Hg and a diastolic pressure less than 80 mm Hg.
explanations.b: Stage 1 hypertension is defined as a systolic pressure between 130-139 mm Hg or a diastolic pressure between 80-89 mm Hg.
explanations.c: Stage 2 hypertension is defined as a systolic pressure of at least 140 mm Hg or a diastolic pressure of at least 90 mm Hg.
explanations.d: Hypertensive emergency involves severely elevated blood pressure with evidence of acute end-organ damage, which is not present here.
explanations.e: Normal blood pressure is defined as less than 120/80 mm Hg; this patient exceeds those limits.

ankiCards: Stage 1 hypertension is defined by a systolic range of {{c1::130-139}} mm Hg.
A diastolic pressure of {{c1::80-89}} mm Hg falls under Stage 1 hypertension.
Elevated blood pressure involves a systolic of {{c1::120-129}} and diastolic <80.
Stage 2 hypertension begins at a systolic pressure of {{c1::140}} mm Hg.
The 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines classify a BP of 135/85 as {{c1::Stage 1 hypertension}}.
keyPoints: Hypertension is a major risk factor for MI, stroke, and heart failure.
The 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines lowered the threshold for diagnosing hypertension.
Stage 1 is 130-139 systolic or 80-89 diastolic.
Stage 2 is ≥140 systolic or ≥90 diastolic.
Elevated blood pressure is 120-129 systolic and <80 diastolic.
Treatment is generally recommended for both Stage 1 and Stage 2 patients.
microReview: Hypertension classification is essential for determining the intensity of therapy. Stage 1 (130-139/80-89) marks the beginning of clinical hypertension, whereas Stage 2 (≥140/90) typically requires more aggressive multi-drug intervention.
examinerTraps: A common trap is using the older JNC 7 guidelines where 140/90 was the cutoff for Stage 1; current guidelines use 130/80.
sourceQuote: According to the 2017 guidelines, average systolic pressure greater than 120 but less than 130 mm Hg is considered elevated, pressure equal to or greater than 130/80 mm Hg but less than 140/89 is considered stage 1 hypertension.

stem: A researcher is studying the transport of neurotransmitters in sympathetic nerve terminals. They identify a specific protein responsible for the reuptake of norepinephrine from the synaptic cleft back into the cytoplasm. Which of the following best identifies this transporter?

explanations.a: VMAT is responsible for transporting catecholamines from the cytoplasm into storage vesicles, not for reuptake from the synapse.
explanations.b: Choline acetyltransferase is involved in the synthesis of acetylcholine, not norepinephrine transport.
explanations.c: The catecholamine reuptake pump, or norepinephrine transporter (NET), is the primary mechanism for recycling norepinephrine from the synapse.
explanations.d: MAO is an enzyme that degrades monoamines within the mitochondria or cytoplasm, not a transporter.
explanations.e: COMT is an enzyme involved in the degradation of catecholamines in the synaptic space, not their reuptake.

ankiCards: The catecholamine reuptake pump is also known as {{c1::NET (Norepinephrine Transporter)}}.
The transporter responsible for recycling NE from the synapse is {{c1::NET}}.
NET is located on the {{c1::presynaptic nerve terminal}} membrane.
Function of NET is to terminate the signal by {{c1::reuptake}} of norepinephrine.
Inhibition of {{c1::NET}} increases the concentration of NE in the synaptic cleft.
keyPoints: NET (Norepinephrine Transporter) is the primary reuptake pump for NE.
This mechanism helps maintain blood pressure homeostasis by regulating synaptic NE levels.
VMAT (Vesicle Monoamine Transporter) differs from NET as it acts on internal storage.
Sympathoplegic drugs can target these transport mechanisms.
Recycling neurotransmitters is more efficient than de novo synthesis.
microReview: The recycling of norepinephrine involves two distinct steps: reuptake from the synapse into the cytoplasm (NET) and storage from the cytoplasm into vesicles (VMAT).
examinerTraps: Students often confuse NET (synaptic reuptake) with VMAT (vesicular storage). NET acts on the plasma membrane; VMAT acts on the vesicle membrane.
sourceQuote: Catecholamine reuptake pump: Nerve terminal transporter responsible for recycling norepinephrine after release into the synapse; also called norepinephrine transporter (NET).

stem: A pharmacological agent is administered that is taken up into sympathetic nerve terminals and stored in vesicles, where it displaces norepinephrine. However, when this agent is released, it is significantly less effective at activating adrenergic receptors than the original transmitter. Which of the following terms best describes this substance?

explanations.a: Ganglionic blockers act on nicotinic receptors in autonomic ganglia, not within the nerve terminal vesicles.
explanations.b: Partial agonists activate receptors with lower efficacy but are not necessarily stored/released in place of a natural transmitter.
explanations.c: A false transmitter is a substance (like octopamine) stored and released like a neurotransmitter but possessing much lower efficacy at the receptor.
explanations.d: Irreversible antagonists bind permanently to receptors; they do not replace neurotransmitters in vesicles.
explanations.e: Postganglionic neuron blockers prevent transmission at the terminal but don't necessarily act as a replacement signaling molecule.

ankiCards: A {{c1::false transmitter}} is a substance stored in vesicles that lacks the effectiveness of norepinephrine.
{{c1::Octopamine}} is a classic example of a false transmitter.
False transmitters are released into the {{c1::synaptic cleft}} during nerve stimulation.
The storage of false transmitters occurs in the {{c1::synaptic vesicles}}.
False transmitters result in {{c1::decreased}} sympathetic effect upon release.
keyPoints: False transmitters mimic the storage and release of norepinephrine.
They result in reduced physiological responses compared to the true transmitter.
Octopamine is the prototype example.
This is one mechanism by which certain drugs reduce sympathetic tone.
They effectively dilute the pool of available norepinephrine.
microReview: False transmitters provide a 'decoy' signal. They occupy the machinery of the sympathetic terminal but fail to produce the same postsynaptic results, lowering blood pressure.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse 'false transmitter' with 'competitive antagonist.' A false transmitter is released from the nerve; an antagonist is a drug that blocks the receptor directly.
sourceQuote: False transmitter: Substance, for example, octopamine, stored in vesicles and released into synaptic cleft but lacking the effectiveness of the true transmitter, norepinephrine.

stem: A 64-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with severe headache and confusion. Her blood pressure is 210/125 mm Hg. Fundoscopic examination reveals bilateral retinal hemorrhages and papilledema. Urinalysis shows proteinuria and red blood cell casts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: Secondary hypertension refers to high BP caused by a specific abnormality (e.g., renal artery stenosis), but doesn't specifically describe this acute crisis.
explanations.b: Hypertensive emergency (malignant hypertension) is characterized by severe hypertension with evidence of acute end-organ damage (retina, brain, kidneys).
explanations.c: Stage 2 is any BP ≥140/90. While she has this, it does not capture the severity or the acute organ damage.
explanations.d: Essential hypertension is high BP of unknown etiology, usually a chronic condition without acute symptoms.
explanations.e: Elevated blood pressure is a much lower range (120-129 systolic).

ankiCards: {{c1::Hypertensive emergency}} is severe hypertension with rapidly progressing end-organ damage.
End-organ damage in hypertensive emergency can include {{c1::retinal hemorrhages}}, stroke, or renal damage.
Malignant hypertension is another term for {{c1::hypertensive emergency}}.
A key clinical sign of hypertensive emergency in the eye is {{c1::papilledema}}.
Encephalopathy and angina are clinical signs of {{c1::hypertensive emergency}}.
keyPoints: Hypertensive emergency requires immediate, controlled reduction of blood pressure.
End-organ damage is the distinguishing factor from hypertensive urgency.
Common presentations include encephalopathy, MI, or renal failure.
Retinal hemorrhages are a classic physical exam finding.
It is an accelerated form of severe hypertension.
Untreated, it can lead to stroke or death.
microReview: A hypertensive emergency is defined by the *effect* of the pressure on the body (organ damage), not just the absolute number, although the numbers are typically extremely high (e.g., >180/120).
examinerTraps: The trap is choosing 'Stage 2 hypertension' which is technically true but clinically incomplete given the end-organ damage presented in the vignette.
sourceQuote: Hypertensive emergency (“malignant hypertension”): An accelerated form of severe hypertension associated with rising blood pressure and rapidly progressing damage to vessels and end organs.

stem: In the management of hypertension, several classes of sympathoplegic drugs are utilized. Which of the following drugs acts specifically by blocking transmission at the level of the autonomic ganglia?

explanations.a: Prazosin is an alpha-1 receptor blocker, acting at the receptor level.
explanations.b: Propranolol is a beta-receptor blocker, acting at the receptor level.
explanations.c: Clonidine acts in the CNS to reduce sympathetic outflow.
explanations.d: Hexamethonium is a nicotinic antagonist that blocks transmission in the autonomic ganglia.
explanations.e: Guanethidine acts at the nerve terminals to prevent norepinephrine release.

ankiCards: {{c1::Hexamethonium}} is a drug that blocks autonomic ganglia.
Ganglionic blockers prevent transmission from {{c1::preganglionic}} to postganglionic neurons.
Clonidine reduces sympathetic outflow from the {{c1::CNS}}.
Guanethidine and reserpine act at the {{c1::nerve terminals}}.
Prazosin and propranolol are examples of {{c1::receptor}} blockers.
keyPoints: Sympathoplegic drugs are classified by their site of action.
Sites include CNS, ganglia, nerve terminals, and receptors.
Ganglionic blockers like hexamethonium are rarely used now due to broad side effects.
CNS-active drugs include clonidine and methyldopa.
Receptor blockers (alpha and beta) are common first-line or second-line agents.
microReview: The sympathetic chain can be interrupted at various points. Ganglionic blockers provide a complete 'shutdown' of autonomic control at the relay station, making them very potent but poorly tolerated.
examinerTraps: Often, students confuse 'ganglionic blockers' with 'postganglionic neuron blockers'. Ganglionic = relay point; Postganglionic = the terminal itself (e.g., Guanethidine).
sourceQuote: Sympathoplegics—blockers of: ... Ganglia (hexamethonium)

stem: When a vasodilator is administered to a patient, there is often a compensatory increase in heart rate. This physiological response is mediated by sensory input from the carotid sinus and aorta. Which of the following terms best describes this mechanism?

explanations.a: Orthostatic hypotension is the drop in BP upon standing, not the compensatory mechanism for low BP.
explanations.b: The baroreceptor reflex is the primary autonomic mechanism for BP homeostasis, involving sensory input to the vasomotor center to adjust sympathetic/parasympathetic output.
explanations.c: Rebound hypertension occurs after stopping a drug, not as a direct reflex to a vasodilator.
explanations.d: False neurotransmission involves replacement of NE with a weaker molecule.
explanations.e: End-organ damage is the consequence of chronic or severe hypertension.

ankiCards: The {{c1::baroreceptor reflex}} is the primary mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis.
Baroreceptor sensors are located in the {{c1::carotid sinus}} and {{c1::aorta}}.
The baroreceptor reflex output travels via {{c1::parasympathetic}} and sympathetic nerves.
Lowering blood pressure often triggers {{c1::reflex tachycardia}} via baroreceptors.
The {{c1::vasomotor center}} receives sensory input for the baroreceptor reflex.
keyPoints: The baroreceptor reflex counteracts rapid changes in blood pressure.
Sensors are found in the carotid sinus and aortic arch.
The reflex can limit the effectiveness of certain antihypertensive drugs (e.g., vasodilators).
Reflex tachycardia is a common side effect of direct vasodilators.
It involves both sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system adjustments.
microReview: The body treats a drug-induced drop in blood pressure as an 'error' and uses the baroreceptor reflex to try and pull it back up, primarily by increasing heart rate and peripheral resistance.
examinerTraps: Be careful not to confuse the 'reflex' (the mechanism) with 'reflex tachycardia' (the result). The question asks for the mechanism.
sourceQuote: Baroreceptor reflex: Primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis; involves sensory input from carotid sinus and aorta to the vasomotor center.

stem: A 68-year-old man is started on a new antihypertensive medication. A week later, he reports feeling lightheaded and faint every time he gets out of bed in the morning or stands up quickly from a chair. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?

explanations.a: Reflex tachycardia is an increase in heart rate, which might cause palpitations but doesn't typically cause postural fainting.
explanations.b: Rebound hypertension is a sudden spike in BP, not a drop upon standing.
explanations.c: Orthostatic (postural) hypotension is a significant drop in blood pressure when assuming an upright posture, commonly caused by sympathoplegic drugs.
explanations.d: Essential hypertension is the baseline high BP he was likely being treated for.
explanations.e: Hypertensive emergency involves extremely high BP, not low BP.

ankiCards: {{c1::Orthostatic hypotension}} is defined as hypotension on assuming an upright posture.
Orthostatic hypotension is also known as {{c1::postural}} hypotension.
Sympathoplegic drugs frequently cause {{c1::orthostatic hypotension}} as a side effect.
Fainting when standing up quickly is a symptom of {{c1::orthostatic hypotension}}.
The failure of the baroreceptor reflex to compensate for gravity results in {{c1::orthostatic hypotension}}.
keyPoints: Orthostatic hypotension is a common side effect of many antihypertensives.
It occurs because the body fails to constrict veins/arteries upon standing.
Drugs that interfere with sympathetic signaling are the most common culprits.
It is particularly common in elderly patients.
It can lead to falls and syncope.
microReview: Gravity pools blood in the legs when we stand. Normally, the sympathetic system kicks in to squeeze the vessels. Drugs that block this system (sympathoplegics) leave the blood in the legs, starving the brain of pressure temporarily.
examinerTraps: Watch for the difference between 'reflex tachycardia' (the heart speeding up) and 'orthostatic hypotension' (the pressure dropping). Both can happen together, but the faintness is due to the pressure drop.
sourceQuote: Orthostatic hypotension: Hypotension on assuming upright posture; postural hypotension.

stem: Inside a sympathetic nerve terminal, norepinephrine is synthesized in the cytoplasm but must be transported into specialized organelles for storage and subsequent release. Which of the following transporters performs this specific function?

explanations.a: NET is on the plasma membrane and moves NE from the synapse to the cytoplasm.
explanations.b: The catecholamine vesicle pump, or VMAT, pumps catecholamines from the neural cytoplasm into the storage vesicle.
explanations.c: Acetylcholine transporters move ACh, not catecholamines like norepinephrine.
explanations.d: Na/K ATPase maintains ion gradients but does not transport neurotransmitters into vesicles.
explanations.e: Calcium sensing receptors regulate calcium levels, not neurotransmitter storage.

ankiCards: The catecholamine vesicle pump is also called {{c1::VMAT (Vesicle Monoamine Transporter)}}.
VMAT moves catecholamines from the {{c1::cytoplasm}} into the storage vesicle.
Reserpine is a drug that inhibits {{c1::VMAT}}.
Storage of NE in {{c1::vesicles}} protects it from degradation by MAO.
VMAT is located on the membrane of the {{c1::storage vesicle}}.
keyPoints: VMAT is essential for protecting NE from cytoplasmic enzymes.
It facilitates the release of neurotransmitters via exocytosis.
Inhibiting VMAT leads to depletion of neurotransmitter stores.
VMAT is distinct from the reuptake pump (NET).
VMAT handles various monoamines, including dopamine and serotonin.
microReview: Think of the cytoplasm as a dangerous place for NE because of MAO. VMAT is the 'security guard' that ushers NE into the 'safe vault' of the vesicle.
examinerTraps: The most frequent trap is confusing VMAT (into vesicle) with NET (into cell). Remember: V is for Vesicle.
sourceQuote: Catecholamine vesicle pump: Storage vesicle transporter that pumps catecholamine from neural cytoplasm into the storage vesicle; also called vesicle monoamine transporter (VMAT).

stem: A 40-year-old patient is diagnosed with hypertension. Extensive diagnostic testing, including renal imaging and endocrine panels, fails to identify a specific underlying cause for the elevated blood pressure. Which of the following terms best categorizes this condition?

explanations.a: Secondary hypertension is caused by a diagnosable abnormality (e.g., aortic coarctation).
explanations.b: Malignant hypertension is an accelerated form with organ damage.
explanations.c: Essential hypertension (also called primary hypertension) is high blood pressure of unknown etiology.
explanations.d: Hypertensive urgency is severely high BP without organ damage.
explanations.e: Refractory hypertension is high BP that does not respond to multiple medications.

ankiCards: Hypertension of unknown etiology is called {{c1::essential}} or primary hypertension.
{{c1::Secondary}} hypertension is caused by a diagnosable abnormality.
About 90-95% of hypertension cases are classified as {{c1::essential}} hypertension.
Examples of {{c1::secondary}} hypertension include renal artery stenosis and coarctation of the aorta.
The term {{c1::primary}} hypertension is synonymous with essential hypertension.
keyPoints: Most cases of hypertension are essential (primary).
Secondary hypertension is rare but important to identify as it may be curable.
Aortic coarctation and renal artery stenosis are classic causes of secondary HTN.
Essential hypertension likely involves multiple genetic and environmental factors.
Diagnosis of essential HTN is often a diagnosis of exclusion.
microReview: If you find a cause (like a tumor or a narrow artery), it's secondary. If you don't (which is the case for most people), it's essential.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'essential' with 'idiopathic'; while they mean similar things, 'essential' is the standard medical term in this context.
sourceQuote: Essential hypertension: Hypertension of unknown etiology; also called primary hypertension. ... Secondary hypertension: Hypertension caused by a diagnosable abnormality, eg, aortic coarctation, renal artery stenosis.

stem: A patient who has been taking a high dose of a centrally acting sympathoplegic drug for several months suddenly stops taking the medication. Within 24 hours, their blood pressure rises significantly above the original pretreatment levels. Which of the following terms describes this phenomenon?

explanations.a: Reflex tachycardia is a heart rate response to acute BP lowering.
explanations.b: Rebound hypertension is the elevation of BP (often above baseline) resulting from the sudden loss of an antihypertensive drug effect.
explanations.c: Tachyphylaxis is a rapid decrease in response to a drug after repeated doses.
explanations.d: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in BP upon standing.
explanations.e: False neurotransmission involves the use of ineffective transmitters.

ankiCards: {{c1::Rebound hypertension}} occurs after the abrupt cessation of certain antihypertensive drugs.
Rebound hypertension often results in BP levels {{c1::above}} pretreatment levels.
{{c1::Clonidine}} is a classic drug associated with rebound hypertension.
The mechanism involves a sudden surge in {{c1::sympathetic}} activity.
To avoid rebound hypertension, drugs should be {{c1::tapered}} slowly.
keyPoints: Abrupt withdrawal of drugs like clonidine can cause a hypertensive crisis.
This is known as rebound hypertension.
The resulting pressure can be higher than before the patient started the drug.
It is caused by the sudden restoration of sympathetic tone that was being suppressed.
Gradual tapering of medication is necessary to prevent this.
microReview: When you suppress the sympathetic system for a long time, the body 'pushes back' to compensate. If you suddenly remove the suppression, that 'push' is unopposed, leading to a massive spike in pressure.
examinerTraps: Distinguish between 'withdrawal' (general symptoms) and 'rebound' (the specific return of the condition being treated, but worse).
sourceQuote: Rebound hypertension: Elevated blood pressure (usually above pretreatment levels) resulting from loss of antihypertensive drug effect.

stem: A pharmacologist is studying the mechanism of neurotransmitter homeostasis within the sympathetic nerve terminal. They identify a specific transporter responsible for the ATP-dependent movement of norepinephrine from the neuronal cytoplasm into storage vesicles. Inhibition of this specific transporter leads to the depletion of catecholamines over time. Which of the following best identifies this transport mechanism?

explanations.a: NET, or the catecholamine reuptake pump, is responsible for recycling norepinephrine from the synaptic cleft back into the cytoplasm, not into storage vesicles.
explanations.b: The catecholamine vesicle pump (VMAT) is the transporter that pumps catecholamines from the neural cytoplasm into the storage vesicle.
explanations.c: SERT is responsible for the reuptake of serotonin from the synaptic cleft, not the vesicular storage of norepinephrine.
explanations.d: Choline acetyltransferase is an enzyme involved in the synthesis of acetylcholine, not a catecholamine transporter.
explanations.e: Acetylcholinesterase is the enzyme responsible for the degradation of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft.

ankiCards: The {{c1::catecholamine vesicle pump}} (VMAT) moves norepinephrine from the cytoplasm into storage vesicles.
The {{c1::norepinephrine transporter}} (NET) is responsible for the reuptake of norepinephrine from the synapse.
Inhibition of the vesicle monoamine transporter (VMAT) results in the {{c1::depletion}} of catecholamine stores.
The transport of norepinephrine into vesicles is dependent on {{c1::ATP}}.
The synonym for the catecholamine vesicle pump is {{c1::VMAT}}.
keyPoints: VMAT (catecholamine vesicle pump) transports neurotransmitters into vesicles.
NET (catecholamine reuptake pump) recycles neurotransmitters from the synapse.
Drug-induced inhibition of VMAT (e.g., by reserpine) leads to catecholamine depletion.
The pump is essential for maintaining the pool of neurotransmitter available for release.
This mechanism is a key target in autonomic and cardiovascular pharmacology.
microReview: Norepinephrine synthesis occurs in the cytoplasm, but it must be sequestered into vesicles via VMAT to prevent degradation by MAO and to allow for quantal release. NET is the primary mechanism for terminating the signal in the synapse.
examinerTraps: A common mistake is confusing NET (reuptake from cleft) with VMAT (transport into vesicles). Both are transporters, but their locations and directions differ.
sourceQuote: Catecholamine vesicle pump: Storage vesicle transporter that pumps catecholamine from neural cytoplasm into the storage vesicle; also called vesicle monoamine transporter (VMAT)

stem: According to the 2017 American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) guidelines, which range of average systolic blood pressure is defined as Stage 1 hypertension?

explanations.a: Values below 120 mm Hg are considered normal blood pressure.
explanations.b: 120–129 mm Hg is classified as elevated blood pressure, not Stage 1 hypertension.
explanations.c: Stage 1 hypertension is defined as a systolic pressure between 130 and 139 mm Hg (or a diastolic pressure between 80 and 89 mm Hg).
explanations.d: Stage 2 hypertension begins at a systolic pressure of 140 mm Hg or higher.
explanations.e: Pressures equal to or greater than 140/90 mm Hg are classified as Stage 2 hypertension.

ankiCards: Stage 1 hypertension (AHA/ACC) is defined as a systolic BP of {{c1::130–139}} mm Hg.
Elevated blood pressure is defined as a systolic BP of {{c1::120–129}} mm Hg with a diastolic < 80.
Stage 2 hypertension is defined as a systolic BP equal to or greater than {{c1::140}} mm Hg.
Stage 1 hypertension requires a diastolic BP between {{c1::80–89}} mm Hg.
According to 2017 guidelines, Stage 2 hypertension starts at {{c1::140/90}} mm Hg.
keyPoints: Normal BP: <120 / <80.
Elevated BP: 120-129 / <80.
Systolic pressure is now considered as important as diastolic pressure for risk assessment.
microReview: The 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines lowered the threshold for hypertension diagnosis to encourage earlier intervention and risk reduction for cardiovascular events like stroke and MI.
examinerTraps: Watch for the distinction between 'Elevated' and 'Stage 1'. Elevated is 120-129; Stage 1 begins at 130.
sourceQuote: pressure equal to or greater than 130/80 mm Hg but less than 140/89 is considered stage 1 hypertension, while pressures equal to or greater than 140/90 are considered stage 2 hypertension.

stem: A 58-year-old male with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease presents to the clinic for a follow-up on his blood pressure. His current readings average 155/95 mm Hg. He is prescribed a potent direct-acting vasodilator to manage his condition. Shortly after starting the medication, he reports a racing heart rate. Which of the following physiological mechanisms best explains his new symptom?

explanations.a: Orthostatic hypotension refers to a drop in blood pressure upon standing, which might occur with these drugs but does not describe the increased heart rate directly.
explanations.b: Reflex tachycardia is the compensatory increase in heart rate resulting from the lowering of blood pressure, mediated by the baroreceptor reflex.
explanations.c: Rebound hypertension is an elevated BP following the cessation of a drug, not a side effect of initiating a vasodilator.
explanations.d: Vagal stimulation would cause bradycardia (a slow heart rate), the opposite of the patient's symptoms.
explanations.e: Direct vasodilators do not act as beta-1 agonists; the tachycardia is an indirect reflex effect via the sympathetic nervous system.

ankiCards: {{c1::Reflex tachycardia}} is the tachycardia resulting from a rapid lowering of blood pressure.
The reflex tachycardia response is mediated by the {{c1::baroreceptor}} reflex.
Direct-acting vasodilators often cause {{c1::reflex tachycardia}} as a compensatory response.
The baroreceptor reflex involves sensory input from the {{c1::carotid sinus}} and aorta.
Output from the vasomotor center during reflex tachycardia is via {{c1::sympathetic}} motor nerves.
keyPoints: Vasodilators reduce peripheral resistance and blood pressure.
Reduced BP triggers the baroreceptor reflex.
The reflex increases sympathetic outflow to the heart.
This result is an increased heart rate (reflex tachycardia).
Beta-blockers are often co-administered to prevent this effect.
