stem: Which of the following describes a substance that is stored in synaptic vesicles and released into the synaptic cleft, but lacks the physiological effectiveness of the natural neurotransmitter norepinephrine?

explanations.a: The norepinephrine transporter is a protein involved in reuptake, not a released chemical substance.
explanations.b: A false transmitter (e.g., octopamine) is a substance that replaces norepinephrine in vesicles but has little effect on receptors upon release.
explanations.c: Renin inhibitors like aliskiren block the enzymatic activity of renin, they are not stored in vesicles.
explanations.d: Vasodilators act on vascular smooth muscle to cause relaxation, not by acting as inactive neurotransmitters.
explanations.e: Ganglionic blockers (e.g., hexamethonium) inhibit transmission at the nicotinic receptors of the autonomic ganglia.

ankiCards: A substance stored in vesicles and released but lacking effective neurotransmitter action is a {{c1::false transmitter}}.
An example of a false transmitter mentioned in the text is {{c1::octopamine}}.
False transmitters replace {{c1::norepinephrine}} in the storage vesicles.
The use of false transmitters is a mechanism of certain {{c1::sympathoplegic}} drugs.
Octopamine is stored in {{c1::vesicles}} and released into the synaptic cleft.
keyPoints: False transmitters are structurally similar to neurotransmitters.
They are taken up into vesicles by VMAT.
They are released by exocytosis upon nerve stimulation.
Because they are weakly active at receptors, they reduce sympathetic transmission.
Octopamine is the classic biochemical example.
microReview: False transmitters (like Octopamine) 'trick' the vesicle into storing them instead of NE. When the nerve fires, 'blanks' are released instead of the active hormone.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'Octopamine' as a specific example. Don't confuse it with 'antagonist'—the transmitter is released, it just doesn't work.
sourceQuote: False transmitter: Substance, for example, octopamine, stored in vesicles and released into synaptic cleft but lacking the effectiveness of the true transmitter, norepinephrine

stem: A 30-year-old male with a history of hypertension is evaluated for a recent change in symptoms. He reports that since starting a new antihypertensive medication, he feels dizzy and lightheaded whenever he stands up quickly from a seated position. Physical examination confirms a significant drop in blood pressure upon standing. Which of the following terms describes this clinical finding?

explanations.a: Reflex tachycardia is an increase in heart rate following a drop in blood pressure, not the drop in pressure itself.
explanations.b: Rebound hypertension is a sudden rise in blood pressure after stopping a medication.
explanations.c: Orthostatic hypotension (postural hypotension) is defined as a significant drop in blood pressure upon assuming an upright posture.
explanations.d: Essential hypertension is the diagnosis of high blood pressure of unknown cause.
explanations.e: Secondary hypertension is high blood pressure with a specific identifiable cause.

ankiCards: Hypotension on assuming an upright posture is called {{c1::orthostatic}} hypotension.
Another name for orthostatic hypotension is {{c1::postural}} hypotension.
Dizziness upon standing in a hypertensive patient is often a side effect of {{c1::sympathoplegic}} or {{c2::vasodilator}} drugs.
Orthostatic hypotension involves a failure of the {{c1::baroreceptor reflex}} to maintain BP during postural changes.
The clinical term for feeling lightheaded when standing up is {{c1::orthostasis}}.
keyPoints: Orthostatic hypotension is a common side effect of many antihypertensive drugs.
It is defined by a drop in BP when changing from supine/seated to standing.
Commonly caused by drugs that interfere with sympathetic outflow or venodilation.
Symptoms include dizziness, lightheadedness, and syncope.
The baroreceptor reflex normally prevents this by increasing peripheral resistance and heart rate.
microReview: Stand up -> Gravity pulls blood down -> BP drops -> Baroreceptors usually fix it. If drugs block the fix (sympathoplegics), you get Orthostatic Hypotension.
examinerTraps: Commonly confused with 'reflex tachycardia'. Tachycardia is what the heart does to *fix* the drop; orthostatic hypotension is the *drop itself*.
sourceQuote: Orthostatic hypotension: Hypotension on assuming upright posture; postural hypotension

stem: In the management of hypertension, several drug classes target the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). A specific drug acts by directly binding to and inhibiting the enzyme responsible for the rate-limiting step of this cascade, preventing the formation of Angiotensin I. Which drug class does this represent?

explanations.a: ACE inhibitors (e.g., captopril) block the conversion of Angiotensin I to Angiotensin II.
explanations.b: Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs, e.g., losartan) block the binding of Angiotensin II to its receptor.
explanations.c: Renin inhibitors (e.g., aliskiren) inhibit the enzymatic activity of renin, which is the first and rate-limiting step in the RAAS pathway.
explanations.d: Calcium channel blockers (e.g., nifedipine) act on vascular smooth muscle to cause vasodilation.
explanations.e: Sympathoplegics (e.g., clonidine, propranolol) reduce sympathetic outflow or its effects on the heart and vessels.

ankiCards: The drug class that directly inhibits the enzyme renin is called {{c1::renin inhibitors}}.
An example of a renin inhibitor mentioned in the text is {{c1::aliskiren}}.
ACE inhibitors, such as {{c1::captopril}}, block the production of Angiotensin II.
Angiotensin antagonists, such as {{c1::losartan}}, are also known as {{c2::receptor blockers}}.
The RAAS system can be blocked at three levels: Renin, {{c1::ACE}}, and {{c2::Angiotensin receptors}}.
keyPoints: Renin is the enzyme that converts Angiotensinogen to Angiotensin I.
Aliskiren is the primary direct renin inhibitor (DRI).
ACE inhibitors (captopril) act downstream of renin.
ARBs (losartan) act at the receptor level.
All three classes eventually decrease Angiotensin II effects but at different stages.
microReview: RAAS targets: Aliskiren (Renin), -pril (ACE), -sartan (ARB). Aliskiren is the only one that stops the very first step (Renin).
examinerTraps: The examiner might ask for the 'rate-limiting step' of RAAS. That is always Renin, making renin inhibitors the correct answer.
sourceQuote: Angiotensin antagonists: Renin inhibitor (aliskiren), ACE inhibitors (captopril), Receptor blockers (losartan)

stem: Which of the following best describes the physiological phenomenon where blood pressure rises, often above pretreatment levels, following the sudden discontinuation of an antihypertensive medication?

explanations.a: Hypertensive emergency is characterized by acute end-organ damage, not just the cause of the BP rise.
explanations.b: Secondary hypertension is due to a separate disease process like renal artery stenosis.
explanations.c: Reflex tachycardia is a heart rate change, not a primary blood pressure rise phenomenon.
explanations.d: Rebound hypertension is the elevation of BP resulting from the loss of drug effect after sudden withdrawal.
explanations.e: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in blood pressure when standing up.

ankiCards: Elevated blood pressure resulting from loss of drug effect is called {{c1::rebound hypertension}}.
Rebound hypertension usually results in BP levels {{c1::above}} pretreatment levels.
Sudden withdrawal of {{c1::clonidine}} is a classic cause of rebound hypertension.
Rebound hypertension is a risk when patients {{c1::suddenly stop}} their medications.
The physiological response to drug withdrawal that spikes BP is {{c1::rebound hypertension}}.
keyPoints: Rebound hypertension occurs upon sudden cessation of certain drugs.
It can be more severe than the patient's original baseline hypertension.
Centrally acting alpha-2 agonists are frequently associated with this.
It can potentially lead to hypertensive crises.
Tapering medications slowly is the standard method to prevent this effect.
microReview: Stop drug fast -> Sympathetic system 'overshoots' because it was suppressed -> BP spikes higher than before = Rebound Hypertension.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse rebound hypertension with 'refractory hypertension' (hypertension that won't respond to 3+ drugs).
sourceQuote: Rebound hypertension: Elevated blood pressure (usually above pretreatment levels) resulting from loss of antihypertensive drug effect

stem: A 25-year-old woman is found to have a blood pressure of 160/100 mm Hg. Further investigation reveals a significant narrowing of the left renal artery. This specific type of hypertension, which results from a diagnosable abnormality, is classified as which of the following?

explanations.a: Essential hypertension is hypertension of unknown etiology.
explanations.b: Primary hypertension is another name for essential hypertension (unknown etiology).
explanations.c: Secondary hypertension is caused by a diagnosable abnormality such as renal artery stenosis or aortic coarctation.
explanations.d: Malignant hypertension refers to the severity and presence of end-organ damage, not the etiology.
explanations.e: Rebound hypertension occurs after drug withdrawal.

ankiCards: Hypertension of unknown etiology is called {{c1::essential}} (or primary) hypertension.
Hypertension caused by a diagnosable abnormality is called {{c1::secondary}} hypertension.
Two examples of causes for secondary hypertension are {{c1::aortic coarctation}} and {{c2::renal artery stenosis}}.
Primary hypertension is also known as {{c1::essential}} hypertension.
Renal artery stenosis is a common cause of {{c1::secondary}} hypertension.
keyPoints: 90-95% of hypertension is 'Essential' (unknown cause).
Secondary hypertension implies an underlying, often treatable, condition.
Renal causes (stenosis, parenchymal disease) are most common.
Mechanical causes like aortic coarctation are also secondary.
Endocrine disorders (like Conn's syndrome) are other causes of secondary HTN.
microReview: Cause unknown = Essential/Primary. Cause found (e.g., Renal Artery Stenosis) = Secondary.
examinerTraps: The terms 'Essential' and 'Primary' are synonyms. If both are options, look for a third option like 'Secondary' if a cause is mentioned.
sourceQuote: Secondary hypertension: Hypertension caused by a diagnosable abnormality, eg, aortic coarctation, renal artery stenosis

stem: Sympathoplegic drugs can act at various levels of the nervous system to reduce blood pressure. Which of the following sites of action is matched with the correct drug example provided in the classification scheme?

explanations.a: Clonidine acts on CNS sympathetic outflow, not at the ganglia.
explanations.b: Hexamethonium is a ganglionic blocker, not a CNS acting drug.
explanations.c: Guanethidine and reserpine are drugs that act at the nerve terminals to block transmission.
explanations.d: Nifedipine is a calcium channel blocker (vasodilator), while alpha or beta receptor blockers are drugs like prazosin or propranolol.
explanations.e: Reserpine is a nerve terminal sympathoplegic, not a direct vasodilator.

ankiCards: The drug {{c1::clonidine}} acts on CNS sympathetic outflow.
Guanethidine acts on {{c1::nerve terminals}} to block transmission.
Hexamethonium is classified as a {{c1::ganglia}} blocker.
Prazosin and propranolol are sympathoplegics that block {{c1::alpha or beta receptors}}.
Nifedipine belongs to the {{c1::calcium blocker}} class of vasodilators.
keyPoints: Sympathoplegics are categorized by their site of action.
CNS: Clonidine.
Ganglia: Hexamethonium.
Nerve terminals: Guanethidine, Reserpine.
Receptors: Alpha blockers (prazosin), Beta blockers (propranolol).
microReview: Where does it work? Brain (Clonidine), Ganglia (Hexamethonium), Nerve ends (Guanethidine), Receptors (Propranolol).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the 'nerve terminal' drugs (Reserpine/Guanethidine) with the 'receptor' drugs (Prazosin/Propranolol).
sourceQuote: Sympathoplegics—blockers of: CNS sympathetic outflow (clonidine), Ganglia (hexamethonium), Nerve terminals (guanethidine, reserpine), Alpha or beta receptors (prazosin, propranolol)

stem: A 52-year-old male presents for a routine checkup. He has no significant past medical history. Physical examination reveals a heart rate of 72 bpm and an average blood pressure of 136/84 mm Hg across multiple readings. The patient is otherwise asymptomatic. According to current American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology guidelines, which of the following is the most appropriate classification for this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Elevated blood pressure is defined as a systolic pressure between 120 and 129 mm Hg and a diastolic pressure less than 80 mm Hg.
explanations.b: Stage 1 hypertension is defined as a systolic pressure between 130 and 139 mm Hg or a diastolic pressure between 80 and 89 mm Hg.
explanations.c: Stage 2 hypertension is defined as a systolic pressure equal to or greater than 140 mm Hg or a diastolic pressure equal to or greater than 90 mm Hg.
explanations.d: Hypertensive emergency involves severe blood pressure elevations accompanied by evidence of acute, progressing end-organ damage, not present here.
explanations.e: Secondary hypertension refers to hypertension caused by a specific, identifiable underlying cause, which is not suggested by this patient's initial screening.

ankiCards: Stage 1 hypertension is defined as a systolic pressure of {{c1::130-139}} mm Hg or a diastolic pressure of {{c2::80-89}} mm Hg.
Stage 2 hypertension begins at a blood pressure of {{c1::140/90}} mm Hg.
Elevated blood pressure is defined as systolic {{c1::120-129}} mm Hg and diastolic {{c2::<80}} mm Hg.
The 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines consider increased {{c1::systolic}} pressure to be at least as important as elevated diastolic pressure.
Most patients with Stage 1 or Stage 2 hypertension are considered {{c1::deserving of treatment}} according to modern guidelines.
keyPoints: The 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines lowered the threshold for diagnosing hypertension.
Stage 1 HTN: 130–139 SBP or 80–89 DBP.
Stage 2 HTN: ≥140 SBP or ≥90 DBP.
Elevated BP: 120–129 SBP and <80 DBP.
Hypertension is a major risk factor for MI, heart failure, and stroke.
microReview: Hypertension classification is based on the highest category if systolic and diastolic fall into different stages. Management starts with lifestyle changes for Stage 1 (if low risk) and medication for Stage 2.
examinerTraps: A common trap is confusing 'Elevated' with 'Stage 1'. Remember that 130/80 is the new cutoff for Stage 1.
sourceQuote: pressure equal to or greater than 130/80 mm Hg but less than 140/89 is considered stage 1 hypertension, while pressures equal to or greater than 140/90 are considered stage 2 hypertension.

stem: A new antihypertensive agent is developed that acts primarily as a potent vasodilator of peripheral arterioles. During clinical trials, subjects are observed to have a significant increase in heart rate shortly after administration. Which of the following physiological mechanisms is primarily responsible for this observed increase in heart rate?

options.b: Inhibition of the vagal motor center
options.d: Stimulation of the catecholamine vesicle pump

explanations.a: While heart rate increases via beta-1, the primary reflex trigger in response to vasodilation is the baroreceptor reflex, not direct drug activation.
explanations.b: Vagal tone might decrease as part of the reflex, but the reflex pathway itself is the primary mechanism.
explanations.c: The baroreceptor reflex is the homeostatic mechanism that increases sympathetic outflow and decreases parasympathetic tone in response to a drop in blood pressure caused by vasodilation, resulting in reflex tachycardia.
explanations.d: The catecholamine vesicle pump (VMAT) is involved in storage, not the acute reflex response to peripheral vasodilation.
explanations.e: Norepinephrine transporters (NET) recycle neurotransmitters; their upregulation would not explain acute reflex tachycardia.

ankiCards: The {{c1::baroreceptor reflex}} is the primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis.
Lowering blood pressure with vasodilators often causes {{c1::reflex tachycardia}}.
The baroreceptor reflex involves sensory input from the {{c1::carotid sinus}} and {{c2::aorta}}.
Vasomotor center output in response to low BP involves {{c1::increased}} sympathetic and {{c2::decreased}} parasympathetic activity.
{{c1::Reflex tachycardia}} results from the baroreceptor reflex sensing a decrease in peripheral resistance.
keyPoints: Vasodilators reduce peripheral resistance, lowering BP.
Decreased BP is sensed by baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch.
The CNS responds by increasing sympathetic output.
Reflex tachycardia is a common side effect of direct-acting vasodilators.
Beta-blockers are often co-administered with vasodilators to blunt this reflex.
microReview: Homeostatic reflexes (like the baroreceptor reflex) often oppose the primary effect of antihypertensive drugs, which is why multi-drug regimens are frequently necessary.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the reflex (mediated by the CNS and baroreceptors) with the direct action of the drug on the heart. Direct vasodilators do not hit cardiac receptors; the heart rate change is indirect.
sourceQuote: Baroreceptor reflex Primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis; involves sensory input from carotid sinus and aorta to the vasomotor center and output via the parasympathetic and sympathetic motor nerves

stem: In the neurochemical regulation of blood pressure, specific transporters are responsible for the storage and recycling of neurotransmitters. Which of the following proteins is specifically responsible for transporting catecholamines from the neural cytoplasm into storage vesicles?

explanations.a: NET (norepinephrine transporter) is the catecholamine reuptake pump that recycles NE from the synapse back into the cytoplasm.
explanations.b: VMAT (vesicle monoamine transporter), also called the catecholamine vesicle pump, moves catecholamines from the cytoplasm into storage vesicles.
explanations.c: MAO is an enzyme that degrades monoamines in the cytoplasm, not a transporter.
explanations.d: COMT is an enzyme involved in the degradation of catecholamines, not transport into vesicles.
explanations.e: ChAT is the enzyme responsible for synthesizing acetylcholine, unrelated to catecholamine transport.

ankiCards: The {{c1::catecholamine vesicle pump}} is also known as VMAT.
VMAT transports catecholamines from the {{c1::neural cytoplasm}} into the {{c2::storage vesicle}}.
The catecholamine reuptake pump is also called {{c1::NET (norepinephrine transporter)}}.
{{c1::NET}} is responsible for recycling norepinephrine after release into the synapse.
Reserpine is a drug that historically targeted the {{c1::VMAT/vesicle pump}}.
keyPoints: Catecholamine signaling depends on proper storage and reuptake.
VMAT handles transport into vesicles (storage).
NET handles transport from the synapse to cytoplasm (reuptake).
Disrupting these transporters can lower sympathetic tone and BP.
High-yield term differentiation: Vesicle pump (VMAT) vs. Reuptake pump (NET).
microReview: VMAT packs the 'ammunition' (NE) into 'granules' (vesicles). NET 'recycles' the spent ammunition from the 'field' (synapse) back to the 'base' (cytoplasm).
examinerTraps: Students often swap the functions of NET and VMAT. Remember: NET = Network/External (synapse); VMAT = Vesicle (internal storage).
sourceQuote: Catecholamine vesicle pump Storage vesicle transporter that pumps catecholamine from neural cytoplasm into the storage vesicle; also called vesicle monoamine transporter (VMAT)

stem: A 64-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department complaining of a severe headache and blurred vision. Her blood pressure is 210/130 mm Hg. Physical examination reveals flame-shaped hemorrhages and papilledema on fundoscopy. Laboratory studies show an elevated serum creatinine. Which of the following terms best describes this patient's clinical presentation?

explanations.a: Essential hypertension is primary hypertension of unknown etiology; while she has high BP, the acute presentation describes a more specific emergency.
explanations.b: While her BP meets the numerical criteria for Stage 2, the presence of acute end-organ damage (retinal hemorrhages, renal issues) elevates the diagnosis.
explanations.c: Hypertensive emergency (malignant hypertension) is characterized by severe hypertension with rapidly progressing damage to end organs like the eyes, kidneys, and brain.
explanations.d: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in blood pressure upon standing, the opposite of this presentation.
explanations.e: Rebound hypertension occurs after the sudden withdrawal of antihypertensive drugs; while possible, the clinical focus here is the acute emergency state.

ankiCards: {{c1::Hypertensive emergency}} is characterized by severe hypertension with rapidly progressing end-organ damage.
Signs of hypertensive emergency include {{c1::renal damage}}, {{c2::encephalopathy}}, and {{c3::retinal hemorrhages}}.
End-organ damage in hypertension typically involves the heart, {{c1::kidney}}, {{c2::retina}}, or {{c3::brain}}.
Malignant hypertension is an older term for {{c1::hypertensive emergency}}.
Acute rising BP with stroke or MI signals a {{c1::hypertensive emergency}}.
keyPoints: Hypertensive emergency requires immediate but controlled BP reduction.
The definition relies on end-organ damage, not just a BP number.
Common signs include papilledema and retinal hemorrhages.
Renal failure (rising creatinine) is a common complication.
Encephalopathy and stroke are neurological manifestations of the condition.
microReview: Distinguish Urgency (High BP, no end-organ damage) from Emergency (High BP + end-organ damage). The presence of retinal hemorrhages or high creatinine in a patient with 210/130 marks an Emergency.
examinerTraps: A trap is focusing only on the numbers. 180/120 without symptoms is an 'Urgency'. Once symptoms like blurred vision or retinal changes appear, it's an 'Emergency'.
sourceQuote: Hypertensive emergency... An accelerated form of severe hypertension associated with rising blood pressure and rapidly progressing damage to vessels and end organs.

stem: Sympathoplegic drugs are classified based on the anatomical site where they disrupt the sympathetic reflex arc. A specific drug used in experimental settings works by blocking transmission at the nicotinic receptors of the autonomic ganglia. Which of the following drugs is the prototypical agent for this mechanism?

explanations.a: Clonidine acts centrally by stimulating alpha-2 receptors to reduce sympathetic outflow from the CNS.
explanations.b: Prazosin is an alpha-1 receptor antagonist acting at the vascular smooth muscle.
explanations.c: Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker acting on cardiac and vascular receptors.
explanations.d: Hexamethonium is a prototypical ganglion-blocking drug that interrupts transmission between pre- and post-ganglionic neurons.
explanations.e: Guanethidine acts at the nerve terminal to inhibit the release of norepinephrine.

ankiCards: {{c1::Hexamethonium}} is a prototypical drug that blocks autonomic ganglia.
Ganglion-blocking drugs interfere with transmission between {{c1::preganglionic}} and {{c2::postganglionic}} neurons.
{{c1::Clonidine}} acts on the CNS to reduce sympathetic outflow.
{{c1::Guanethidine}} and {{c2::reserpine}} act at the nerve terminals.
Prazosin and Propranolol are examples of {{c1::receptor blockers}}.
keyPoints: Sympathoplegics reduce BP by decreasing sympathetic tone.
Sites of action include: CNS, Ganglia, Nerve terminals, and Receptors.
Ganglionic blockers are rarely used clinically due to non-specific side effects.
Clonidine (CNS) is used for hypertension and withdrawal syndromes.
Receptor blockers (Alpha/Beta) are common first- or second-line agents.
microReview: Think of the sympathetic path: CNS (Clonidine) -> Ganglia (Hexamethonium) -> Nerve Terminal (Guanethidine) -> Receptors (Prazosin/Propranolol).
examinerTraps: Hexamethonium is often used in physiology/pharmacology questions as a tool to 'isolate' the heart or vessels from the autonomic nervous system.
sourceQuote: Sympathoplegics—blockers of... Ganglia (hexamethonium)

stem: Which of the following substances acts as a 'false transmitter' by being stored in synaptic vesicles and released into the synaptic cleft, but fails to activate adrenergic receptors as effectively as norepinephrine?

explanations.a: Dopamine is a precursor to norepinephrine and a potent agonist at its own receptors.
explanations.b: Octopamine is a prototypical false transmitter that displaces norepinephrine in vesicles but has little effect on postsynaptic receptors.
explanations.c: Epinephrine is a potent endogenous catecholamine and the primary hormone of the adrenal medulla.
explanations.d: Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor peptide, not a small-molecule neurotransmitter.
explanations.e: Aldosterone is a steroid hormone that promotes sodium retention in the kidney.

ankiCards: A {{c1::false transmitter}} is stored in vesicles and released but lacks the effectiveness of norepinephrine.
{{c1::Octopamine}} is a classic example of a false transmitter.
False transmitters replace {{c1::norepinephrine}} in the synaptic cleft.
The use of certain drugs can lead to the accumulation of {{c1::false transmitters}} in nerve terminals.
False transmitters result in {{c1::decreased}} sympathetic efficacy.
keyPoints: False transmitters are structural analogs of real neurotransmitters.
They are synthesized or taken up and stored just like NE.
Upon nerve stimulation, they are released but produce no/little response.
This leads to a 'functional' sympathoplegia.
Octopamine is the most common board-relevant example.
microReview: False transmitters are like 'blanks' in a gun. They fit in the chamber (vesicle) and can be fired (released), but they don't hit the target (receptor).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse a false transmitter with an antagonist. An antagonist blocks the receptor; a false transmitter reduces the amount of effective ligand being released.
sourceQuote: False transmitter Substance, for example, octopamine, stored in vesicles and released into synaptic cleft but lacking the effectiveness of the true transmitter, norepinephrine

stem: A 48-year-old man with a long history of hypertension has been managed with several medications. He recently ran out of his prescription for a centrally acting antihypertensive and did not refill it for three days. He now presents to the urgent care clinic with a blood pressure of 190/115 mm Hg, sweating, and palpitations. This phenomenon is best defined as:

explanations.a: Essential hypertension is the baseline chronic condition, not the acute spike due to drug cessation.
explanations.b: The blood pressure of 190/115 exceeds the criteria for Stage 1.
explanations.c: Secondary hypertension implies a structural or hormonal cause like renal artery stenosis, not drug withdrawal.
explanations.d: Rebound hypertension is an elevated blood pressure, often exceeding pretreatment levels, resulting from the sudden loss of an antihypertensive drug's effect (e.g., Clonidine).
explanations.e: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in BP upon standing, not an acute hypertensive spike.

ankiCards: {{c1::Rebound hypertension}} occurs after the sudden loss of a drug's antihypertensive effect.
Rebound hypertension often results in BP levels {{c1::above}} pretreatment levels.
Sudden withdrawal of {{c1::clonidine}} is a classic cause of rebound hypertension.
Symptoms of rebound hypertension can include {{c1::sweating}}, tachycardia, and anxiety.
To avoid rebound, centrally acting drugs should be {{c1::tapered}} slowly.
keyPoints: Rebound hypertension is a withdrawal phenomenon.
It is most common with sympathoplegics like clonidine.
Pathophysiology involves a sudden surge in sympathetic activity.
It can mimic a hypertensive emergency.
Patients must be educated on the dangers of sudden medication cessation.
microReview: Stopping a drug like Clonidine (which 'muffles' the sympathetic system) is like removing a dam; the sympathetic 'water' (NE) rushes back with excessive force, causing a spike in BP.
examinerTraps: Examiners often use Clonidine withdrawal vignettes to test the concept of rebound hypertension.
sourceQuote: Rebound hypertension Elevated blood pressure (usually above pretreatment levels) resulting from loss of antihypertensive drug effect

stem: A patient is prescribed a medication that inhibits the conversion of Angiotensin I to Angiotensin II. This mechanism classifies the drug under which of the following categories of antihypertensive agents?

explanations.a: Calcium blockers like nifedipine inhibit calcium entry into smooth muscle, not peptide conversion.
explanations.b: ACE (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme) inhibitors like captopril block the conversion of Angiotensin I to Angiotensin II.
explanations.c: Receptor blockers (ARBs) like losartan block the AT1 receptor, but do not prevent the conversion of Angiotensin I.
explanations.d: Renin inhibitors like aliskiren block the enzyme renin, which converts Angiotensinogen to Angiotensin I.
explanations.e: Parenteral vasodilators like nitroprusside act directly on vessels, often via nitric oxide, not the RAAS pathway enzymes.

ankiCards: {{c1::ACE inhibitors}} block the conversion of Angiotensin I to Angiotensin II.
{{c1::Captopril}} is an example of an ACE inhibitor.
{{c1::Losartan}} is an example of an Angiotensin Receptor Blocker (ARB).
{{c1::Aliskiren}} is a drug that inhibits renin.
Angiotensin antagonists include ACE inhibitors, {{c1::ARBs}}, and renin inhibitors.
keyPoints: The Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) is a major target for HTN.
ACE inhibitors (e.g., Captopril) are first-line for many patients.
They prevent the formation of the potent vasoconstrictor Angiotensin II.
By doing so, they also reduce aldosterone secretion.
Common side effects include cough and angioedema (due to bradykinin).
microReview: RAAS Cascade: Angiotensinogen --(Renin)--> Angiotensin I --(ACE)--> Angiotensin II --(AT1 Receptor)--> Vasoconstriction. ACE inhibitors hit the middle step.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse ARBs with ACE inhibitors. ACE inhibitors prevent the synthesis of ATII; ARBs block the action of ATII at the receptor level.
sourceQuote: Angiotensin antagonists... ACE inhibitors (captopril)

stem: Which of the following classes of antihypertensive drugs is characterized by its ability to cause hypotension specifically when a patient assumes an upright posture?

explanations.a: Diuretics reduce volume; while they can contribute to low BP, they aren't the primary class defined by orthostatic changes in the way sympathoplegics are.
explanations.b: Vasodilators lower BP but usually cause more reflex tachycardia than severe orthostatic changes unless combined with other drugs.
explanations.c: Sympathoplegics (especially those acting on ganglia or nerve terminals) interfere with the sympathetic response needed to constrict vessels upon standing, leading to orthostatic hypotension.
explanations.d: ACE inhibitors generally preserve autonomic reflexes and rarely cause severe orthostatic hypotension on their own.
explanations.e: Renin inhibitors, like ACE inhibitors, typically don't cause significant orthostatic hypotension.

ankiCards: {{c1::Orthostatic hypotension}} is defined as hypotension on assuming an upright posture.
Orthostatic hypotension is also called {{c1::postural hypotension}}.
{{c1::Sympathoplegics}} are the drug class most associated with orthostatic hypotension.
The reflex that prevents orthostatic hypotension is the {{c1::baroreceptor reflex}}.
Postganglionic neuron blockers can cause severe {{c1::orthostatic/postural}} hypotension.
keyPoints: Standing up causes blood to pool in the lower extremities.
Normally, the baroreceptor reflex increases sympathetic tone to maintain BP.
Sympathoplegics block this compensatory constriction.
This results in a significant drop in BP (orthostatic hypotension).
Common with older drugs like Guanethidine or Hexamethonium.
microReview: Posture = Postural Hypotension. Sympathetic nervous system = The system that prevents you from fainting when you stand up. Sympatho-plegic = Paralyzing that system.
examinerTraps: A common trap is assuming all BP meds cause orthostatic hypotension. Centrally acting or peripherally acting sympathoplegics are much more likely to cause it than ACE inhibitors or ARBs.
sourceQuote: Orthostatic hypotension Hypotension on assuming upright posture; postural hypotension

stem: A pharmacological agent is used to lower blood pressure by reducing the storage of norepinephrine in the peripheral adrenergic nerve endings. It achieves this by inhibiting the catecholamine vesicle pump. Which drug serves as the prototype for this specific mechanism?

explanations.a: Hydralazine is an older oral vasodilator acting directly on vascular smooth muscle.
explanations.b: Nifedipine is a calcium channel blocker.
explanations.c: Reserpine is the prototypical drug that acts on nerve terminals by inhibiting the vesicle monoamine transporter (VMAT), depleting catecholamine stores.
explanations.d: Prazosin is an alpha-receptor blocker.
explanations.e: Nitroprusside is a parenteral vasodilator used for hypertensive emergencies.

ankiCards: {{c1::Reserpine}} acts on nerve terminals by inhibiting the catecholamine vesicle pump.
Inhibition of the vesicle pump results in the {{c1::depletion}} of norepinephrine stores.
Reserpine and {{c1::guanethidine}} are categorized as nerve terminal blockers.
{{c1::Nerve terminal blockers}} are a sub-class of sympathoplegics.
Hydralazine and Nifedipine are {{c1::vasodilators}}, not sympathoplegics.
keyPoints: Reserpine blocks VMAT.
Without VMAT, NE is degraded by MAO in the cytoplasm.
This leads to long-term depletion of neurotransmitters.
It was one of the first effective antihypertensives but is rarely used now due to CNS side effects (depression).
It represents the 'nerve terminal' site of sympathoplegic action.
microReview: Reserpine 'leaks' the storage tanks. By blocking the pump (VMAT) that puts NE into vesicles, the NE stays in the cytoplasm where it is 'eaten' by MAO, eventually leaving the nerve terminal empty.
examinerTraps: Be careful to distinguish between 'nerve terminal' blockers (Reserpine/Guanethidine) and 'receptor' blockers (Prazosin/Propranolol).
sourceQuote: Sympathoplegics—blockers of... Nerve terminals (guanethidine, reserpine)

stem: A 52-year-old male presents for a routine check-up. His average blood pressure reading in the clinic today is 146/92 mm Hg. He has no significant past medical history and feels well. Physical examination is unremarkable, and there are no signs of end-organ damage. Based on current guidelines, which of the following is the most accurate classification of this patient's blood pressure status?

explanations.a: Elevated blood pressure is defined as a systolic pressure between 120 and 129 mm Hg with a diastolic pressure less than 80 mm Hg.
explanations.b: Stage 1 hypertension is defined as a systolic pressure between 130-139 mm Hg or a diastolic pressure between 80-89 mm Hg.
explanations.c: Stage 2 hypertension is defined as a systolic pressure equal to or greater than 140 mm Hg or a diastolic pressure equal to or greater than 90 mm Hg.
explanations.d: Hypertensive emergency involves severely elevated blood pressure (usually >180/120 mm Hg) with evidence of acute end-organ damage, which is not present here.
explanations.e: Secondary hypertension refers to hypertension with a specific, identifiable cause; there is no evidence provided to suggest an underlying abnormality yet.

ankiCards: Stage 2 hypertension is defined as a BP equal to or greater than {{c1::140/90}} mm Hg.
According to 2017 guidelines, a systolic BP of 125 mm Hg is categorized as {{c1::elevated}}.
Stage 1 hypertension is diagnosed when systolic BP is {{c1::130–139}} or diastolic BP is 80–89.
The American Heart Association guidelines emphasize that {{c1::systolic}} pressure is at least as important as diastolic pressure.
Hypertension is a major risk factor for myocardial infarction, heart failure, and {{c1::stroke}}.
keyPoints: Normal blood pressure is generally under 120/80 mm Hg.
Elevated BP (120-129 systolic) requires lifestyle monitoring.
Stage 1 hypertension begins at 130/80 mm Hg.
Stage 2 hypertension begins at 140/90 mm Hg.
Systolic elevation is recognized as a critical predictor of cardiovascular risk.
Treatment is recommended for both Stage 1 and Stage 2 in most patients.
microReview: Hypertension is classified by severity: Elevated (120-129/<80), Stage 1 (130-139/80-89), and Stage 2 (≥140/≥90). Classification directs the urgency and type of clinical intervention required.
examinerTraps: A common trap is confusing the 2017 Stage 1 threshold (130/80) with the older Stage 1 threshold (140/90), which is now considered Stage 2.
sourceQuote: pressures equal to or greater than 140/90 are considered stage 2 hypertension. Increased systolic pressure is now considered at least as important as elevated diastolic.

stem: A pharmacologist is studying the primary autonomic mechanism responsible for blood pressure homeostasis. This mechanism involves sensory input from the carotid sinus and aorta traveling to the vasomotor center, with compensatory output via motor nerves. Which of the following is the term for this regulatory pathway?

explanations.a: The baroreceptor reflex is the primary autonomic mechanism for BP homeostasis, using sensory input from the carotid sinus/aorta to adjust sympathetic/parasympathetic output.
explanations.b: The renin-angiotensin cascade is a hormonal system, not the primary rapid autonomic reflex path.
explanations.c: The corticospinal tract is a motor pathway involved in voluntary muscle control, not BP homeostasis.
explanations.d: Tubuloglomerular feedback is a renal mechanism relating to GFR and sodium delivery, not the systemic autonomic reflex.
explanations.e: The Frank-Starling mechanism relates to the relationship between ventricular end-diastolic volume and stroke volume.

ankiCards: The {{c1::baroreceptor reflex}} is the primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis.
Sensory input for the baroreceptor reflex originates in the {{c1::carotid sinus}} and aorta.
The baroreceptor reflex sends sensory input to the {{c1::vasomotor center}}.
Output from the baroreceptor reflex is carried via the {{c1::parasympathetic}} and sympathetic motor nerves.
Lowering blood pressure often triggers a compensatory {{c1::reflex tachycardia}} via the baroreceptor reflex.
keyPoints: The baroreceptor reflex provides rapid, beat-to-beat BP regulation.
It senses changes in arterial wall stretch.
Sensors are located in the carotid sinus and the aortic arch.
The brainstem vasomotor center processes the input.
Autonomic adjustments involve both the heart and peripheral resistance.
microReview: Homeostasis of blood pressure is largely maintained by the baroreceptor reflex, which detects pressure changes and modulates autonomic output to correct them, often causing reflex heart rate changes when peripheral resistance drops.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse the baroreceptor reflex (fast, autonomic) with the RAAS (slower, endocrine/hormonal) response to low blood pressure.
sourceQuote: Baroreceptor reflex: Primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis; involves sensory input from carotid sinus and aorta to the vasomotor center

stem: Which of the following transport mechanisms is specifically responsible for moving catecholamines from the neural cytoplasm into the storage vesicles within the nerve terminal?

explanations.a: The NET, or catecholamine reuptake pump, moves norepinephrine from the synaptic cleft back into the neural cytoplasm.
explanations.b: The VMAT, or catecholamine vesicle pump, transports catecholamines from the cytoplasm into storage vesicles.
explanations.c: The Na+/K+ ATPase maintains the resting membrane potential and is not specific to catecholamine storage.
explanations.d: Choline acetyltransferase is an enzyme involved in the synthesis of acetylcholine.
explanations.e: MAO is an enzyme that degrades catecholamines in the cytoplasm, not a transporter.

ankiCards: The {{c1::catecholamine vesicle pump}} is also known as VMAT.
{{c1::VMAT}} pumps catecholamines from the neural cytoplasm into storage vesicles.
The catecholamine reuptake pump is also called {{c1::NET}} (norepinephrine transporter).
NET is responsible for recycling norepinephrine after release into the {{c1::synapse}}.
Reserpine is a drug that inhibits the {{c1::catecholamine vesicle pump (VMAT)}}.
keyPoints: NET (Norepinephrine Transporter) handles reuptake from the synapse.
VMAT (Vesicle Monoamine Transporter) handles storage within vesicles.
VMAT can be blocked by drugs like reserpine.
Effective neurotransmission requires sequestration of catecholamines into vesicles.
Cytoplasmic catecholamines not sequestered are subject to degradation by MAO.
microReview: Catecholamine handling involves two main transporters: NET for reuptake from the synapse (recycling) and VMAT (vesicle pump) for sequestration into vesicles for future release.
examinerTraps: Students often swap the functions of NET and VMAT. Remember: NET is 'External' (reuptake from outside), VMAT is 'Vesicular' (storage inside).
sourceQuote: Catecholamine vesicle pump: Storage vesicle transporter that pumps catecholamine from neural cytoplasm into the storage vesicle; also called vesicle monoamine transporter (VMAT)

stem: A 64-year-old female is brought to the emergency department with a severe headache, confusion, and blurry vision. Her blood pressure is 210/130 mm Hg. Fundoscopic examination reveals retinal hemorrhages and papilledema. Urinalysis shows proteinuria and red cell casts. Which of the following terms best describes this clinical presentation?

explanations.a: Essential hypertension is hypertension without a known cause, usually chronic and not implying the acute severity seen here.
explanations.b: Stage 1 hypertension is much lower in pressure (130-139/80-89).
explanations.c: Primary hypertension is a synonym for essential hypertension.
explanations.d: Hypertensive emergency is characterized by severe hypertension with rapidly progressing end-organ damage (e.g., encephalopathy, retinal hemorrhage, renal damage).
explanations.e: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in blood pressure upon standing, the opposite of the current presentation.

ankiCards: A {{c1::hypertensive emergency}} is severe hypertension associated with rapidly progressing damage to vessels and end organs.
Signs of end-organ damage in hypertensive emergency include encephalopathy, stroke, and {{c1::retinal hemorrhages}}.
Hypertensive emergency was historically called {{c1::malignant}} hypertension.
Renal damage and {{c1::angina}} are common clinical signals of a hypertensive emergency.
Diminished perfusion to the heart, kidney, or brain due to vascular damage is called {{c1::end-organ damage}}.
keyPoints: Hypertensive emergency requires immediate but controlled BP reduction.
Presence of end-organ damage defines 'emergency' vs 'urgency'.
End-organs include the brain, heart, kidneys, and eyes.
Retinal hemorrhages are a classic sign of 'malignant' progression.
Common complications include stroke, MI, and renal failure.
microReview: Hypertensive emergency involves extremely high blood pressure coupled with acute target organ damage. This is a medical emergency requiring parenteral antihypertensive therapy.
examinerTraps: Do not select 'Stage 2' simply because the BP is high; if there is active organ damage (confusion, retinal bleeds), the more specific and urgent term 'Hypertensive emergency' is correct.
sourceQuote: Hypertensive emergency: An accelerated form of severe hypertension associated with rising blood pressure and rapidly progressing damage to vessels and end organs.

stem: Which of the following drug classes acts as a sympathoplegic by specifically blocking the central nervous system (CNS) sympathetic outflow to lower blood pressure?

explanations.a: ACE inhibitors work on the renin-angiotensin system in the periphery.
explanations.b: Calcium channel blockers work on vascular smooth muscle and the heart.
explanations.c: Drugs like clonidine (alpha-2 agonists) act on the CNS to reduce sympathetic outflow.
explanations.d: ARBs (e.g., losartan) block angiotensin receptors in the periphery.
explanations.e: Direct vasodilators (e.g., hydralazine) act directly on vascular smooth muscle.

ankiCards: {{c1::Clonidine}} is a sympathoplegic drug that blocks CNS sympathetic outflow.
Sympathoplegics can act at the CNS, ganglia, nerve terminals, or {{c1::receptors}}.
A drug that blocks transmission at the terminals of postganglionic nerves is a {{c1::postganglionic neuron blocker}}.
Prazosin and propranolol are examples of sympathoplegics that block {{c1::alpha or beta receptors}}.
{{c1::Hexamethonium}} is an example of a drug that acts at the ganglia to block sympathetic transmission.
keyPoints: Sympathoplegics reduce blood pressure by decreasing sympathetic influence.
Sites of action include the CNS (clonidine).
Ganglionic blockers (hexamethonium) are now rarely used.
Nerve terminal blockers include reserpine and guanethidine.
Adrenoceptor blockers include alpha (prazosin) and beta (propranolol) blockers.
microReview: Sympathoplegics are categorized by their site of action: CNS (clonidine), Ganglia (hexamethonium), Nerve Terminals (reserpine), or Receptors (prazosin/propranolol). All aim to reduce sympathetic tone.
examinerTraps: Commonly, students confuse the site of action for clonidine (CNS) with prazosin (Peripheral receptors). Both are sympathoplegics but have different anatomical targets.
sourceQuote: Sympathoplegics—blockers of: CNS sympathetic outflow (clonidine); Nerve terminals (guanethidine, reserpine); Ganglia (hexamethonium)

stem: Which of the following substances acts as a 'false transmitter' by being stored in synaptic vesicles and released into the cleft, but lacking the effectiveness of norepinephrine?

explanations.a: Dopamine is a functional catecholamine and a precursor to norepinephrine.
explanations.b: Octopamine is a classic example of a false transmitter that displaces norepinephrine but has little effect on receptors.
explanations.c: Serotonin is an active neurotransmitter in the CNS and periphery, not a false transmitter of the sympathetic system.
explanations.d: Epinephrine is a highly potent endogenous catecholamine.
explanations.e: Isoproterenol is a potent synthetic beta-agonist, not a false transmitter.

ankiCards: {{c1::Octopamine}} is an example of a false transmitter.
A {{c1::false transmitter}} is stored in vesicles but lacks the effectiveness of norepinephrine.
False transmitters are released into the {{c1::synaptic cleft}} upon nerve stimulation.
The use of certain drugs can lead to the accumulation of {{c1::false transmitters}} in sympathetic nerves.
False transmitters compete with {{c1::norepinephrine}} for storage in vesicles.
keyPoints: False transmitters displace the real neurotransmitter from vesicles.
They are released like normal transmitters but fail to activate receptors effectively.
Octopamine is the most frequently cited example.
This process results in a net decrease in sympathetic signaling.
It is one mechanism by which certain older antihypertensives functioned.
microReview: False transmitters are 'decoy' molecules that take the place of norepinephrine in vesicles but don't work at the synapse, leading to reduced sympathetic response.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse a 'false transmitter' (like octopamine) with a 'receptor blocker' (like prazosin). One prevents the signal from being 'sent' effectively; the other prevents it from being 'received'.
sourceQuote: False transmitter: Substance, for example, octopamine, stored in vesicles and released into synaptic cleft but lacking the effectiveness of the true transmitter, norepinephrine

stem: Which of the following drug classes is most directly associated with the compensatory development of reflex tachycardia as a result of its primary pharmacological action?

explanations.a: Beta-blockers lower heart rate and would actually prevent reflex tachycardia.
explanations.b: Direct vasodilators lower blood pressure, which triggers the baroreceptor reflex, leading to a compensatory increase in heart rate (reflex tachycardia).
explanations.c: ACE inhibitors have a lower incidence of reflex tachycardia compared to direct vasodilators.
explanations.d: Centrally acting alpha-2 agonists (like clonidine) decrease sympathetic outflow, suppressing heart rate.
explanations.e: Ganglionic blockers inhibit the reflex arc itself by blocking the ganglia, preventing reflex tachycardia.

ankiCards: {{c1::Reflex tachycardia}} results from the lowering of blood pressure via the baroreceptor reflex.
Direct {{c1::vasodilators}} are highly likely to cause reflex tachycardia.
Reflex tachycardia is mediated by an increase in {{c1::sympathetic}} activity to the heart.
Beta-blockers are often used to suppress {{c1::reflex tachycardia}} caused by other drugs.
{{c1::Nitroprusside}} is an example of a parenteral vasodilator that can trigger reflex responses.
keyPoints: Reflex tachycardia is a compensatory response to hypotension.
It is mediated by the baroreceptor reflex.
Vasodilators that act directly on vessels often trigger this response.
This can limit the antihypertensive efficacy of the drug.
Co-administration with a beta-blocker often manages this side effect.
microReview: Vasodilation reduces peripheral resistance and blood pressure, causing the baroreceptors to signal the brain to increase heart rate (reflex tachycardia) to maintain cardiac output.
examinerTraps: Remember that ganglionic blockers (like hexamethonium) *prevent* reflex tachycardia because they block the signal from the CNS to the heart at the nicotinic receptors in the ganglia.
sourceQuote: Reflex tachycardia: Tachycardia resulting from lowering of blood pressure; mediated by the baroreceptor reflex

stem: A 28-year-old woman is evaluated for hypertension. Her blood pressure is consistently 165/105 mm Hg. Physical exam reveals a bruit over the right renal artery. Laboratory studies show elevated plasma renin activity. Which of the following terms best describes her hypertension?

explanations.a: Essential hypertension is defined as hypertension of unknown etiology.
explanations.b: Primary hypertension is another name for essential hypertension.
explanations.c: Secondary hypertension is caused by a diagnosable abnormality, such as renal artery stenosis.
explanations.d: Elevated blood pressure refers to a specific range (120-129 SBP) and is not a descriptive category for the cause.
explanations.e: Malignant hypertension involves severe BP with end-organ damage; while this patient's BP is high, the focus of the question is the etiology (bruit).

ankiCards: Hypertension caused by a diagnosable abnormality is called {{c1::secondary}} hypertension.
Hypertension of unknown etiology is called {{c1::essential}} or primary hypertension.
Renal artery stenosis is a common cause of {{c1::secondary}} hypertension.
{{c1::Aortic coarctation}} is a mechanical cause of secondary hypertension.
Primary hypertension is also known as {{c1::essential}} hypertension.
keyPoints: Most hypertension (90-95%) is primary/essential.
Secondary hypertension should be suspected in young patients or resistant cases.
Renal artery stenosis causes high renin levels.
Treatment involves addressing the underlying cause.
Physical signs like bruits or pulse discrepancies point toward secondary causes.
microReview: Primary (essential) hypertension has no single identifiable cause. Secondary hypertension results from a specific underlying condition (e.g., renal artery stenosis, pheochromocytoma, or coarctation of the aorta).
examinerTraps: A bruit and high renin in a young person are classic 'red flags' for secondary hypertension. Don't label it 'essential' just because it's high blood pressure.
sourceQuote: Secondary hypertension: Hypertension caused by a diagnosable abnormality, eg, aortic coarctation, renal artery stenosis

stem: Which of the following mechanisms best explains 'orthostatic hypotension' experienced by patients on certain antihypertensive medications?

options.a: Excessive activation of the renin-angiotensin system
options.b: Failure of the baroreceptor reflex to compensate for posture changes
options.d: Inhibition of the catecholamine vesicle pump
options.e: Reduced blood volume due to excessive water intake

explanations.a: RAAS activation would help maintain blood pressure, not cause hypotension.
explanations.b: Orthostatic (postural) hypotension occurs when the autonomic system (baroreceptor reflex) fails to constrict vessels sufficiently upon standing.
explanations.c: Increased catecholamine reuptake would decrease sympathetic tone but is not the primary mechanism of postural drops.
explanations.d: VMAT inhibition (e.g., reserpine) can cause orthostatic hypotension, but it is through the failure of sympathetic transmission, not the transporter action itself.
explanations.e: Reduced blood volume causes hypotension, but it is caused by low intake or high loss, not excessive intake.

ankiCards: {{c1::Orthostatic}} hypotension is defined as a drop in blood pressure when assuming an upright posture.
Another term for orthostatic hypotension is {{c1::postural}} hypotension.
Many sympathoplegic drugs cause orthostatic hypotension by interfering with the {{c1::baroreceptor}} reflex.
Assuming an upright posture normally causes gravity-induced venous {{c1::pooling}}.
The baroreceptor reflex maintains blood pressure during posture changes by increasing {{c1::sympathetic}} tone.
keyPoints: Standing up causes blood to pool in the lower extremities.
The baroreceptor reflex normally counteracts this via vasoconstriction and increased HR.
Drugs that block sympathetic nerves or receptors impair this response.
Symptoms include dizziness, lightheadedness, or syncope.
Common in the elderly and those on alpha-blockers.
microReview: Orthostatic hypotension happens when the body's rapid autonomic response (baroreceptor reflex) to the gravitational shift of blood is blunted, often by antihypertensive drugs that block sympathetic output.
examinerTraps: Distinguish between reflex tachycardia (a response to low BP) and orthostatic hypotension (a failure to maintain BP). They often occur together with vasodilators.
sourceQuote: Orthostatic hypotension: Hypotension on assuming upright posture; postural hypotension

stem: Which of the following antihypertensive drug classes works by specifically inhibiting the enzyme responsible for converting Angiotensin I to the potent vasoconstrictor Angiotensin II?

explanations.a: Diuretics lower blood pressure by increasing sodium and water excretion.
explanations.b: ACE inhibitors (e.g., captopril) inhibit Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme, preventing the formation of Angiotensin II.
explanations.c: ARBs (e.g., losartan) block the binding of Angiotensin II to its receptor.
explanations.d: Renin inhibitors (e.g., aliskiren) inhibit the enzymatic activity of renin itself.
explanations.e: Calcium channel blockers inhibit the entry of calcium into muscle cells to cause vasodilation.

ankiCards: Captopril is an example of an {{c1::ACE inhibitor}}.
Losartan is an example of an {{c1::Angiotensin antagonist (ARB)}}.
Aliskiren is an example of a {{c1::Renin inhibitor}}.
ACE inhibitors prevent the formation of {{c1::Angiotensin II}}.
The RAAS system is a major target for drugs used in {{c1::hypertension}}.
keyPoints: The RAAS pathway: Renin -> Angiotensin I -> Angiotensin II.
Renin inhibitors (Aliskiren) block the first step.
ACE inhibitors (Captopril) block the conversion step.
ARBs (Losartan) block the final receptor interaction.
All three classes effectively reduce the vasoconstrictive effects of Angiotensin II.
microReview: Drugs targeting the Renin-Angiotensin system work at different stages: Aliskiren (Renin inhibitor), ACE inhibitors (Captopril), and ARBs (Losartan). Each reduces Angiotensin II activity differently.
examinerTraps: Carefully read if the question asks for the drug that 'prevents formation' (ACE inhibitor) versus the drug that 'blocks the receptor' (ARB).
sourceQuote: Angiotensin antagonists: Receptor blockers (losartan). ACE inhibitors (captopril). Renin inhibitor (aliskiren).

stem: A 54-year-old male with a history of obesity and a sedentary lifestyle presents for a routine physical examination. His blood pressure, measured on three separate occasions during the visit, averages 146/92 mm Hg. He reports no headaches, visual changes, or chest pain. Which of the following best describes this patient's cardiovascular status?

explanations.a: Elevated blood pressure is defined as a systolic pressure between 120 and 129 mm Hg with a diastolic pressure less than 80 mm Hg.
explanations.b: Stage 1 hypertension is defined as a systolic pressure between 130 and 139 mm Hg or a diastolic pressure between 80 and 89 mm Hg.
explanations.c: Stage 2 hypertension is defined as a systolic pressure equal to or greater than 140 mm Hg or a diastolic pressure equal to or greater than 90 mm Hg.
explanations.d: Hypertensive emergency requires an accelerated form of severe hypertension associated with rapidly progressing end-organ damage, such as renal failure or encephalopathy, which is not present in this asymptomatic patient.
explanations.e: Normal blood pressure is defined as less than 120/80 mm Hg.

ankiCards: Stage 2 hypertension is defined as a systolic blood pressure ≥{{c1::140}} mm Hg or a diastolic pressure ≥{{c1::90}} mm Hg.
Elevated blood pressure is defined as systolic {{c1::120-129}} mm Hg and diastolic <{{c1::80}} mm Hg.
Stage 1 hypertension is defined as systolic {{c1::130-139}} mm Hg or diastolic {{c1::80-89}} mm Hg.
The primary risk factors for lethal cardiovascular conditions including MI and stroke involve {{c1::hypertension}}.
Hypertensive emergency is characterized by severe hypertension with evidence of {{c1::end-organ damage}}.
keyPoints: Blood pressure categories are determined by the higher of the systolic or diastolic value.
Stage 2 hypertension begins at 140/90 mm Hg.
Stage 1 hypertension begins at 130/80 mm Hg.
Elevated blood pressure is a precursor to hypertension, starting at 120 systolic.
Hypertension is a major risk factor for myocardial infarction, heart failure, and stroke.
microReview: Blood pressure classification: Normal (<120/80), Elevated (120-129/<80), Stage 1 (130-139/80-89), Stage 2 (≥140/≥90). Stage 2 requires treatment in most patients.
examinerTraps: A common mistake is using the older 140/90 threshold for Stage 1; the 2017 guidelines lowered the thresholds, making 140/90 the start of Stage 2.
sourceQuote: average systolic pressure greater than 120 but less than 130 mm Hg is considered elevated, pressure equal to or greater than 130/80 mm Hg but less than 140/89 is considered stage 1 hypertension, while pressures equal to or greater than 140/90 are considered stage 2 hypertension.

stem: A pharmacological agent is administered that significantly decreases peripheral vascular resistance. Shortly thereafter, the patient's heart rate increases significantly. This compensatory response is primarily mediated by which of the following physiological components?

explanations.a: The nerve terminal transporter (NET) is responsible for recycling norepinephrine, not for the reflex increase in heart rate.
explanations.b: The vesicle monoamine transporter (VMAT) pumps catecholamines into storage vesicles and does not mediate systemic homeostatic reflexes.
explanations.c: The baroreceptor reflex is the primary mechanism for BP homeostasis; it involves sensory input to the vasomotor center and motor output via sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves to adjust heart rate in response to BP changes.
explanations.d: While the RAAS affects blood pressure long-term, the rapid, acute increase in heart rate in response to falling BP is mediated by the baroreceptor reflex.
explanations.e: Postganglionic neuron blockers inhibit transmission, which would prevent rather than cause a reflex increase in heart rate.

ankiCards: The primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis is the {{c1::baroreceptor reflex}}.
Reflex tachycardia is a response to lowering blood pressure mediated by the {{c1::baroreceptor reflex}}.
Sensory input for the baroreceptor reflex originates in the {{c1::carotid sinus}} and {{c1::aorta}}.
The {{c1::vasomotor center}} receives baroreceptor input and coordinates autonomic output.
Autonomic output for BP homeostasis is carried by the {{c1::parasympathetic}} and {{c1::sympathetic}} nerves.
keyPoints: Baroreceptor reflex provides acute homeostasis for blood pressure.
Lowering BP triggers a reduction in baroreceptor firing.
The result is reflex tachycardia and increased sympathetic tone.
The sensory organs are the carotid sinus and the aortic arch.
The integration center is the vasomotor center in the brainstem.
microReview: Baroreceptor Reflex: Low BP -> Vasomotor Center -> Increased Sympathetic/Decreased Parasympathetic output -> Reflex Tachycardia.
examinerTraps: Distinguish between the receptor (carotid sinus/aorta) and the effector (sympathetic nerves) or the mediator (baroreceptor reflex).
sourceQuote: Baroreceptor reflex: Primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis; involves sensory input from carotid sinus and aorta to the vasomotor center and output via the parasympathetic and sympathetic motor nerves

stem: Which of the following proteins is specifically responsible for the transport of catecholamines from the neural cytoplasm into storage vesicles within the nerve terminal?

explanations.a: The norepinephrine transporter (NET), or catecholamine reuptake pump, moves norepinephrine from the synapse back into the cytoplasm.
explanations.b: The vesicle monoamine transporter (VMAT), or catecholamine vesicle pump, moves catecholamines from the cytoplasm into the storage vesicles.
explanations.c: AChT is involved in cholinergic transmission, not catecholamine transport.
explanations.d: This is another name for NET, which moves substances across the plasma membrane, not the vesicle membrane.
explanations.e: The ganglionic nicotinic receptor is involved in signal transmission at the ganglia, not intracellular transport.

ankiCards: The catecholamine vesicle pump is also known as {{c1::VMAT (vesicle monoamine transporter)}}.
{{c1::VMAT}} pumps catecholamine from neural cytoplasm into storage vesicles.
The catecholamine reuptake pump is also known as {{c1::NET (norepinephrine transporter)}}.
{{c1::NET}} is responsible for recycling norepinephrine after release into the synapse.
Storage vesicles release neurotransmitters into the {{c1::synaptic cleft}}.
keyPoints: VMAT is the vesicle pump (cytoplasm to vesicle).
NET is the reuptake pump (synapse to cytoplasm).
Both are critical for adrenergic nerve terminal function.
Drugs like reserpine target the vesicle pump.
Inhibition of these pumps alters neurotransmitter availability.
microReview: Transporter comparison: NET = Synapse to Cytoplasm (Recycling). VMAT = Cytoplasm to Vesicle (Storage).
examinerTraps: Confusing NET and VMAT is common. Remember 'V' for Vesicle.
sourceQuote: Catecholamine vesicle pump: Storage vesicle transporter that pumps catecholamine from neural cytoplasm into the storage vesicle; also called vesicle monoamine transporter (VMAT)

stem: A 62-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with a sudden onset of confusion and blurred vision. Her blood pressure is 210/130 mm Hg. Fundoscopic examination reveals retinal hemorrhages and papilledema. Urinalysis shows proteinuria and red blood cell casts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.a: While the BP is in the range of Stage 2, the presence of acute end-organ damage (encephalopathy, retinal hemorrhage, renal damage) elevates the diagnosis to an emergency.
explanations.b: Secondary hypertension refers to hypertension with a diagnosable cause (like renal artery stenosis), which may or may not be an emergency.
explanations.c: Hypertensive emergency is defined by severe hypertension with rapidly progressing damage to end organs like the brain, retina, and kidneys.
explanations.d: Reflex tachycardia is a physiological response to BP lowering, not a diagnosis for severe BP elevation.
explanations.e: Rebound hypertension occurs upon sudden withdrawal of antihypertensive medication, but 'hypertensive emergency' better describes the current clinical severity.
explanations.f: Essential hypertension is hypertension of unknown etiology and typically follows a chronic, non-emergency course.

ankiCards: An accelerated form of severe hypertension with rapidly progressing end-organ damage is called {{c1::hypertensive emergency}}.
Common signs of end-organ damage in hypertensive emergency include {{c1::encephalopathy}}, {{c1::retinal hemorrhages}}, and {{c1::renal damage}}.
Hypertensive emergency was historically called {{c1::malignant hypertension}}.
End-organ damage results from diminished {{c1::perfusion}} due to vascular damage.
Clinical signals of hypertensive emergency include {{c1::angina}}, {{c1::stroke}}, or {{c1::myocardial infarction}}.
keyPoints: Hypertensive emergency involves acute BP elevation + end-organ damage.
End organs include the brain, heart, kidneys, and eyes.
Encephalopathy and retinal hemorrhage are classic indicators.
It requires immediate, usually parenteral, intervention.
It was formerly known as 'malignant' hypertension.
microReview: Hypertensive Emergency: High BP + End-organ damage (Brain/Heart/Kidney/Retina). Requires rapid controlled BP reduction.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'Hypertensive Urgency' (High BP, no damage) with 'Hypertensive Emergency' (High BP + damage). Only the latter is described by the provided signs.
sourceQuote: Hypertensive emergency: An accelerated form of severe hypertension associated with rising blood pressure and rapidly progressing damage to vessels and end organs. Often signaled by renal damage, encephalopathy, and retinal hemorrhages

stem: A patient is treated with a drug that leads to the accumulation of octopamine within sympathetic storage vesicles. Octopamine is released into the synaptic cleft upon nerve stimulation but produces a significantly weaker effect on postjunctional receptors compared to norepinephrine. Octopamine is best classified as which of the following?

explanations.a: Postganglionic neuron blockers inhibit the release or transmission directly but do not necessarily involve the storage of a weak replacement substance.
explanations.b: A nerve terminal transporter is a protein (like NET) used for reuptake, not the substance itself.
explanations.c: A false transmitter is a substance like octopamine that is stored and released like the true transmitter (norepinephrine) but lacks its physiological effectiveness.
explanations.d: The catecholamine vesicle pump is the transporter (VMAT), not the chemical stored.
explanations.e: Octopamine in this context is a byproduct of pharmacological interference, not an agent causing secondary hypertension.

ankiCards: A substance stored in vesicles and released but lacking the effectiveness of norepinephrine is a {{c1::false transmitter}}.

stem: A 54-year-old male is initiated on hydralazine for the management of resistant hypertension. Three days later, he returns to the clinic complaining of palpitations and a racing heart. Physical examination reveals a blood pressure of 138/88 mmHg and a heart rate of 118 beats per minute. Which of the following physiological processes is most likely responsible for his increased heart rate?

options.b: Inhibition of the catecholamine reuptake pump
options.c: Direct stimulation of the sinoatrial node
options.d: Blockade of the catecholamine vesicle pump
options.e: Activation of the parasympathetic motor nerves

explanations.a: Hydralazine is a vasodilator that lowers blood pressure, which triggers the baroreceptor reflex. This compensatory mechanism increases sympathetic output to the heart, causing reflex tachycardia.
explanations.b: Inhibition of the reuptake pump (NET) would increase synaptic norepinephrine but is not the primary mechanism of tachycardia induced by vasodilators.
explanations.c: Hydralazine does not have direct agonist activity on the sinoatrial node; the tachycardia is a secondary reflex response.
explanations.d: Blockade of the vesicle pump (VMAT), as seen with reserpine, would deplete catecholamines and typically leads to bradycardia, not tachycardia.
explanations.e: The baroreceptor reflex in response to low blood pressure involves a decrease in parasympathetic output and an increase in sympathetic output.

examinerTraps: A common mistake is assuming the drug directly stimulates the heart; remember the tachycardia is a compensatory 'reflex' to the drop in blood pressure.
