keyPoints: 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines lowered the threshold for hypertension.
Elevated BP: 120-129 / <80.
Systolic blood pressure carries significant prognostic weight for cardiovascular risk.
Early intervention is urged for both stage 1 and stage 2 patients.
microReview: Hypertension classification changed in 2017 to promote earlier intervention. Stage 1 starts at 130/80, whereas Stage 2 starts at 140/90. 'Elevated' BP is a pre-hypertensive state starting at 120 systolic.
examinerTraps: Students often confuse the 2017 Stage 1 threshold (130/80) with the old JNC 7 threshold (140/90).
sourceQuote: According to the 2017 guidelines, average systolic pressure greater than 120 but less than 130 mm Hg is considered elevated, pressure equal to or greater than 130/80 mm Hg but less than 140/89 is considered stage 1 hypertension

stem: A pharmacologist is studying a drug that inhibits the vesicle monoamine transporter (VMAT). This mechanism directly interferes with the storage of norepinephrine in the nerve terminals. Which of the following terms best describes the physiological phenomenon where blood pressure drops significantly when a patient moves from a supine to a standing position, a common side effect of drugs acting on sympathetic nerve terminals?

explanations.a: Reflex tachycardia is the heart's compensatory increase in rate in response to a drop in BP, not the drop itself.
explanations.b: Rebound hypertension is the elevation of BP above baseline following the abrupt cessation of an antihypertensive drug.
explanations.c: Orthostatic hypotension (or postural hypotension) is defined as a drop in blood pressure upon assuming an upright posture, often caused by sympathoplegic drugs.
explanations.d: Hypertensive emergency involves severely elevated BP with evidence of acute end-organ damage.
explanations.e: The baroreceptor reflex is the homeostatic mechanism that normally prevents orthostatic hypotension; its failure or inhibition leads to the condition.

ankiCards: {{c1::Orthostatic hypotension}} is defined as hypotension occurring when assuming an upright posture.
The catecholamine vesicle pump is also known as {{c1::VMAT (vesicle monoamine transporter)}}.
VMAT is responsible for pumping catecholamines from the {{c1::neural cytoplasm}} into {{c2::storage vesicles}}.
Drugs that block sympathetic nerve terminals often cause {{c1::postural/orthostatic}} hypotension.
The {{c1::baroreceptor reflex}} is the primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis.
keyPoints: VMAT (Vesicle Monoamine Transporter) stores NE in vesicles.
Inhibition of NE storage leads to decreased sympathetic tone.
Orthostatic hypotension is a failure of the baroreceptor-mediated compensation for gravity-induced venous pooling.
Sympathoplegic drugs commonly disrupt this postural response.
Postganglionic neuron blockers act at the nerve terminal level.
microReview: Orthostatic hypotension occurs when drugs (like Reserpine or Guanethidine) interfere with the sympathetic nervous system's ability to constrict vessels quickly upon standing. This is a hallmark of sympathoplegic agents.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the mechanism (VMAT inhibition) with the clinical sign (Orthostatic hypotension) or the compensatory response (Reflex tachycardia).
sourceQuote: Orthostatic hypotension: Hypotension on assuming upright posture; postural hypotension... Catecholamine vesicle pump: Storage vesicle transporter that pumps catecholamine from neural cytoplasm into the storage vesicle

stem: A 54-year-old male presents to the clinic for a routine check-up. He has no symptoms but his blood pressure today is 145/95 mm Hg. A repeat measurement ten minutes later is 142/92 mm Hg. According to the 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines, which of the following best describes this patient's condition and the recommended initial approach?

options.a: Elevated blood pressure; lifestyle modification only
options.c: Stage 1 hypertension; lifestyle modification and consider pharmacotherapy
options.d: Stage 2 hypertension; lifestyle modification and pharmacotherapy

explanations.a: Elevated BP is 120-129 systolic; this patient is significantly higher.
explanations.b: Stage 1 ends at 139/89; this patient is at 142/92.
explanations.c: Stage 1 ends at 139/89; this patient's BP is ≥140/90.
explanations.d: Pressure equal to or greater than 140/90 mm Hg is considered Stage 2 hypertension. Both stage 1 and 2 are deserving of treatment.
explanations.e: The patient is asymptomatic and does not show signs of end-organ damage, so this is not a hypertensive emergency.

ankiCards: Stage 2 hypertension starts at a blood pressure of {{c1::140/90}} mm Hg.
According to 2017 guidelines, Stage 2 hypertension warrants {{c1::lifestyle modification}} and {{c2::pharmacotherapy}}.
{{c1::Systolic}} pressure is considered at least as important as diastolic in the 2017 guidelines.
The 2017 guidelines urge more active {{c1::prevention}} and {{c2::treatment}} of hypertension.
A blood pressure of 145/95 is classified as {{c1::Stage 2}} hypertension.
keyPoints: Stage 2 hypertension is defined as ≥140/90 mm Hg.
Management of Stage 2 usually requires immediate initiation of medication.
Asymptomatic high BP is not a hypertensive emergency.
Repeat measurements are necessary for diagnosis.
Lifestyle modifications are universal for all stages of hypertension.
microReview: Stage 2 hypertension (≥140/90) requires more aggressive management than Stage 1 (130-139/80-89). The patient's reading of 142/92 places him squarely in Stage 2.
examinerTraps: The trap is using the old Stage 1 definition (140/90). In the current guidelines, 140/90 is already Stage 2.
sourceQuote: while pressures equal to or greater than 140/90 are considered stage 2 hypertension... Both stage 1 and stage 2 hypertension are deserving of treatment

stem: Which of the following describes the mechanism of a 'false transmitter' in the context of antihypertensive therapy?

options.a: A drug that blocks the alpha-1 receptor directly on the vascular smooth muscle
options.b: A substance stored in vesicles and released but lacks the efficacy of norepinephrine
options.c: A molecule that prevents the reuptake of norepinephrine into the nerve terminal
options.d: A peptide that inhibits the conversion of Angiotensin I to Angiotensin II
options.e: A ligand that binds to central alpha-2 receptors to reduce sympathetic outflow

explanations.a: This describes alpha-blockers like prazosin.
explanations.b: A false transmitter (e.g., octopamine) is stored in vesicles and released into the synaptic cleft but does not trigger the same effective response as the true transmitter, norepinephrine.
explanations.c: This describes the action of the catecholamine reuptake pump (NET), or drugs that inhibit it (like cocaine/TCAs).
explanations.d: This describes ACE inhibitors like captopril.
explanations.e: This describes central sympathoplegics like clonidine.

ankiCards: A {{c1::false transmitter}} is a substance stored in vesicles that lacks the effectiveness of norepinephrine.
An example of a false transmitter is {{c1::octopamine}}.
False transmitters are released into the {{c1::synaptic cleft}}.
False transmitters compete with {{c1::norepinephrine}} for storage in vesicles.
Antihypertensive effects of some drugs are mediated by the production of {{c1::false transmitters}}.
keyPoints: False transmitters are stored and released like normal neurotransmitters.
They have significantly lower potency at the postsynaptic receptor.
Octopamine is the classic example.
This process displaces normal norepinephrine from the synapse.
It represents a unique mechanism within the sympathoplegic class.
microReview: False transmitters 'trick' the neuron into releasing a dud signal. They are packaged into vesicles instead of NE but don't activate the receptors effectively, leading to reduced sympathetic activity.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse false transmitters with competitive antagonists. Antagonists block the receptor; false transmitters are released from the presynaptic neuron.
sourceQuote: False transmitter: Substance, for example, octopamine, stored in vesicles and released into synaptic cleft but lacking the effectiveness of the true transmitter, norepinephrine

stem: A 62-year-old woman with a history of chronic hypertension is brought to the emergency department with a severe headache, confusion, and blurry vision. Her blood pressure is 210/130 mm Hg. Fundoscopy reveals retinal hemorrhages. Which of the following terms best describes this clinical presentation?

explanations.a: While her BP is high enough to be Stage 2, the presence of end-organ damage (retinal hemorrhages, encephalopathy) upgrades the diagnosis.
explanations.b: Essential hypertension refers to the etiology (unknown), not the severity of the presentation.
explanations.c: Hypertensive emergency is characterized by severe hypertension with rapidly progressing damage to end organs like the retina, brain, or kidneys.
explanations.d: Secondary hypertension refers to a known cause (e.g., renal artery stenosis), which is not specified here.
explanations.e: Rebound hypertension is a withdrawal phenomenon, not defined by end-organ damage in the primary definition.

ankiCards: {{c1::Hypertensive emergency}} is severe hypertension associated with rapidly progressing damage to vessels and end organs.
Common signs of a hypertensive emergency include {{c1::encephalopathy}}, {{c2::retinal hemorrhages}}, and {{c3::renal damage}}.
Hypertensive emergency is also known as {{c1::malignant hypertension}}.
An accelerated form of severe hypertension signaled by stroke or MI is a {{c1::hypertensive emergency}}.
End-organ damage in the {{c1::retina}} can be visualized via fundoscopy during a hypertensive crisis.
keyPoints: Hypertensive emergency requires BP >180/120 AND end-organ damage.
End-organs include brain, heart, kidneys, and eyes.
Malignant hypertension is an older term for the same phenomenon.
It represents a medical emergency requiring parenteral treatment.
Retinal hemorrhages are a pathognomonic finding for 'malignant' severity.
microReview: Hypertensive emergency = Very high BP + end-organ damage (stroke, MI, renal failure, or retinopathy). Stage 2 is just a BP number (≥140/90).
examinerTraps: The examiner provides high BP numbers and asks for the diagnosis. Look specifically for end-organ damage (confusion, vision loss) to differentiate Stage 2 from an Emergency.
sourceQuote: Hypertensive emergency (“malignant hypertension”): An accelerated form of severe hypertension associated with rising blood pressure and rapidly progressing damage to vessels and end organs.

stem: A new antihypertensive drug is designed to target the primary autonomic mechanism responsible for blood pressure homeostasis. This mechanism involves sensory input from the carotid sinus and aorta to the vasomotor center. What is the name of this mechanism?

explanations.a: The catecholamine reuptake pump (NET) recycles NE but is not a reflex arc involving the carotid sinus.
explanations.b: The renin-angiotensin system is a hormonal system, not the primary autonomic reflex arc.
explanations.c: The baroreceptor reflex is the primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis via the carotid sinus, aorta, and vasomotor center.
explanations.d: Postganglionic blockade refers to a drug's action site, not the homeostatic reflex itself.
explanations.e: The catecholamine vesicle pump (VMAT) handles intracellular storage of NE.

ankiCards: The {{c1::baroreceptor reflex}} is the primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis.
Sensory input for the baroreceptor reflex comes from the {{c1::carotid sinus}} and {{c2::aorta}}.
The baroreceptor reflex sends output via {{c1::parasympathetic}} and {{c2::sympathetic}} motor nerves.
The {{c1::vasomotor center}} receives input from the baroreceptors to regulate blood pressure.
{{c1::Reflex tachycardia}} results when the baroreceptor reflex compensates for a drop in blood pressure.
keyPoints: Baroreceptors are stretch receptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch.
They provide the rapid, second-to-second regulation of BP.
Vasomotor center in the medulla integrates this information.
Autonomic output (PSNS/SNS) is adjusted to maintain set-point BP.
Many drugs (vasodilators) trigger this reflex, leading to tachycardia.
microReview: The baroreceptor reflex is the body's 'thermostat' for BP. It uses the carotid sinus/aorta as sensors and the vasomotor center as the controller to adjust heart rate and vascular tone.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse the 'catecholamine reuptake pump' (a cellular transporter) with the 'baroreceptor reflex' (a systemic circuit).
sourceQuote: Baroreceptor reflex: Primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis; involves sensory input from carotid sinus and aorta to the vasomotor center

stem: Which of the following best defines the role of the catecholamine reuptake pump (NET) in the sympathetic nerve terminal?

options.a: Pumping norepinephrine from the neural cytoplasm into storage vesicles
options.c: Recycling norepinephrine after its release into the synapse
options.d: Facilitating the release of norepinephrine into the synaptic cleft
options.e: Degrading norepinephrine within the synaptic cleft

explanations.a: This is the function of the catecholamine vesicle pump (VMAT), not NET.
explanations.b: Synthesis is performed by enzymes like dopamine beta-hydroxylase.
explanations.c: The catecholamine reuptake pump (also called norepinephrine transporter or NET) is responsible for recycling norepinephrine after its release.
explanations.d: Release is triggered by calcium-mediated exocytosis.
explanations.e: Degrading in the cleft is handled by enzymes (though mostly NE is recycled), but NET is a transporter, not an enzyme.

ankiCards: The catecholamine reuptake pump is also known as {{c1::NET (norepinephrine transporter)}}.
NET is responsible for {{c1::recycling}} norepinephrine after release.
NET moves norepinephrine from the {{c1::synapse/synaptic cleft}} back into the {{c2::nerve terminal}}.
NET is located on the {{c1::nerve terminal}} membrane.
Blocking {{c1::NET}} would increase the concentration of norepinephrine in the synaptic cleft.
keyPoints: NET (Norepinephrine Transporter) is the 'reuptake' pump.
It terminates the signal by removing NE from the synapse.
It is distinct from VMAT (the vesicle pump).
Drugs that inhibit NET (e.g., cocaine) increase synaptic NE.
It is a crucial target in autonomic pharmacology.
microReview: NET = Reuptake from synapse to cytoplasm. VMAT = Transport from cytoplasm into vesicles. They are the two main 'pumps' in the sympathetic terminal.
examinerTraps: A common mistake is swapping the functions of NET and VMAT. Remember: NET is for 'Netting' the NE back from the synapse; VMAT is for 'Vesicles'.
sourceQuote: Catecholamine reuptake pump: Nerve terminal transporter responsible for recycling norepinephrine after release into the synapse; also called norepinephrine transporter (NET)

stem: A 45-year-old woman is evaluated for a new diagnosis of hypertension. After laboratory testing and imaging, she is found to have significant narrowing of her right renal artery. Which of the following terms correctly classifies her hypertension?

explanations.a: Essential hypertension means the cause is unknown; here, the cause (renal artery stenosis) is known.
explanations.b: Primary hypertension is a synonym for essential hypertension.
explanations.c: Secondary hypertension is hypertension caused by a diagnosable abnormality, such as renal artery stenosis or aortic coarctation.
explanations.d: Malignant hypertension refers to the clinical severity (end-organ damage), not the underlying etiology.
explanations.e: Elevated blood pressure refers to a specific BP range (120-129), not the type/cause of hypertension.

ankiCards: {{c1::Secondary}} hypertension is caused by a diagnosable abnormality (e.g., renal artery stenosis).
{{c1::Essential}} hypertension is of unknown etiology.
Another name for essential hypertension is {{c1::primary}} hypertension.
Aortic coarctation is a cause of {{c1::secondary}} hypertension.
Renal artery stenosis leads to {{c1::secondary}} hypertension.
keyPoints: Most hypertension (90-95%) is primary/essential.
Secondary hypertension has a specific, treatable cause.
Common causes of secondary HTN include renal disease and endocrine disorders.
Aortic coarctation is a classic structural cause.
Identifying secondary causes is vital because they may be curable.
microReview: If you can name the specific medical condition causing the high BP (like renal artery stenosis), it is 'Secondary'. If you can't, it is 'Essential' or 'Primary'.
examinerTraps: The examiner will often provide a clear cause (like a tumor or stenosis) and ask for the classification. Don't pick 'Essential' if a cause is present.
sourceQuote: Secondary hypertension: Hypertension caused by a diagnosable abnormality, eg, aortic coarctation, renal artery stenosis... Essential hypertension: Hypertension of unknown etiology

stem: Which of the following antihypertensive drug classes is correctly matched with its specific drug example as listed in the provided pharmacological classifications?

explanations.a: Losartan is an Angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB), not an ACE inhibitor.
explanations.b: Aliskiren is a Renin inhibitor, not a calcium channel blocker (Nifedipine is an example).
explanations.c: Clonidine is correctly classified as a drug that acts on CNS sympathetic outflow (a central sympathoplegic).
explanations.d: Prazosin is an Alpha receptor blocker, not a ganglion blocker (Hexamethonium is the example).
explanations.e: Captopril is an ACE inhibitor, not a renin inhibitor.

ankiCards: Clonidine acts by reducing {{c1::CNS sympathetic outflow}}.
An example of a Renin inhibitor is {{c1::Aliskiren}}.
An example of a Receptor blocker (Angiotensin antagonist) is {{c1::Losartan}}.
Captopril belongs to the {{c1::ACE inhibitor}} class.
Hexamethonium is a drug that blocks {{c1::ganglia}}.

Clonidine and Methyldopa act in the CNS.

stem: Which of the following terms describes the phenomenon of elevated blood pressure, often exceeding pretreatment levels, following the sudden withdrawal of an antihypertensive medication?

explanations.a: Hypertensive emergency is defined by end-organ damage, not by the cause of the BP spike (though rebound can lead to an emergency).
explanations.b: Rebound hypertension is defined as elevated BP resulting from the loss of an antihypertensive drug's effect, usually after abrupt cessation.
explanations.c: Reflex tachycardia is a heart rate increase, not a BP increase upon drug cessation.
explanations.d: Essential hypertension is a long-term classification of unknown etiology.
explanations.e: Postganglionic blockade is a drug mechanism, not a withdrawal effect.

ankiCards: {{c1::Rebound hypertension}} occurs after the loss of an antihypertensive drug's effect.
Rebound hypertension levels are usually {{c1::above}} pretreatment levels.
Abruptly stopping certain antihypertensives like {{c1::clonidine}} can cause rebound hypertension.
Rebound hypertension is a risk associated with sudden {{c1::withdrawal/cessation}} of therapy.
{{c1::Reflex tachycardia}} is a different concept, involving compensatory HR increase during active drug effect.
keyPoints: Rebound hypertension is a 'withdrawal' phenomenon.
It is commonly associated with central alpha-2 agonists and beta-blockers.
BP can spike to dangerous levels.
Prevention involves tapering the dose of the medication.
It is a distinct term from 'treatment failure'.
microReview: Stop the drug abruptly -> BP shoots up higher than it was before = Rebound Hypertension. This is why many BP meds must be tapered.
examinerTraps: The examiner may describe a patient who ran out of meds and now has a BP of 180/110. The term for this specific event is 'rebound', not just 'stage 2'.
sourceQuote: Rebound hypertension: Elevated blood pressure (usually above pretreatment levels) resulting from loss of antihypertensive drug effect

stem: A 54-year-old man presents for a routine physical examination. His blood pressure readings, taken on two separate occasions over two weeks, show an average of 136/84 mm Hg. He has no significant past medical history and is currently asymptomatic. Based on the 2017 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines, which of the following best describes this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Elevated blood pressure is defined as a systolic pressure between 120-129 mm Hg and a diastolic pressure less than 80 mm Hg.
explanations.b: Stage 1 hypertension is defined as a systolic pressure between 130-139 mm Hg or a diastolic pressure between 80-89 mm Hg. This patient's reading of 136/84 mm Hg falls within this range.
explanations.c: Stage 2 hypertension is defined as a systolic pressure of 140 mm Hg or higher, or a diastolic pressure of 90 mm Hg or higher.
explanations.d: Hypertensive emergency involves severe hypertension (usually >180/120 mm Hg) with evidence of acute end-organ damage, which is not present here.
explanations.e: Secondary hypertension refers to high blood pressure caused by an identifiable underlying cause (e.g., renal artery stenosis), which is not the primary classification based on pressure readings alone.

ankiCards: According to 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines, Stage 1 hypertension is defined as {{c1::130-139}}/{{c1::80-89}} mm Hg.
Elevated blood pressure is defined as a systolic range of {{c1::120-129}} mm Hg with a diastolic less than {{c1::80}} mm Hg.
Stage 2 hypertension requires a systolic pressure equal to or greater than {{c1::140}} mm Hg.
Primary hypertension is also known as {{c1::essential}} hypertension.
The definition of Stage 1 hypertension includes a diastolic range of {{c1::80–89}} mm Hg.
keyPoints: 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines lowered the threshold for hypertension diagnosis.
Stage 1 HTN: 130-139 SBP or 80-89 DBP.
Stage 2 HTN: ≥140 SBP or ≥90 DBP.

Diagnosis requires multiple readings over time.

sourceQuote: average systolic pressure greater than 120 but less than 130 mm Hg is considered elevated, pressure equal to or greater than 130/80 mm Hg but less than 140/89 is considered stage 1 hypertension

stem: A patient is prescribed a potent vasodilator to manage resistant hypertension. Shortly after administration, the patient experiences a significant increase in heart rate. This physiological response is mediated by sensory input from the carotid sinus to the vasomotor center. Which of the following terms best describes this mechanism?

explanations.a: The baroreceptor reflex is the primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis, responding to pressure changes via sensory input from the carotid sinus and aorta.
explanations.b: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in blood pressure upon standing, not the compensatory mechanism for drug-induced vasodilation.
explanations.c: Rebound hypertension is an increase in blood pressure following the cessation of a drug.
explanations.d: Vascular remodeling refers to structural changes in vessel walls due to chronic hypertension, not an acute reflex.
explanations.e: Postganglionic blockade refers to drugs that stop nerve transmission at the terminal, not the reflex pathway itself.

ankiCards: The {{c1::baroreceptor reflex}} is the primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis.
Sensory input for the baroreceptor reflex comes from the {{c1::carotid sinus}} and {{c2::aorta}}.

stem: Which of the following transporters is specifically responsible for moving catecholamines from the neural cytoplasm into storage vesicles within the nerve terminal?

stem: A 62-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with a blood pressure of 210/130 mm Hg. She complains of a severe headache and blurred vision. Fundoscopic examination reveals retinal hemorrhages and papilledema. Which of the following is the most accurate diagnosis for this clinical presentation?

explanations.a: Essential hypertension refers to primary hypertension of unknown cause, which may or may not be severe.
explanations.b: While her pressure meets the criteria for Stage 2 (≥140/90), the presence of acute end-organ damage (retinal hemorrhage, papilledema) upgrades the diagnosis.

ankiCards: A hypertensive emergency is characterized by severe hypertension and rapid damage to {{c1::end organs}}.

Centrally acting drugs like {{c1::clonidine}} are classic causes of rebound hypertension.
Suddenly stopping antihypertensive medication can lead to {{c1::rebound}} hypertension.
Rebound hypertension is often associated with symptoms of {{c1::sympathetic}} overactivity.
keyPoints: Rebound hypertension occurs with abrupt withdrawal of certain drugs.
Commonly associated with Clonidine (CNS sympathoplegic).
BP can exceed original hypertensive levels.
Caused by sudden up-regulation of receptors or sudden surge in catecholamines.
Patients should be tapered off these medications.
microReview: Rebound Hypertension: Abrupt cessation of drug (e.g., Clonidine) -> Sympathetic surge -> Massive BP spike.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'Rebound hypertension' with 'Hypertensive emergency'. While rebound can *lead* to an emergency, the term for the drug-withdrawal phenomenon is 'rebound'.
sourceQuote: Rebound hypertension Elevated blood pressure (usually above pretreatment levels) resulting from loss of antihyperten- sive drug effect

stem: Which of the following drugs specifically acts by inhibiting the enzyme responsible for the rate-limiting step of the angiotensin cascade, rather than blocking receptors or the conversion of angiotensin I?

explanations.a: Captopril is an ACE inhibitor, which blocks the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II.
explanations.b: Losartan is an Angiotensin Receptor Blocker (ARB).
explanations.c: Aliskiren is a renin inhibitor, which acts at the very beginning of the cascade (the rate-limiting step).
explanations.d: Nifedipine is a calcium channel blocker.
explanations.e: Prazosin is an alpha-1 receptor antagonist.

ankiCards: {{c1::Aliskiren}} is a direct renin inhibitor.
{{c1::Captopril}} is an example of an ACE inhibitor.
{{c1::Losartan}} acts as an angiotensin receptor antagonist.
The rate-limiting step in the angiotensin cascade is the action of {{c1::renin}}.
ACE inhibitors block the conversion of {{c1::angiotensin I}} to {{c2::angiotensin II}}.
keyPoints: Renin is the rate-limiting enzyme in the RAAS.
Aliskiren = Direct Renin Inhibitor.
ACEIs (e.g., Captopril) block ACE.
ARBs (e.g., Losartan) block AT1 receptors.
All three classes eventually decrease Angiotensin II effects.
microReview: RAAS blockers: Aliskiren (Renin), Captopril (ACE), Losartan (AT1 Receptor).
examinerTraps: Confusing the site of action: Renin (Aliskiren) vs. ACE (Captopril).
sourceQuote: Angiotensin antagonists: Renin inhibitor (aliskiren), ACE inhibitors (captopril), Receptor blockers (losartan)

stem: Hypertension resulting from a specific, diagnosable abnormality such as aortic coarctation or renal artery stenosis is classified as:

explanations.a: Essential hypertension is hypertension of unknown etiology.
explanations.b: Primary hypertension is a synonym for essential hypertension.
explanations.c: Secondary hypertension is defined as hypertension caused by a diagnosable abnormality (e.g., renal or vascular issues).
explanations.d: Malignant hypertension refers to the severity and rapid progression, not the underlying cause (though secondary causes can lead to it).
explanations.e: Idiopathic is a synonym for unknown cause (essential).

ankiCards: {{c1::Secondary}} hypertension is caused by a diagnosable abnormality.
Aortic coarctation is a cause of {{c1::secondary}} hypertension.
Renal artery stenosis is a common cause of {{c1::secondary}} hypertension.
Hypertension of unknown etiology is called {{c1::essential}} or {{c2::primary}} hypertension.
Most cases of hypertension are classified as {{c1::essential/primary}}.
keyPoints: Essential/Primary HTN = 90-95% of cases, unknown cause.
Secondary HTN = Identifiable cause.
Common secondary causes: Renal artery stenosis, Pheochromocytoma, Coarctation of aorta.
Treatment of secondary HTN often focuses on the underlying cause.
Secondary HTN should be suspected in very young patients or sudden onset.
microReview: HTN Etiology: Essential (Unknown) vs. Secondary (Known cause like Renovascular or Coarctation).
examinerTraps: Assuming 'Secondary' describes the *severity* of hypertension; it actually describes the *origin*.
sourceQuote: Secondary hypertension Hypertension caused by a diagnosable abnormality, eg, aortic coarctation, renal artery stenosis

stem: A patient is treated with hexamethonium in an experimental setting. This drug blocks transmission at the autonomic ganglia. Which category of antihypertensive drugs does this drug belong to according to its site of action?

explanations.a: CNS sympathoplegics (e.g., clonidine) work in the brain's vasomotor centers.
explanations.b: Nerve terminal blockers (e.g., guanethidine) work at the postganglionic neuron endings.
explanations.c: Ganglion blockers (e.g., hexamethonium) act on the nicotinic receptors within the autonomic ganglia.
explanations.d: Alpha-receptor blockers (e.g., prazosin) act on the effector organ receptors.
explanations.e: Beta-receptor blockers (e.g., propranolol) act on the effector organ receptors.

ankiCards: Hexamethonium is a drug that acts at the {{c1::ganglia}}.
Drugs acting at the nerve terminals include {{c1::guanethidine}} and {{c2::reserpine}}.
Clonidine acts on the {{c1::CNS}} sympathetic outflow.
Prazosin and Propranolol block {{c1::alpha}} or {{c2::beta}} receptors.
Sympathoplegics are classified by their site of action: CNS, ganglia, nerve terminals, or {{c1::receptors}}.
keyPoints: Sympathoplegics reduce sympathetic tone.
Ganglion blockers (Hexamethonium) are rarely used now due to lack of selectivity.
CNS sympathoplegics (Clonidine) reduce outflow from the brain.
Nerve terminal blockers (Guanethidine) prevent NE release.
Receptor blockers (Prazosin/Propranolol) are the most selective.
microReview: Sympathoplegic sites: CNS (Clonidine) -> Ganglia (Hexamethonium) -> Terminals (Guanethidine) -> Receptors (Prazosin).
examinerTraps: Confusing 'Nerve terminal' action with 'Ganglion' action. Terminals are the end of the postganglionic neuron; ganglia are the synapse between pre- and postganglionic neurons.
sourceQuote: Sympathoplegics— blockers of... Ganglia (hexamethonium)

stem: A 50-year-old patient has a blood pressure of 145/95 mm Hg. He is otherwise healthy. According to the 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines, what is the correct classification for this patient's blood pressure, and what is the clinical significance?

options.c: Stage 2 hypertension; deserving of treatment in most patients

explanations.a: Elevated BP is 120-129/<80. This patient is much higher.
explanations.b: Stage 1 is 130-139/80-89. This patient's 145/95 exceeds those limits.
explanations.c: Stage 2 hypertension (≥140/90) is deserving of treatment in most patients according to the guidelines.
explanations.d: Hypertensive emergency requires much higher BP and end-organ damage symptoms.
explanations.e: Normal BP is <120/80.

ankiCards: Stage 2 hypertension is defined as BP equal to or greater than {{c1::140/90}} mm Hg.
Both Stage 1 and Stage 2 hypertension are deserving of {{c1::treatment}} in most patients.
Average systolic pressure between 130 and 139 is {{c1::Stage 1}} hypertension.
Average diastolic pressure of 95 mm Hg indicates {{c1::Stage 2}} hypertension.
The 2017 guidelines urge more active {{c1::prevention}} and treatment of hypertension.
keyPoints: Stage 2 HTN: ≥140/90 mm Hg.
Treatment is indicated for both Stage 1 and Stage 2 in most cases.
The 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines emphasize aggressive BP management.
HTN is a major risk factor for MI, heart failure, and stroke.
Increased systolic pressure is as important as diastolic.
microReview: HTN Stages: 120-129 (Elevated), 130-139/80-89 (Stage 1), ≥140/90 (Stage 2).
examinerTraps: Assuming that 140/90 is still 'Stage 1'—the 2017 guidelines shifted the definitions downward.
sourceQuote: pressures equal to or greater than 140/90 are considered stage 2 hypertension... Both stage 1 and stage 2 hypertension are deserving of treatment in most patients

stem: A 52-year-old man presents for a follow-up blood pressure check. Over three separate visits, his average blood pressure is 144/92 mm Hg. He has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. Physical examination and basic metabolic panel are unremarkable. Under the 2017 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) guidelines, how should this patient's condition be classified?

explanations.a: Elevated blood pressure is defined as a systolic pressure between 120-129 mm Hg and a diastolic pressure less than 80 mm Hg.
explanations.b: Stage 1 hypertension is defined as a systolic pressure of 130-139 mm Hg or a diastolic pressure of 80-89 mm Hg.
explanations.c: Stage 2 hypertension is defined as a systolic pressure of 140 mm Hg or greater, or a diastolic pressure of 90 mm Hg or greater. This patient's 144/92 mm Hg meets both criteria.
explanations.d: Hypertensive urgency involves significantly higher pressures (usually >180/120 mm Hg) without acute end-organ damage, which is not present here.
explanations.e: Normal blood pressure is defined as less than 120/80 mm Hg.

ankiCards: AHA/ACC 2017: Stage 2 Hypertension is defined as systolic BP ≥ {{c1::140}} or diastolic BP ≥ {{c1::90}} mm Hg.
AHA/ACC 2017: Stage 1 Hypertension is defined as systolic BP {{c1::130-139}} or diastolic BP {{c1::80-89}} mm Hg.
AHA/ACC 2017: Elevated blood pressure is systolic {{c1::120-129}} and diastolic < {{c1::80}} mm Hg.
Hypertension is a major risk factor for {{c1::myocardial infarction}}, heart failure, and {{c1::stroke}}.
According to current guidelines, increased {{c1::systolic}} pressure is considered at least as important as elevated diastolic pressure.
keyPoints: The 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines lowered the thresholds for diagnosing hypertension.
Stage 2: ≥140/90 mm Hg.
Elevated BP: 120-129/<80 mm Hg.
Systolic blood pressure is a critical predictor of cardiovascular risk.
Both Stage 1 and Stage 2 hypertension typically require treatment intervention.
microReview: Hypertension classification has evolved to emphasize earlier intervention. Stage 2 starts at 140/90, while Stage 1 begins at 130/80. Systolic elevation is now viewed with equal or greater clinical weight than diastolic elevation in predicting lethal outcomes like MI or stroke.
examinerTraps: A common trap is using the older JNC 7 guidelines where Stage 1 started at 140/90. Students must ensure they use the 2017 AHA/ACC definitions.
sourceQuote: According to the 2017 guidelines, average systolic pressure greater than 120 but less than 130 mm Hg is considered elevated, pressure equal to or greater than 130/80 mm Hg but less than 140/89 is considered stage 1 hypertension, while pressures equal to or greater than 140/90 are considered stage 2 hypertension.

stem: A new antihypertensive drug is studied in a clinical trial. It is found to inhibit the transporter responsible for pumping catecholamines from the neural cytoplasm into storage vesicles in the nerve terminal. Inhibition of which of the following proteins describes this mechanism of action?

explanations.a: The norepinephrine transporter (NET) is the catecholamine reuptake pump on the nerve terminal membrane, not the vesicle membrane.
explanations.b: The catecholamine vesicle pump, also known as the vesicle monoamine transporter (VMAT), is responsible for moving catecholamines from the cytoplasm into storage vesicles.
explanations.c: Monoamine oxidase (MAO) is an enzyme that degrades catecholamines in the mitochondria/cytoplasm, not a transporter.
explanations.d: Catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) is an enzyme involved in the extraneuronal metabolism of catecholamines.
explanations.e: ACE is an enzyme in the lungs and vascular endothelium that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II.

ankiCards: The transporter that moves catecholamines into storage vesicles is {{c1::VMAT}} (Catecholamine vesicle pump).
The transporter responsible for recycling norepinephrine from the synapse is {{c1::NET}} (Catecholamine reuptake pump).
The primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis is the {{c1::baroreceptor reflex}}.
{{c1::VMAT}} stands for Vesicle Monoamine Transporter.
{{c1::NET}} stands for Norepinephrine Transporter.
keyPoints: VMAT (Catecholamine vesicle pump) transports neurotransmitters into vesicles.
NET (Catecholamine reuptake pump) recovers neurotransmitters from the synaptic cleft.
Drugs affecting VMAT (like reserpine) deplete neurotransmitter stores.
Sympathoplegics can act at nerve terminals, ganglia, or central sites.
Inhibition of VMAT leads to decreased sympathetic tone.
microReview: Understanding the difference between the reuptake pump (NET) and the storage pump (VMAT) is vital. VMAT packages norepinephrine for release; if inhibited, norepinephrine is exposed to degradation by MAO in the cytoplasm, leading to depletion.
examinerTraps: Confusing VMAT with NET is the most frequent error. Remember: 'V' for Vesicle (storage) and 'N' for Norepinephrine (reuptake from synapse).
sourceQuote: Catecholamine vesicle pump: Storage vesicle transporter that pumps catecholamine from neural cytoplasm into the storage vesicle; also called vesicle monoamine transporter (VMAT)

stem: A 45-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department due to a sudden onset of a splitting headache and confusion. Her blood pressure is 220/140 mm Hg. Fundoscopic examination reveals bilateral papilledema and retinal hemorrhages. Laboratory studies show an acute rise in serum creatinine. Which of the following terms best describes her current clinical state?

explanations.a: Secondary hypertension refers to high blood pressure with a specific, identifiable cause (e.g., renal artery stenosis).
explanations.b: Essential hypertension is high blood pressure of unknown etiology.
explanations.c: A hypertensive emergency (historically called malignant hypertension) is severe hypertension with evidence of rapidly progressing end-organ damage (e.g., encephalopathy, retinal damage, renal failure).
explanations.d: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in blood pressure upon standing.
explanations.e: Rebound hypertension is an increase in blood pressure following the withdrawal of an antihypertensive drug.

ankiCards: A hypertensive emergency is severe hypertension associated with {{c1::end-organ damage}}.
Signs of end-organ damage in hypertensive emergency include {{c1::retinal hemorrhages}}, encephalopathy, and renal damage.
The historical term for a hypertensive emergency with rapidly progressing damage is {{c1::malignant hypertension}}.
End-organ damage results in diminished {{c1::perfusion}} to the heart, kidney, retina, or brain.
Essential hypertension is also known as {{c1::primary}} hypertension.
keyPoints: Hypertensive emergency requires immediate but controlled blood pressure reduction.
Defining feature: Acute end-organ damage (brain, heart, kidneys, eyes).
Clinical signs include papilledema, hematuria, or focal neurological deficits.
It is distinguished from hypertensive urgency by the presence of organ damage.
Prompt recognition is necessary to prevent permanent stroke or renal failure.
microReview: A hypertensive emergency is defined by the degree of end-organ risk rather than an absolute pressure number alone. The presence of 'malignant' features like retinal hemorrhages or encephalopathy necessitates parenteral therapy.
examinerTraps: The examiner might provide high blood pressure (e.g., 200/120) without organ damage and ask for the diagnosis; that would be 'urgency' rather than 'emergency'. Always look for evidence of damage (creatinine, vision, CNS).
sourceQuote: Hypertensive emergency (“malignant hypertension”): An accelerated form of severe hypertension associated with rising blood pressure and rapidly progressing damage to vessels and end organs.

stem: The American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology suggest that most patients diagnosed with either Stage 1 or Stage 2 hypertension should receive treatment. What is the specific systolic blood pressure threshold at which Stage 1 hypertension is first recognized?

explanations.a: 120 mm Hg is the upper limit of 'Normal' and the start of 'Elevated' blood pressure.
explanations.b: 125 mm Hg falls within the 'Elevated' category (120-129).
explanations.c: Stage 1 hypertension begins at a systolic pressure of 130 mm Hg.
explanations.d: 135 mm Hg is within the Stage 1 range (130-139).
explanations.e: 140 mm Hg marks the beginning of Stage 2 hypertension.

ankiCards: Stage 1 Hypertension begins at a systolic pressure of {{c1::130}} mm Hg.
Stage 2 Hypertension begins at a systolic pressure of {{c1::140}} mm Hg.
Elevated Blood Pressure is defined as systolic between {{c1::120}} and {{c1::129}} mm Hg.
Normal blood pressure is defined as systolic less than {{c1::120}} mm Hg.
Current guidelines emphasize that increased {{c1::systolic}} pressure is at least as important as diastolic.
keyPoints: Treatment is urged for both Stage 1 and Stage 2 hypertension.
Stage 1: 130-139 systolic.
Stage 2: ≥140 systolic.
Hypertension is a primary risk factor for lethal cardiovascular events.
Prevention and active treatment are stressed in 2017 guidelines.
microReview: Memory Tool: Normal <120, Elevated 120-129, Stage 1 130-139, Stage 2 ≥140. For diastolic: Normal <80, Elevated <80, Stage 1 80-89, Stage 2 ≥90.
examinerTraps: Wait for 'and' vs 'or'. Hypertension is diagnosed if *either* the systolic or diastolic pressure meets the threshold. Many students forget that 130/78 is still Stage 1.
sourceQuote: According to the 2017 guidelines... pressure equal to or greater than 130/80 mm Hg but less than 140/89 is considered stage 1 hypertension

stem: When a vasodilator like nifedipine is administered to a patient with hypertension, it results in a rapid decrease in blood pressure. This drop in pressure is often followed by a compensatory increase in heart rate. Which mechanism is primarily responsible for this compensatory increase?

options.b: Inhibition of the catecholamine reuptake pump

explanations.a: While the RAAS may be activated, the rapid, beat-to-beat compensatory tachycardia is primarily mediated by the autonomic baroreceptor reflex.
explanations.b: Inhibition of NET (reuptake pump) would increase norepinephrine in the synapse, but this is not the mechanism of compensatory tachycardia following vasodilation.
explanations.c: The baroreceptor reflex is the primary autonomic mechanism for BP homeostasis. A drop in BP reduces baroreceptor firing, leading to increased sympathetic and decreased parasympathetic output, resulting in tachycardia.
explanations.d: Vasodilators like nifedipine do not directly stimulate beta receptors; the stimulation is indirect via the reflex.
explanations.e: Parasympathetic outflow is decreased as part of the reflex, but the reflex itself is the overarching mechanism.

ankiCards: The primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis is the {{c1::baroreceptor reflex}}.
Reflex tachycardia results from a lowering of blood pressure and is mediated by the {{c1::baroreceptor}} reflex.
The baroreceptor reflex involves sensory input from the {{c1::carotid sinus}} and {{c1::aorta}}.
Input from baroreceptors is processed in the {{c1::vasomotor}} center of the brain.
Vasodilators often trigger {{c1::reflex tachycardia}} as a side effect.
keyPoints: Baroreceptor reflex: Carotid sinus/aorta → Vasomotor center → Autonomic nerves.
Vasodilation → Decreased MAP → Decreased Baroreceptor stretch → Increased Sympathetic outflow.
Clinical result: Reflex tachycardia and increased cardiac output.
This reflex can counteract the blood-pressure-lowering effects of certain drugs.
Beta-blockers are often used with vasodilators to blunt this reflex.
microReview: The baroreceptor reflex is a negative feedback loop. If BP goes down, the reflex pulls it up (tachycardia, vasoconstriction). If BP goes up, the reflex pulls it down (bradycardia, vasodilation).
examinerTraps: The examiner may ask for the sensors (carotid sinus/aorta) or the effector (sympathetic/parasympathetic nerves). Ensure you distinguish between the sensors and the reflex itself.
sourceQuote: Baroreceptor reflex: Primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis; involves sensory input from carotid sinus and aorta to the vasomotor center and output via the parasympathetic and sympathetic motor nerves

stem: Which of the following describes a substance that is stored in synaptic vesicles and released upon nerve stimulation but lacks the potency and effectiveness of the endogenous neurotransmitter norepinephrine?

explanations.a: End-organ damage refers to the clinical outcome of severe hypertension, not a neurotransmitter substitute.
explanations.b: Secondary transmitter is not a standard term for this phenomenon.
explanations.c: A false transmitter (e.g., octopamine) is a substance stored and released like a neurotransmitter but possessing much lower efficacy at the receptor.
explanations.d: Postganglionic blockers are drugs that inhibit transmission at nerve terminals but do not necessarily act as substitute transmitters.
explanations.e: Rebound transmitter is not a standard pharmacological term.

ankiCards: A {{c1::false transmitter}} is a substance stored in vesicles and released but lacking the effectiveness of norepinephrine.
An example of a false transmitter mentioned in high-yield terms is {{c1::octopamine}}.
False transmitters replace {{c1::norepinephrine}} in the synaptic vesicles.
The clinical result of a false transmitter is reduced {{c1::sympathetic}} effectiveness.
False transmitters are stored in vesicles via the {{c1::VMAT}} (Catecholamine vesicle pump).
keyPoints: False transmitters compete with norepinephrine for storage in vesicles.
They are released by the same mechanisms as the true transmitter.
Their low efficacy results in a net decrease in sympathetic signaling.
This mechanism contributes to the action of some sympathoplegic drugs.
Octopamine is the classic example.
microReview: Think of a 'false transmitter' as a 'decoy'. The nerve fires and releases the decoy, but the 'decoy' cannot turn on the receptor as effectively as the real 'key' (norepinephrine), leading to lower blood pressure.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse 'false transmitter' with 'competitive antagonist'. A competitive antagonist blocks the receptor; a false transmitter is actually released from the presynaptic neuron.
sourceQuote: False transmitter: Substance, for example, octopamine, stored in vesicles and released into synaptic cleft but lacking the effectiveness of the true transmitter, norepinephrine

stem: A 24-year-old male with no medical history is found to have a blood pressure of 170/110 mm Hg during a pre-employment physical. Physical examination reveals a loud bruit in the flank and a significant difference in blood pressure between the arms and legs. Further workup identifies a coarctation of the aorta. Which term best classifies his hypertension?

explanations.a: Essential hypertension has no known cause.
explanations.b: Primary hypertension is a synonym for essential hypertension.
explanations.c: Secondary hypertension is caused by a diagnosable abnormality, such as aortic coarctation or renal artery stenosis.
explanations.d: Malignant hypertension refers to the severity and presence of end-organ damage, not the underlying etiology.
explanations.e: Orthostatic hypertension refers to a rise in BP upon standing, which is the opposite of the more common orthostatic hypotension.

ankiCards: Hypertension caused by a diagnosable abnormality (e.g., aortic coarctation) is called {{c1::secondary}} hypertension.
Hypertension of unknown etiology is called {{c1::essential}} or {{c2::primary}} hypertension.
Examples of secondary hypertension include {{c1::renal artery stenosis}} and {{c1::aortic coarctation}}.
The 2017 guidelines urge active prevention and treatment of {{c1::hypertension}}.
Secondary hypertension is less common than {{c1::essential}} hypertension.
keyPoints: Essential/Primary: No specific cause found (90-95% of cases).
Secondary: Result of another medical condition (5-10% of cases).
Clues to secondary HTN: Young age of onset, sudden onset, or poor response to meds.
Identifying the cause in secondary HTN can sometimes lead to a cure.
Renal artery stenosis is a common cause of secondary hypertension.
microReview: Primary = Unknown cause. Secondary = Second to something else (another disease). Aortic coarctation is a classic board-exam 'Secondary' cause found in younger patients.
examinerTraps: Examiners often use 'Primary' and 'Essential' interchangeably to confuse students. If both are listed and the question asks for a type with a known cause, neither can be the answer.
sourceQuote: Secondary hypertension: Hypertension caused by a diagnosable abnormality, eg, aortic coarctation, renal artery stenos

stem: A patient abruptly stops taking a centrally acting sympathoplegic medication. Within 24 hours, the patient's blood pressure rises to 190/110 mm Hg, which is higher than their baseline pressure before starting the drug. This clinical phenomenon is known as:

explanations.a: Reflex tachycardia is an increase in heart rate following a decrease in blood pressure.
explanations.b: Postganglionic blockade refers to the mechanism of certain drugs, not the withdrawal effect.
explanations.c: Rebound hypertension is the elevation of blood pressure (usually above pretreatment levels) resulting from the loss of an antihypertensive drug's effect, typically after sudden cessation.
explanations.d: While this patient's pressure is high, the specific term for this withdrawal-induced rise is rebound hypertension. It could lead to an emergency, but 'rebound' is the specific description.
explanations.e: Secondary hypertension refers to a specific underlying disease cause, not drug withdrawal.

ankiCards: {{c1::Rebound hypertension}} is defined as elevated BP resulting from the loss of an antihypertensive drug effect.
Rebound hypertension often occurs when a drug is {{c1::abruptly}} discontinued.
In rebound hypertension, blood pressure usually rises above {{c1::pretreatment}} levels.
Centrally acting drugs like {{c1::clonidine}} are notoriously associated with rebound hypertension.
To avoid rebound hypertension, drugs should be {{c1::tapered}} slowly.
keyPoints: Rebound hypertension: Sudden cessation → Sympathetic 'overshoot'.
Pressure often exceeds original baseline levels.
Associated with sympathoplegics (e.g., clonidine).
Can cause symptoms like nervousness, tachycardia, and headache.
Management requires restarting the drug or using alpha/beta blockers.
microReview: Stop the drug fast = Pressure goes up fast. This is the 'rebound' effect. It occurs because receptors upregulate or compensatory mechanisms are suddenly unleashed.
examinerTraps: The question might ask for the specific drug. Clonidine is the 'classic' culprit for rebound hypertension on board exams.
sourceQuote: Rebound hypertension: Elevated blood pressure (usually above pretreatment levels) resulting from loss of antihypertensive drug effect

stem: Which of the following antihypertensive agents is classified as a centrally acting sympathoplegic that affects central nervous system sympathetic outflow?

explanations.a: Losartan is an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB).
explanations.b: Clonidine is a CNS-active sympathoplegic that reduces sympathetic outflow from the vasomotor center.
explanations.c: Prazosin is an alpha-receptor blocker (peripheral).
explanations.d: Guanethidine is a nerve terminal blocker (postganglionic).
explanations.e: Hexamethonium is a ganglion blocker.

ankiCards: Clonidine acts on {{c1::CNS}} sympathetic outflow.
Guanethidine and reserpine act at the {{c1::nerve terminals}}.
Hexamethonium is a blocker of the {{c1::ganglia}}.
Prazosin blocks {{c1::alpha}} receptors.
Losartan is an example of an {{c1::Angiotensin}} receptor blocker.
keyPoints: Sympathoplegics are categorized by their site of action.
CNS: Clonidine, Methyldopa.
Ganglia: Hexamethonium (rarely used).
Nerve Terminals: Guanethidine, Reserpine.
Receptors: Prazosin (alpha), Propranolol (beta).
microReview: Map the sympathetic path: Brain (Clonidine) → Ganglia (Hexamethonium) → Nerve Terminal (Guanethidine) → Receptor (Prazosin/Propranolol).
examinerTraps: Make sure to distinguish between 'nerve terminal' blockers and 'receptor' blockers. They both work peripherally but at different anatomical points in the synapse.
sourceQuote: Sympathoplegics—blockers of... CNS sympathetic outflow (clonidine)... Nerve terminals (guanethidine, reserpine)... Ganglia (hexamethonium)

stem: A patient experiences a sharp drop in blood pressure when moving from a supine to a standing position. This condition is categorized as:

explanations.a: Reflex tachycardia is a heart rate response to low BP, not the BP drop itself.
explanations.b: Hypertensive urgency is severe high BP without organ damage.
explanations.c: Essential hypertension is chronic high BP of unknown cause.
explanations.d: Orthostatic (or postural) hypotension is a decrease in blood pressure upon assuming an upright posture.
explanations.e: End-organ damage is the result of chronic or severe hypertension.

ankiCards: {{c1::Orthostatic hypotension}} is hypotension on assuming an upright posture.
Another name for orthostatic hypotension is {{c1::postural}} hypotension.
The baroreceptor reflex normally prevents {{c1::orthostatic}} hypotension.
Many antihypertensive drugs, especially sympathoplegics, can cause {{c1::orthostatic hypotension}} as a side effect.
Orthostatic hypotension involves a failure of the {{c1::autonomic}} system to compensate for gravity.
keyPoints: Orthostatic hypotension = BP drop on standing.
Commonly caused by drugs that interfere with sympathetic reflexes.
Symptoms: Dizziness, lightheadedness, syncope.
Physiological cause: Gravity pools blood in the legs; reflex fails to constrict veins/arteries fast enough.
It is a significant safety concern, especially in elderly patients on medication.
microReview: Orthostatic = Posture. Hypotension = Low BP. Orthostatic Hypotension = Low BP due to posture change. Usually occurs because the baroreceptor reflex is blocked or 'lazy'.
examinerTraps: Sometimes confused with 'postural tachycardia syndrome' (POTS). In POTS, the heart rate goes up significantly without a major drop in BP. In orthostatic hypotension, the BP drop is the defining feature.
sourceQuote: Orthostatic hypotension: Hypotension on assuming upright posture; postural hypotension

stem: According to the 2017 American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) guidelines, a patient with an average blood pressure reading of 126/78 mm Hg is classified into which category?

explanations.a: Normal blood pressure is defined as less than 120/80 mm Hg.
explanations.b: Elevated blood pressure is defined as a systolic pressure between 120–129 mm Hg and a diastolic pressure less than 80 mm Hg.
explanations.c: Stage 1 hypertension starts at a systolic of 130 mm Hg or a diastolic of 80 mm Hg.
explanations.d: Stage 2 hypertension is defined as systolic pressure equal to or greater than 140 mm Hg or diastolic equal to or greater than 90 mm Hg.
explanations.e: Hypertensive emergency involves severely elevated blood pressure with evidence of acute end-organ damage.

ankiCards: A systolic pressure of {{c1::120-129}} mm Hg with a diastolic < 80 is classified as elevated blood pressure.
Stage 1 hypertension is defined by a systolic pressure of {{c1::130-139}} or a diastolic of 80-89 mm Hg.
Stage 2 hypertension begins at a blood pressure of {{c1::140/90}} mm Hg or higher.
The 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines consider elevated {{c1::systolic}} pressure to be at least as important as diastolic pressure.
Normal blood pressure is defined as a reading less than {{c1::120/80}} mm Hg.
keyPoints: Normal BP: <120/80 mm Hg
Elevated BP: 120-129 / <80 mm Hg
Stage 1 HTN: 130-139 / 80-89 mm Hg
Stage 2 HTN: ≥140 / ≥90 mm Hg
Systolic pressure is prioritized in current guidelines for cardiovascular risk assessment.
Active prevention is urged for readings above normal.
microReview: The 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines lowered the threshold for hypertension to 130/80 mm Hg (Stage 1) to encourage earlier intervention and reduce risks of MI and stroke.
examinerTraps: Students often confuse 'Elevated' with 'Stage 1'. Elevated is the intermediate step (120-129 systolic) before the hypertension diagnosis at 130.
sourceQuote: average systolic pressure greater than 120 but less than 130 mm Hg is considered elevated, pressure equal to or greater than 130/80 mm Hg but less than 140/89 is considered stage 1 hypertension

stem: Which of the following describes the physiological mechanism responsible for reflex tachycardia when a vasodilator drug is administered to a patient with hypertension?

options.a: Inhibition of the catecholamine reuptake pump (NET)
options.b: Activation of the catecholamine vesicle pump (VMAT)
options.d: Direct stimulation of the vasomotor center by the drug
options.e: Release of false transmitters from postganglionic nerves

explanations.a: NET inhibition increases synaptic norepinephrine but does not define the reflex response to pressure drops.
explanations.b: VMAT is a storage transporter; its activation does not mediate the baroreceptor reflex.
explanations.c: The baroreceptor reflex involves sensory input from the carotid sinus and aorta; a drop in BP leads to increased sympathetic output, causing reflex tachycardia.
explanations.d: Vasodilators lower BP; the tachycardia is a secondary reflex response, not usually direct CNS stimulation.
explanations.e: False transmitters like octopamine reduce sympathetic effectiveness rather than causing tachycardia.

ankiCards: The primary autonomic mechanism for blood pressure homeostasis is the {{c1::baroreceptor reflex}}.
Sensory input for the baroreceptor reflex comes from the {{c1::carotid sinus}} and aorta.
Reflex tachycardia results from the lowering of blood pressure and is mediated by {{c1::sympathetic}} output.
The vasomotor center receives input from baroreceptors and regulates output via {{c1::parasympathetic and sympathetic}} nerves.
A sudden drop in blood pressure triggers the baroreceptor reflex to increase {{c1::heart rate}}.
keyPoints: The baroreceptor reflex is the main homeostatic mechanism for BP.
Sensors are located in the carotid sinus and the aortic arch.
Vasodilators trigger this reflex by lowering peripheral resistance.
Reflex tachycardia is a common side effect of rapid-acting antihypertensives.
Efferent pathways involve both sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves.
microReview: Decreased BP -> Decreased baroreceptor firing -> Vasomotor center increases sympathetic/decreases parasympathetic drive -> Increased Heart Rate (Reflex Tachycardia).
examinerTraps: Distinguish between the drug's direct action (vasodilation) and the body's compensatory action (reflex tachycardia).
sourceQuote: Reflex tachycardia Tachycardia resulting from lowering of blood pressure; mediated by the baroreceptor reflex

stem: A 55-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a severe headache and blurred vision. His blood pressure is 210/130 mm Hg. Physical examination reveals retinal hemorrhages and signs of encephalopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate classification for this patient's condition?

explanations.a: Essential hypertension is hypertension of unknown etiology, not a description of this acute presentation.
explanations.b: Secondary hypertension refers to hypertension with a specific diagnosable cause (e.g., renal artery stenosis).
explanations.c: While his BP meets Stage 2 criteria, the presence of acute end-organ damage (retinal hemorrhage, encephalopathy) upgrades it to an emergency.
explanations.d: Hypertensive emergency (malignant hypertension) is characterized by severe BP elevation with rapidly progressing damage to end organs like the brain and retina.
explanations.e: Rebound hypertension occurs after stopping a drug; it does not specifically define the clinical severity of end-organ damage.

ankiCards: Severe hypertension with acute end-organ damage (e.g., encephalopathy) is called a {{c1::hypertensive emergency}}.
Malignant hypertension is another term for {{c1::hypertensive emergency}}.
End-organ damage in hypertension can manifest in the {{c1::heart, kidney, retina, or brain}}.
A systolic pressure ≥ 140 or diastolic ≥ 90 is categorized as {{c1::Stage 2}} hypertension.
Hypertensive emergency is often signaled by {{c1::renal damage, encephalopathy, and retinal hemorrhages}}.
keyPoints: Hypertensive emergency requires immediate BP reduction to prevent further damage.
End-organ damage is the key differentiator from hypertensive urgency.
Symptoms include encephalopathy, retinal changes, and renal failure.
Also historically known as malignant hypertension.
Stage 2 is a chronic classification, whereas Emergency is an acute clinical state.
microReview: Hypertensive Emergency = BP usually >180/120 + End-organ damage (Brain/Heart/Kidney/Eye).
examinerTraps: Do not select 'Stage 2 hypertension' if acute end-organ damage is present; 'Hypertensive emergency' is the specific clinical diagnosis.
sourceQuote: Hypertensive emergency... An accelerated form of severe hypertension associated with rising blood pressure and rapidly progressing damage to vessels and end organs.

stem: A researcher is studying a drug that inhibits the transport of norepinephrine from the neural cytoplasm into storage vesicles. Which of the following components of the sympathetic nerve terminal is the primary target of this drug?

explanations.a: NET (norepinephrine transporter) is responsible for recycling norepinephrine from the synapse back into the cytoplasm.
explanations.b: VMAT (vesicle monoamine transporter), also called the catecholamine vesicle pump, moves catecholamines from the cytoplasm into storage vesicles.
explanations.c: Alpha-1 receptors are postsynaptic targets, not transporters.
explanations.d: Beta-2 receptors are typically postsynaptic and mediate vasodilation or bronchodilation.
explanations.e: Acetylcholine transporters are specific for cholinergic nerves, not catecholamine nerves.

ankiCards: The {{c1::catecholamine vesicle pump (VMAT)}} transports norepinephrine from the neural cytoplasm into storage vesicles.
The {{c1::catecholamine reuptake pump (NET)}} is responsible for recycling norepinephrine from the synapse.
The abbreviation VMAT stands for {{c1::vesicle monoamine transporter}}.
The abbreviation NET stands for {{c1::norepinephrine transporter}}.
Drugs that block {{c1::VMAT}} (like reserpine) deplete norepinephrine stores.
keyPoints: VMAT (Vesicle pump): Cytoplasm -> Vesicle.
NET (Reuptake pump): Synapse -> Cytoplasm.
Blocking VMAT leads to depletion of neurotransmitters.
These pumps are targets for specific sympathoplegic drugs.
VMAT handles various monoamines, not just norepinephrine.
microReview: VMAT = Vesicle (storage). NET = NE Transporter (reuptake from cleft).
examinerTraps: Confusing VMAT (Vesicle) with NET (Nerve terminal reuptake). Both involve norepinephrine transport but in different locations.
sourceQuote: Catecholamine vesicle pump Storage vesicle transporter that pumps catecholamine from neural cytoplasm into the storage vesicle; also called vesicle monoamine transporter (VMAT)

stem: A 42-year-old woman is diagnosed with hypertension. Further investigation reveals that her elevated blood pressure is caused by renal artery stenosis. Which of the following terms best describes her condition?

explanations.a: Essential hypertension is hypertension of unknown etiology.
explanations.b: Primary hypertension is another name for essential hypertension (unknown cause).
explanations.c: Secondary hypertension is hypertension caused by a diagnosable abnormality, such as renal artery stenosis or aortic coarctation.
explanations.d: Idiopathic is a synonym for essential or primary hypertension.
explanations.e: Orthostatic refers to pressure changes related to posture, not the underlying etiology.

ankiCards: {{c1::Secondary}} hypertension is caused by a diagnosable abnormality like renal artery stenosis.
Hypertension of unknown etiology is called {{c1::essential}} or primary hypertension.
Aortic coarctation is a cause of {{c1::secondary}} hypertension.
The most common form of hypertension is {{c1::essential}} hypertension.
Renal artery stenosis is a classic example of {{c1::secondary}} hypertension.
keyPoints: Essential/Primary HTN: No identifiable cause (majority of cases).
Secondary HTN: Identifiable underlying cause.
Common secondary causes: Renal artery stenosis, Coarctation of the aorta.
Treatment of the underlying cause can often cure secondary HTN.
Diagnostic workup for HTN usually aims to rule out secondary causes in young patients.
microReview: Essential = Unknown cause. Secondary = Known cause (Renal, Endocrine, Vascular).
examinerTraps: Students may select 'Essential' if they assume all hypertension is primary, but any specific cause mentioned (like renal artery stenosis) makes it 'Secondary'.
sourceQuote: Secondary hypertension Hypertension caused by a diagnosable abnormality, eg, aortic coarctation, renal artery stenosis

stem: Which of the following substances, if stored in synaptic vesicles and released in place of norepinephrine, would be classified as a 'false transmitter' because it lacks the effectiveness of the true transmitter?

explanations.a: Epinephrine is a highly potent endogenous catecholamine and true transmitter/hormone.
explanations.b: Octopamine is the classic example of a false transmitter that can be stored and released but has very low efficacy at adrenergic receptors.
explanations.c: Dopamine is a precursor to norepinephrine and a true transmitter in its own right.
explanations.d: Acetylcholine is the primary transmitter of the parasympathetic system, not a 'false' version of norepinephrine.
explanations.e: Serotonin is a true monoamine neurotransmitter with its own specific receptors.

ankiCards: A {{c1::false transmitter}} is a substance stored in vesicles and released but lacks the effectiveness of norepinephrine.
An example of a false transmitter is {{c1::octopamine}}.
False transmitters are stored in {{c1::synaptic vesicles}}.
Octopamine replaces {{c1::norepinephrine}} in the synaptic cleft.
False transmitters result in {{c1::diminished}} sympathetic effectiveness.
keyPoints: False transmitters occupy vesicles instead of the real neurotransmitter.
They are released upon nerve stimulation.
They have low or no activity at the postsynaptic receptor.
Octopamine is the prototypical example mentioned in pharmacology.
This mechanism can lead to reduced sympathetic tone.
microReview: False Transmitter = Octopamine. It 'fools' the vesicle but fails to activate the receptor.
examinerTraps: Don't confuse false transmitters with agonists or antagonists; they specifically relate to the storage and release process.
sourceQuote: False transmitter Substance, for example, octopamine, stored in vesicles and released into synaptic cleft but lacking the effectiveness of the true transmitter, norepinephrine

stem: Which drug class is correctly matched with its representative agent as listed in the classification of antihypertensive drugs?

explanations.a: Losartan is an Angiotensin Receptor Blocker (ARB/Antagonist), not an ACE inhibitor.
explanations.b: Nifedipine is a representative calcium channel blocker (CCB).
explanations.c: Captopril is an ACE inhibitor, not an angiotensin antagonist (ARB).
explanations.d: Prazosin is an alpha-receptor blocker, not a CNS sympathetic outflow drug (like clonidine).
explanations.e: Guanethidine is a nerve terminal blocker, not a ganglion blocker (like hexamethonium).

ankiCards: {{c1::Nifedipine}} is an example of a calcium channel blocker used in hypertension.
Captopril belongs to the {{c1::ACE inhibitor}} class.
Losartan is categorized as an {{c1::angiotensin antagonist (or ARB)}}.
{{c1::Clonidine}} is a drug that acts on CNS sympathetic outflow.
Hexamethonium is a representative {{c1::ganglion}} blocker.
keyPoints: ACE Inhibitors: Captopril, Enalapril.
Angiotensin Antagonists (ARBs): Losartan, Valsartan.
Calcium Blockers: Nifedipine, Verapamil, Diltiazem.
CNS Sympathetic Outflow: Clonidine, Methyldopa.
Ganglion Blockers: Hexamethonium (rarely used now).
microReview: Match: ACEi (-pril), ARB (-sartan), CCB (-dipine), alpha-blocker (-zosin).
examinerTraps: ACE inhibitors and ARBs (Angiotensin antagonists) are frequently swapped in questions. Captopril = ACEi, Losartan = ARB.
sourceQuote: Calcium blockers (nifedipine)... ACE inhibitors (captopril)... Angiotensin antagonists Receptor blockers (losartan)

stem: A 68-year-old male with a history of hypertension abruptly stops taking his medication. Two days later, he presents with a blood pressure of 195/115 mm Hg, which is significantly higher than his original untreated baseline. Which of the following terms describes this phenomenon?

explanations.a: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in BP upon standing.
explanations.b: Reflex tachycardia is an increase in heart rate following a drop in BP.
explanations.c: Rebound hypertension is an elevated BP (often above pretreatment levels) resulting from the sudden loss of an antihypertensive drug's effect.
explanations.d: While the pressure is very high, the term for this specific drug-withdrawal event is rebound hypertension.
explanations.e: Secondary hypertension refers to an underlying anatomical or physiological abnormality, not a withdrawal state.

ankiCards: {{c1::Rebound hypertension}} is an elevated BP resulting from the loss of an antihypertensive drug effect.
Rebound hypertension often results in levels {{c1::above}} pretreatment levels.
{{c1::Orthostatic}} hypotension is the term for a drop in BP when assuming an upright posture.
Drugs affecting {{c1::CNS sympathetic outflow}} are commonly associated with rebound hypertension.
Loss of drug effect can cause a rapid {{c1::increase}} in blood pressure.
keyPoints: Rebound HTN occurs after sudden cessation of therapy.
It is most common with clonidine and beta-blockers.
BP can exceed the original baseline.
Orthostatic hypotension is 'postural' hypotension.
Tapering medications helps prevent rebound phenomena.
microReview: Stop drug -> Sudden loss of suppression -> Sympathetic surge -> Rebound HTN.
examinerTraps: Do not confuse 'rebound' (withdrawal) with 'reflex' (immediate compensation to a drug's effect).
sourceQuote: Rebound hypertension Elevated blood pressure (usually above pretreatment levels) resulting from loss of antihypertensive drug effect

stem: Which of the following describes a drug that blocks the transmission of sympathetic signals by acting specifically at the terminals of the postganglionic nerves?

explanations.a: Ganglion blockers (e.g., hexamethonium) act at the autonomic ganglia, not the nerve terminals.
explanations.b: CNS outflow blockers (e.g., clonidine) act within the brain to reduce sympathetic drive.
explanations.c: Postganglionic neuron blockers (e.g., guanethidine, reserpine) act at the distal nerve terminals to prevent transmitter release or storage.
explanations.d: ARBs act at the receptor level in the periphery (vessels/adrenals).
explanations.e: Beta-blockers act on the postsynaptic receptors, not the neuron terminal transmission itself.

ankiCards: A {{c1::postganglionic neuron blocker}} acts in the terminals of the postganglionic nerves.
Guanethidine and {{c1::reserpine}} are examples of nerve terminal blockers.
{{c1::Hexamethonium}} is an example of a drug that blocks autonomic ganglia.
Nerve terminal blockers prevent the {{c1::release or storage}} of norepinephrine.
Postganglionic neuron blockers are a subcategory of {{c1::sympathoplegic}} drugs.
keyPoints: Nerve terminal blockers are distinct from receptor blockers.
They interfere with the 'business end' of the neuron.
Examples include guanethidine and reserpine.
Mechanism involves depleting stores or blocking release.
These drugs are part of the broader group of sympathoplegics.
microReview: Nerve Terminal = Postganglionic neuron blocker. Ganglia = Ganglion blocker.
examinerTraps: Ensure distinction between the 'ganglion' (where pre- and postganglionic neurons meet) and the 'terminal' (where the postganglionic neuron meets the effector organ).
sourceQuote: Postganglionic neuron blocker Drug that blocks transmission by an action in the terminals of the postganglionic nerves

stem: According to the High-Yield Terms, which anatomical structures provide the sensory input to the vasomotor center for the baroreceptor reflex?

explanations.a: The baroreceptor reflex involves sensory input from the carotid sinus and the aorta.
explanations.b: The macula densa in the kidney senses sodium chloride, not part of the primary baroreceptor reflex.
explanations.c: The hypothalamus regulates temperature and other homeostatic functions, but baroreceptor input goes to the vasomotor center (medulla).
explanations.d: Atrial stretch receptors exist but the high-pressure baroreceptor reflex specifically uses the carotid sinus and aorta.
explanations.e: Pulmonary vessels are involved in low-pressure sensing, not the primary arterial baroreceptor reflex described.

ankiCards: The baroreceptor reflex involves sensory input from the {{c1::carotid sinus and aorta}}.
The {{c1::vasomotor center}} receives input from baroreceptors to maintain BP homeostasis.
Output from the vasomotor center travels via {{c1::parasympathetic and sympathetic}} motor nerves.
The carotid sinus is a key sensor for {{c1::blood pressure}}.
The baroreceptor reflex is the primary mechanism for {{c1::blood pressure homeostasis}}.
keyPoints: High-pressure baroreceptors: Carotid sinus, Aortic arch.
Integrator: Vasomotor center in the medulla.
Effectors: Heart and blood vessels.
Fast-acting reflex for moment-to-moment BP control.
Counteracts changes induced by drugs or posture.
microReview: Sensor (Carotid/Aorta) -> Integrator (Vasomotor Center) -> Effector (Symp/Parasymp).
examinerTraps: Don't confuse arterial baroreceptors (Carotid/Aorta) with volume receptors in the atria.
sourceQuote: Baroreceptor reflex... involves sensory input from carotid sinus and aorta to the vasomotor center

stem: A 58-year-old male with a history of sedentary lifestyle and high sodium intake presents for a routine physical examination. His blood pressure readings, taken on three separate occasions, average 146/92 mm Hg. He has no history of previous chronic disease. Under current clinical guidelines, which classification best describes his condition, and what is the generally recommended approach?

options.a: Elevated blood pressure; lifestyle modification only
options.b: Stage 1 hypertension; lifestyle modification and monitoring
options.c: Stage 2 hypertension; pharmacological treatment and lifestyle modification

explanations.a: Elevated blood pressure is defined as systolic 120–129 and diastolic <80 mm Hg. This patient's pressure is higher.
explanations.b: Stage 1 hypertension is defined as 130–139/80–89 mm Hg. This patient exceeds these limits.
explanations.c: Pressures equal to or greater than 140/90 mm Hg are categorized as stage 2 hypertension, and guidelines recommend active prevention and treatment in such cases.
explanations.d: The patient's readings (146/92) exceed the Stage 1 definition of 130-139/80-89 mm Hg.
explanations.e: Hypertensive emergency requires signs of acute end-organ damage and much higher pressures, not seen in this stable patient.

ankiCards: Stage 2 hypertension is defined as a blood pressure equal to or greater than {{c1::140/90}} mm Hg.
The average systolic pressure range for 'elevated' blood pressure is {{c1::120-129}} mm Hg.
According to the 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines, stage 1 hypertension is defined as {{c1::130-139/80-89}} mm Hg.
In modern hypertension management, increased {{c1::systolic}} pressure is considered at least as important as elevated diastolic pressure.
Stage 2 hypertension typically requires both {{c1::pharmacological treatment}} and lifestyle modifications.
keyPoints: Stage 2 hypertension threshold is 140/90 mm Hg.
Systolic blood pressure is a primary focus in modern guidelines.
Most patients with Stage 1 or Stage 2 hypertension require active treatment.
Elevated blood pressure is a precursor stage starting at 120 mm Hg systolic.
Hypertension is a major risk factor for myocardial infarction, stroke, and heart failure.
microReview: Hypertension is categorized by the 2017 AHA/ACC guidelines into Elevated (120-129 systolic), Stage 1 (130-139/80-89), and Stage 2 (>=140/90). Management strategies shift from lifestyle modifications at lower levels to active pharmacological intervention at Stage 2.
examinerTraps: Candidates often confuse the threshold for Stage 1 (130/80) with Stage 2 (140/90). Ensure you distinguish between 'Elevated' and 'Hypertension'.
sourceQuote: pressures equal to or greater than 140/90 are considered stage 2 hypertension . . . Both stage 1 and stage 2 hypertension are deserving of treatment in most patients

stem: A new antihypertensive drug is being studied in a clinical trial. The drug acts by specifically inhibiting the transporter responsible for pumping catecholamines from the neural cytoplasm into storage vesicles. Which of the following terms describes this specific pharmacological target?

explanations.a: NET (catecholamine reuptake pump) is responsible for recycling norepinephrine from the synapse back into the nerve terminal.
explanations.b: The catecholamine vesicle pump, also called VMAT, moves catecholamines from the cytoplasm into storage vesicles.
explanations.c: The baroreceptor sensor is a physiological mechanism in the carotid sinus and aorta, not a molecular pump in the nerve terminal.
explanations.d: Alpha-2 receptors are presynaptic inhibitory receptors, not vesicle transporters.
explanations.e: The postganglionic ganglion is a structural site of synapse, not a specific catecholamine pump.

ankiCards: The catecholamine vesicle pump is also known as {{c1::VMAT (vesicle monoamine transporter)}}.
The pump responsible for recycling norepinephrine from the synapse is the {{c1::NET (norepinephrine transporter)}}.
VMAT functions by pumping catecholamine from the {{c1::neural cytoplasm}} into the storage vesicle.
NET is also referred to as the {{c1::catecholamine reuptake pump}}.
Blocking {{c1::VMAT}} leads to depletion of neurotransmitters in the storage vesicles.
keyPoints: VMAT (Catecholamine vesicle pump) transports neurotransmitters into vesicles.
NET (Catecholamine reuptake pump) returns neurotransmitters to the nerve terminal from the synapse.
Interference with storage (VMAT) or reuptake (NET) alters sympathetic signaling.
These pumps are distinct from the postganglionic neuron blockers.
NET is a key mechanism for terminating the synaptic signal.
microReview: Transporters in the sympathetic nerve terminal regulate catecholamine availability. VMAT handles internal storage within vesicles, while NET handles reuptake from the synaptic cleft.
examinerTraps: Students frequently switch VMAT and NET. Remember: 'V' for Vesicle storage and 'N' for Norepinephrine reuptake.
sourceQuote: Catecholamine vesicle pump Storage vesicle transporter that pumps catecholamine from neural cytoplasm into the storage vesicle; also called vesicle monoamine transporter (VMAT)

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a headache, blurred vision, and a blood pressure of 210/130 mm Hg.
